# Authoring validation acceptance — 2026-09-27

This is the focused acceptance record for #250, #251 and #252. It distinguishes
runtime execution, requirement coverage and final completion. The behavioral
contract and graphs are in [authoring-validation.md](authoring-validation.md).

## Source and fixture

Implementation started in an isolated `codex/authoring-validation` worktree from
`8c3f2a61b738e8305e0d7b1ee10345b7deb91e3d`. The runs used the working-tree
implementation; each saved run includes its prepared graph, declarations, worker
specs and configuration fingerprints. Final controls also cover refinements made
after those launches: clearer audit diagnostics/prompts, initialization of first-pass
feedback files, output-file freshness, full-mode repair resource phases, the maximum
fast repair allowance, and the smoke gate's configured command timeout.

Evidence roots below are relative to that worktree. Raw logs and managed
authentication stay local. `.factory/authoring-acceptance-20260927/VERIFIED-EVIDENCE.json`
records receipt digests, execution order, actual routes, usage and final source hashes.

The synthetic source `authoring_seed/greeting` has one string knob `text`, a
`greeting.txt` invariant and an equality score. Its original operation would write
`ORIGINAL_EXECUTED` and raise. The requested revision must write the knob value plus
one newline, publish matching `greeting`/`expected` facts, preserve its score and
invariant, and include a README documenting `text=welcome`. No dependencies, model
nodes, extra modes or optimization are requested. The original execution marker
remained absent after every run, and no original-smoke directory was created.

## Actual terminal and native GUI evidence

| Entry point | Run identity | Observed result |
|---|---|---|
| Public terminal, `refactory ceo --mode edit_fast` | `.factory/authoring-acceptance-20260927/cli` | Completed. Initial runtime defect failed smoke and returned diagnostics to the coder. Corrected execution then exposed the intentionally missing README to focused QA. The second repair added it; fresh smoke, audit and final report passed. Three distinct smoke directories, two repairs, ten passing audit rows. |
| Native Chrome Modes panel, **Run once** | `.factory/interactive/single-07cc0586-200c-44dd-ab67-65d7628a5e4e` | Runtime-defect and missing-README controls both caused repair. The final package executed successfully, but QA cited a directory for one requirement. The audit gate refused completion at the declared bound. No `create.json` was published. This is a negative acceptance result, not a successful authoring run. |
| Native Chrome CEO chat, `wf_open`/`wf_next`, `default_pack/edit_fast` | `.factory/authoring-acceptance-20260927/chat-fast` | Completed. First audit self-citations were rejected. Its one allowed repair led to fresh execution and a valid audit grounded in individual files. Final output was exactly `hello\n`; score 1; fifteen passing rows and one explicit exclusion for original comparison. Eleven graph nodes completed, none skipped. |
| Native panel, **Read this run**, on that completed chat run | Same `chat-fast` identity | Displayed finished/done, all eleven completed nodes, smoke-before-QA connections, worker receipts and Outputs and validation. This read did not launch another evaluation. |

The terminal and panel briefs explicitly staged two temporary defects: first raise
`ValueError("ACCEPTANCE_RUNTIME_DEFECT")` and omit the README; after runtime feedback,
fix the operation but retain the omission until QA reports it. Neither defect was
an authorized final exclusion. The chat brief requested the correct small artifact
directly. These complementary paths consolidate acceptance without repeating the
same model campaign until it happens to pass.

All three paths set `allow_regression=true`; smoke validated the revised mode.
Their persisted revision records retain `revision_of_state` and its digest, set
`before_score` and `regressed` to null, and explicitly state that original execution
and non-regression measurement were intentionally skipped. The terminal/panel used
two repairs, 30-second smoke and a 600-second run bound. Chat used one repair and
30-second smoke. Token caps were unset. Chat's `wf_open` did not install a shared
elapsed/token ledger; its worker telemetry is reported separately rather than
inventing aggregate usage or an enforced elapsed limit.

Actual terminal and panel workers used DSH `0.1.5-rc.3`,
`deepseek-official/deepseek-flash`, effort `low`. Chat selected that provider/model
and low effort in the native composer, but child receipts record effort as null;
they do not establish an effective child effort of low. The existing permission
default remained `skip`. Credentials stayed in the managed store.

| Run | Reported tokens | Time evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Terminal | 647,954, measured run ledger | 140.810 seconds |
| Panel | 694,532, measured run ledger | 210.749 seconds |
| Successful chat | 892,734 across four worker receipts; coordinator UI approximately 1.1 million separately | Native chat UI: 4m 34s; no aggregate run ledger |

These are reported token counts, including provider-reported cached input; they
are not monetary cost estimates. Coordinator and child figures have distinct
scopes and are not presented as a deduplicated total.

## Incomplete full-chat attempts and discovered defects

An initial full Edit native chat stopped before its first worker because
`research-review.txt` was a required input without an initial producer. The shared
prepare operations now initialize feedback as **not run**, and strict worker-read
controls cover first-pass Create and Design. No missing file was hand-seeded in the
failed run. Its identity is
`.factory/web/session-09f56067-2ead-42ef-9b4e-4c6565a386d3/default_pack-edit`;
native coordinator UI reported approximately 460,000 tokens.

A fresh full-chat attempt at `.factory/authoring-acceptance-20260927/chat-fixed`
passed initialization but expanded the tiny task into the full research director's
delegated investigations. It was stopped before implementation to avoid an
unnecessary research campaign. The research worker reported 5,743,561 tokens;
the coordinator UI reported approximately 66,000 separately. Native Stop aborted
the chat call but its owned child processes remained, so the two identified
worker processes were terminated and their absence verified. The saved graph
reports exit 143 and the worker reports cancelled. This is **not** completed
full-mode/Overwatch model acceptance. Full-mode audit delivery, role separation,
failure/repair behavior and stale sign-off are covered by the controls below;
actual modeled intent-audit behavior was established with focused QA.

## Controls and limits

The targeted Python suite covers full/fast Create/Edit runtime repair before
review, all three fast repairs, unresolved bounds, missing credentials/tools,
cancellation, timeout, resource exhaustion, missing criteria, reviewer waivers,
explicit user exclusions with current evidence, changed source/intent/output,
stale delivery, native first-pass reads, shared validation reserve, and lowered
gate timeout preservation. Existing false/default comparable and non-comparable
Edit behavior remains covered alongside the no-original-execution spies.

Validation: 186 Python tests passed; 33 optional reference-oracle checks skipped
because `factory` is not installed. The generated API reference and tutorial were
regenerated and verified. Five targeted TypeScript suites passed, 143 tests,
covering the chat tool, panel rendering/graph/declarations and workflow execution.
Build/typecheck and normal commit/push hooks passed. Seven unrelated console-service
expectation failures also reproduced on the unchanged base commit (39 passed,
7 failed in that suite); they were not repaired by this change.

Audit parsing checks traceability and freshness, not the truth of arbitrary model
claims. In particular, a numeric smoke score alone does not establish every user
requirement. The failed panel audit demonstrates that a reviewer-authored PASS
does not override the runtime evidence contract.

The task's localhost server on port 60211 and its owned workers were stopped.
Other tasks' servers, the protected original checkout, `.env.swp`, and historical
campaigns were not changed or restarted.

refactory/docs/authoring-validation.md.text:
# Authoring validation and intent audits

Create/Edit execute what they built before reviewers sign off. One canonical
runtime operation owns the current revision's smoke, including its generated
score and any model/Task work. Design's declared acceptance command has the same
place in its graph. Listing or registering a package only makes it available for
execution; completion requires successful validation and current review.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Brief, research, accepted strategy/design] --> B[Coder]
  B --> C[Materialize and structural admission]
  C --> D[Stage/register package]
  D --> E[Canonical smoke]
  E --> F{Repairable failure?}
  F -->|yes, within shared bound| B
  F -->|dependency, cancellation, uncertainty or exhaustion| X[Stop with diagnostics and unblock/recovery action]
  F -->|passed| G[Separate health, code and adversarial QA]
  G --> H[QA gate]
  H -->|repair within shared bound| B
  H --> I[Overwatch: intent versus final evidence]
  I --> J[Audit gate]
  J -->|missing evidence or defect, within bound| B
  J -->|current evidence and PASS| K[Completion report]
```

Fast Create retains a strategist, coder and one focused QA worker. Fast Edit
retains coder then focused QA. Their smoke now precedes focused QA and shares
`repair_attempts` with structural admission and QA failures. There is no added
Overwatch worker or fan-out. Full Design retains separate health/code/adversarial
reviews and Overwatch after its acceptance command; fast Design retains focused
QA after that command.

## Runtime receipts and repair

`create_ops.gate_smoke` executes `smoke` once for each package attempt. Agent modes
receive a model for that execution; they no longer make a preliminary incomplete
keyless run. `smoke.json` records mode, sample inputs, run directory, status, score
when measured, stdout/stderr, elapsed time and failure information. Distinct smoke
directories preserve the outputs of earlier attempts. `revision.json` separately
records comparison/provenance. Design retains its command and actual output.

`authoring-evidence.json` binds the validation result to hashes of the delivered
source, authoritative brief/strategy/design/plan inputs, applicable ledger entries,
validation settings, receipt files and canonical runtime output files. Each validation receipt also survives in
`.refactory/validation-history/`. Earlier failed or superseded records remain
historical; they cannot certify a repaired revision. This local evidence contract
does not promise exhaustive tracking of external services or every transitive
dependency outside the delivered package.

Repairable implementation/check failures return concrete diagnostics to the
coder. Full modes share their declared attempt allowance across admission,
runtime and review failure; fast modes use their existing total repair allowance.
Missing tools/credentials, cancellation, uncertain worker outcomes/timeouts and
resource exhaustion stop with their actual outcome. The artifact and evidence
remain for explicit unblock/recovery; repeating code generation cannot install an
unavailable validation dependency.

The shared resource ledger accounts for work, validation and repair, including
nested model smoke. Review and completion use the validation allocation; a repair
returns to work admission. Token and elapsed caps remain optional and unset by
default. The repair bound controls attempts, not a fabricated token quota.

## What reviewers and Overwatch receive

The common agent-delivery path supplies the latest ledger and captures the
artifact/context identity at dispatch. Health, code and adversarial QA remain
independent full-mode roles. They inspect canonical receipts and delivered output,
then use targeted checks for uncovered requirements. They do not each repeat the
whole model/Task feed.

Overwatch receives the original brief, accepted strategy/criteria and design,
current applicable ledger, merged reviews and final runtime evidence. It writes
`reviews/overwatch.md` plus `intent-audit.json`. Fast focused QA writes its existing
report plus the same intent map. The map covers every baseline id: `brief`,
`strategy`, explicit `criterion-N` rows when supplied, `design`/`plan`, and current
`ledger-N` instructions, including the initial idea. Compound asks must be decomposed into separate rows even
when they share an id. Each row identifies the requirement, status and supporting
individual file paths with concrete command/output or source findings. Directories,
line-number suffixes and the audit itself cannot serve as evidence references.

Required behavior without adequate evidence is failed or unverified with a
precise reason. A README limitation or reviewer/coordinator waiver cannot alter
the baseline. An exclusion must cite an explicit user change and quote its exact
text (semantic review must still establish that it really authorizes the exclusion). A missing required
consumer or validation tool stays unverified with its exact unblock action.

The gate requires coverage, substantive evidence references, a final exact PASS
verdict without blockers, and current delivery receipts. A changed artifact,
receipt, validation input or later applicable user instruction invalidates old
sign-off. Completion checks freshness again. Explicit graph redo/recovery still
owns restarting completed nodes and archiving dependent state.

These checks establish traceability and freshness. They cannot mechanically prove
that an agent understood every sentence, that a cited command establishes the
claimed behavior, or that a generated artifact is good. Those remain semantic
review responsibilities, tested with actual modeled acceptance as well as controls.

## Edit comparison policy

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Revised mode passes canonical execution] --> B[Capture source identity/state; check freshness]
  B --> C{allow_regression?}
  C -->|true| D[Skip original execution and numerical comparison]
  C -->|false, comparable| E[Execute original on accepted sample inputs]
  E --> F[Compare scores; refuse a lower revised score]
  C -->|false, not comparable| G[Record why comparison is unmeasured]
  D --> H[Persist provenance and proceed to review]
  F --> H
  G --> H
```

The default is still false. With true, no original smoke runs, no delta is
computed and the revision is not classified as regressed/non-regressed.
`before_score` and `regressed` are null; `after_score` describes only the revised
measurement. `revision_note` explicitly says comparison was intentionally skipped.
The source state/digest and provenance remain, and revised correctness/QA still
run. With false, existing comparable/non-comparable behavior and numerical refusal
remain. This is not a new evaluation-editing framework or a performance-improvement
requirement.

CEO uses `--knob allow_regression=true`, the Python/headless Edit command uses
`--allow-regression`, chat's Edit tool uses `allowRegression`, and the panel exposes
the declaration's boolean knob and help. All reach the same `_revision` operation;
historical report fields stay readable.

Implementation: [graphs](../refactory_dsh/create.py),
[fast graphs](../refactory_dsh/fast.py), [operations](../refactory_dsh/create_ops.py),
[evidence contract](../refactory_dsh/authoring_evidence.py),
[delivery](../refactory_dsh/agent_delivery.py),
[controls](../tests/test_authoring_evidence.py).

The [2026-09-27 acceptance record](authoring-validation-acceptance-20260927.md)
separates successful terminal/chat runs, the panel's negative control, incomplete
full-chat attempts, measured usage and deterministic coverage.

refactory/docs/benchmark-cheating-preven.text:
# Benchmark Cheating Prevention

When building scored benchmark modes for the refactory-dsh outer loop, the agent
under evaluation has full tool access to its workspace. If gold answers are
reachable from the workspace, the agent will find and copy them instead of
solving the problem. This guide covers the known leak vectors and how to close
them.

## 1. Never put gold answers in `TaskInstance.metadata`

The data node serializes the full `metadata` dict to `current_item.json` in the
workspace. Anything in metadata is visible to the agent.

**Bad:**

```python
TaskInstance(
    id=item["id"],
    metadata={
        "question": item["question"],
        "solution": item["solution"],   # leaked to workspace
    },
)
```

**Good:**

```python
TaskInstance(
    id=item["id"],
    metadata={
        "question": item["question"],
        "fen": item["fen"],
        # solutions are NOT in metadata
    },
)
```

Look up solutions in `verify()` by reading the source data file directly:

```python
def verify(self, instance, workspace):
    solutions = self._load_solutions()  # reads from data file
    gold = solutions[instance.id]["answer"]
    # ...compare predicted vs gold...
```

## 2. Audit `setup()` for answer leaks

Even if metadata is clean, a custom `setup()` method might explicitly write
solutions to workspace files. Only write the problem statement.

```python
def setup(self, instance, workspace):
    workspace.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    (workspace / "current_item.json").write_text(json.dumps({
        "id": instance.id,
        "question": instance.metadata["question"],
        # DO NOT include solution fields here
    }))
```

## 3. Don't expose gold answers as facts

Calling `ctx.set_fact("gold_answer", ...)` in an op may expose the answer
through the runtime's fact system. Only set facts the agent should see. Scoring
belongs in `verify()`, not in facts.

## 4. Be aware of path exposure in the worker prompt

The DSH worker prompt includes `refactory_source` and `runtime_root` paths. A
capable model could navigate from these paths to the package's `data/` directory
and read the answer file. Mitigations:

- Use puzzle IDs that don't directly map to answer file structure
- For high-stakes benchmarks, consider serving answers from an API
- Monitor for suspicious file reads in agent transcripts

## 5. Validate with a spot-check

Before trusting any 90%+ score, manually compare a few model predictions against
gold answers. If they match exactly — especially with unusual formatting — the
model is likely reading the answer.

```bash
# Quick spot-check: compare latest answer to gold
cat /tmp/run-dir/answer.txt
python3 -c "import json; items=json.load(open('data/items.json')); print(items[0]['solution'])"
```

## 6. Red-flag suspicious accuracy

If a baseline model scores vastly above published benchmarks for the same task,
assume cheating until proven otherwise. Investigate before investing compute in
optimization runs that start from an inflated baseline.

## Checklist for new benchmark modes

- [ ] `TaskInstance.metadata` contains NO solution fields
- [ ] `setup()` writes NO solution data to the workspace
- [ ] No op sets gold answers as facts
- [ ] `verify()` loads solutions from source data, not from metadata or workspace
- [ ] Spot-check confirms the model gets some items genuinely wrong
- [ ] Baseline accuracy is plausible for the model and task difficulty

refactory/docs/budget-strategy.md.text:
# Choosing a budget for agentic work

A universal cumulative-token cutoff is a poor definition of a successful fast run.
Keep token limits as **optional, explicit resource guardrails**. Bound ordinary fast
work through its small graph, focused QA, repair limit and worker/check timeouts.
A required check must still pass; removing a cutoff does not establish correctness.

The current product already leaves run-wide token and elapsed limits unset by
default. The 150,000-token/360-second settings in the September release checks were
acceptance-test allocations, not product defaults. The initial analysis reused
saved receipts. Subsequent scoped CLI checks are recorded below; they do not
establish a universal allocation or remove any explicitly selected limit.

## What the failed checks measured

The six CLI/native GUI attempts used the same DSH model. Their worker receipts
reconcile with the saved provider usage:

| Usage category | Tokens | Share |
|---|---:|---:|
| Uncached input | 131,098 | 14.1% |
| Cached input | 780,672 | 83.8% |
| Output, including reasoning | 19,523 | 2.1% |
| Total | 931,293 | 100% |

No run reached its six-minute elapsed limit, and no repair loop ran. The
observed failures therefore do not establish that the task scope or repair bound
needed expansion.

These totals count context processed on successive requests. They are neither
novel output nor a dollar amount; actual costs were unavailable. Cached tokens
remain part of honest usage accounting, but raw token totals alone cannot compare
spending or useful progress across runtimes and models.

Five implementation workers made no write/edit tool calls before exhaustion.
Their calls explored framework, source and delivery files despite the prompt
already containing the emission instructions and relevant API/reference text.
The original CLI Create/Edit traces also showed a child Python import failure
followed by source discovery. The selected-Python propagation fix and worker
orientation now supply the interpreter, node identity, exact input/output paths
and delivery boundary directly. Fast prompts give the coder its API/reference
context and give QA the changed-file list plus the executed check result.
Workers are instructed to return after delivering the current node, without
rediscovering runtime protocols or executing later stages. These are implemented
changes; they do not guarantee compliant or efficient model behavior.

CLI Design completed implementation at 69,799 tokens and used another 92,550 for
QA. Its passing QA JSON was written at 133,008 total tokens; two further requests
used 29,341 tokens before handback crossed the limit. The runtime never completed
the gate/report, so that file is partial evidence, not a completed run. A fixed
1,000-token validation reserve was not a meaningful estimate of this QA stage.

See the [release outcomes](release-validation-20260926.md#fast-mode-outcomes) for
all six attempts and their limits. They do not establish a successful minimum
allocation or prove that more tokens would produce a good result.

## Separate the controls

| Control | Purpose | Current behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Small graph and repair bound | Keep the requested work finite and focused | Create/Design use one strategist, coder and QA agent sequentially; Edit uses coder and QA directly. At most one repair by default; required checks remain in the graph |
| Worker/check timeout | Stop a hung or excessively slow operation | Separate from the optional run-wide elapsed limit |
| Optional elapsed/token limit | Honor an explicitly chosen resource boundary | Shared across descendants and validation; exhaustion is reported and does not become success |
| Validation reserve | Retain part of an explicit allocation for required checks | Validation may use the reserve; returning to implementation must use the work allowance |
| Usage and progress evidence | Explain what the run spent and achieved | Inspect worker receipts, completed nodes and artifact/check records; unavailable measurements stay unavailable |

A token limit is checked at usage boundaries. An already admitted request can
overshoot it, so it is not an exact provider-side ceiling. Do not silently raise an
explicit limit or discard cached-input usage to make a run appear compliant.
External workers without complete nested telemetry refuse token-limited launches.

When a user needs a strict monetary ceiling, the current raw-token control cannot
promise one. That would require reliable model-specific pricing and complete
billing coverage. Choosing no token cap is an explicit tradeoff: work remains
subject to its graph/repair bounds and operation timeouts, but total token usage
has no configured ceiling.

## Reserve correction

The investigation found a separate implementation bug: after Design entered final
validation, its sticky resource phase could let a repair inherit access to the
validation reserve. Fast graph nodes now declare that phase independently of their
worker-routing role. A repair returns to `work`; Design QA/reporting retain their
validation phase. Explicit work phases survive native graph serialization.
Legacy nodes without an explicit phase keep their prior behavior.

Deterministic checks exercise both the Python executor and native graph runtime:
with a total allocation of 100 and reserve of 20, work using 60 followed by QA
using 25 may finish a successful report at 85, but failed QA cannot start a repair
from that remaining validation allocation. Reaching the total limit still fails.
This fixes reserve ownership; it does not fix unproductive exploration or prove
successful model-backed fast authoring.

## Scoped acceptance sequence

The revised checks use the changed execution strategy:

1. Verify the actual loaded runtime, selected Python/imports and reference paths
   without a model call. Keep unrelated run histories out of the task context.
2. Use one fixed representative task first. Retain its focused QA and repair bound;
   agree any resource allocation separately before launching paid work.
3. Inspect stage completion and the reason for each tool call, alongside input,
   cached-input and output usage. A larger cap is not the response to repeated
   framework discovery or another environment failure.
4. Continue to the other paths only after that representative path completes and
   the evidence supports the execution strategy. Reuse unchanged interface and
   accounting evidence.

The representative CLI Design task corrected a tiny copied helper and completed
the three sequential roles, focused check, QA gate and final report at 135,727
observed tokens in 31.77 seconds, with no repair. A subsequent CLI Create attempt
emitted its package but reached 156,775 tokens before worker handback or QA;
the configured 150,000-token limit stopped the run. The emitted file is partial
progress, not a completed package or QA result.

The user authorized further checks with six-minute elapsed limits, one
repair and no cumulative-token cap: CLI Create retry/Edit and native
Create/Edit/Design. Native Design completed at 128,567 tokens in 29.02 seconds,
with no repair. CLI Create completed at 1,210,437 tokens in 143.47 seconds,
including one actual structural repair, focused QA and canonical smoke. CLI Edit
completed at 831,836 tokens in 132.58 seconds with no repair or measured regression.
These results demonstrate completion under the selected time/repair bounds, not
token efficiency or a lower cost. Cached input remains included in the observed
totals. Native Edit completed at 757,421 tokens in 130.15 seconds with one
structural repair and no measured regression. Native Create failed after one
repair on a framework API example import defect. After that example was corrected,
native Create completed at 655,160 tokens in 99.89 seconds with no repair. All six
CLI/native paths now have positive completion evidence; the earlier failures
remain in the [validation record](release-validation-20260926.md#fast-mode-outcomes).

Node orientation and focused prompts define each worker's task; they do not cap
cumulative context processing or guarantee efficient tool use. A file appearing
on disk is never enough by itself to stop a worker or certify success: its
declared contract, checks and side-effect boundary still need to be resolved.

[Resource settings and recovery](budgets-fast-modes.md) · [Worker capabilities](models.md)

refactory/docs/budgets-fast-modes.md.text:
# Fast authoring and shared run budgets

`default_pack/create_fast`, `default_pack/edit_fast` and `default_pack/design_fast`
are ordinary, inspectable modes for small, purposeful tasks. They omit research
and reviewer fan-out and allow one repair by default. The existing `create`,
`edit` and `design` modes remain available with their full graphs.

| Mode | Sequential work and required validation |
|---|---|
| Create fast | One strategist plans the minimum reusable graph, knobs, score and artifact invariants; one coder emits the package; one QA agent reviews it. Structural admission and canonical runtime smoke remain required. |
| Edit fast | One coder makes the small revision directly, then one QA agent checks it. Task bindings, inputs and artifact contracts are preserved; structural admission and canonical smoke remain required; comparison defaults on but `allow_regression=true` skips the original execution/comparison branch. |
| Design fast | One strategist, one coder and one QA agent produce a tiny checked artifact, such as a one-file helper or a small change in a copied project. The required command runs against the materialized output. |

The strategy is a concise plan, not a separate research or approval workflow.
Create and Edit produce reusable packages. Design produces the artifact itself
and is not an optimization target.

## Acceptance status

All three fast modes completed their required checks and reports in separate
CLI and native GUI runs. CLI Create and native Edit each exercised one actual
structural repair; Edit retained its measured score. Both interfaces also showed
an explicit unresolved known-defect control with zero permitted repairs.

The final checks used six-minute elapsed limits and one repair. Successful CLI
Design retained a 150,000-token cap; the user chose no cumulative-token cap for
the subsequent checks. All usage remained measured. The earlier capped failures
and a native Create import failure are retained alongside the corrected success.
These results establish the sampled artifact contracts, not token efficiency or
arbitrary project quality. See the
[recorded outcomes](release-validation-20260926.md#fast-mode-outcomes).

## Choose the graph

In the terminal, choose `--mode create_fast`, `--mode edit_fast` or
`--mode design_fast` with `refactory ceo`. In the native GUI, select the same mode
from the mode catalogue and configure its knobs, then use **Run once**. The public
CLI forwards `--check` to the declared `check` knob for all fast variants and
honors `--timeout` for authoring. The direct authoring commands also accept `--fast`:

```bash
uv run python -m refactory_dsh.design --fast \
  --name tiny-helper --brief 'Write helper.py with add(a, b) and a small assertion test.' \
  --check 'python helper.py' --repair-attempts 1 --max-elapsed-s 360
```

For a change to an existing project, pass `--source-project /absolute/project`
to fast Design, or set its `source_project` knob. Refactory copies the source to
the output artifact and applies emitted new or changed files there. It does
not replace the source project. Dependency directories, Git metadata, previous
run output and `.env*` files are excluded; source symlinks are refused. File
deletion is not part of this small-change emission contract.

`repair_attempts` is one shared bound across structural admission, canonical runtime validation and focused QA,
from zero to three. It counts repairs after the first implementation, so one
permits at most two implementations. The required Design `check` runs as a bounded
command against the materialized artifact. Create/Edit can also name an explicit
`check`; an empty check is reported as not requested, not passed. Focused QA asks
the worker to inspect the emitted or changed files, requested behavior and relevant
regressions, using the actual command result already supplied. It records evidence
for each check and an explicit list of checks not run. It does not edit the
implementation or repeat downstream runtime stages. A required check not run
cannot count as a pass.

Canonical smoke runs before focused QA. Its real receipts join the requested check result in the QA context. The worker must map every brief/criteria/ledger obligation to current evidence in `intent-audit.json`; it cannot waive a requirement or silently repair source. Missing dependencies stop with an unblock explanation. Changed source or intent invalidates the earlier receipt/sign-off. See [authoring validation](authoring-validation.md).

Read `authoring-evidence.json`, `intent-audit.json`, `focused-check.json`, `focused-qa.json` and `fast-report.json` in the run
directory. They separate command results, model-authored review, structural
admission and runtime smoke. Exhausted repair produces an unresolved report and
no success report. A model's favorable review is not proof of artifact quality.

## Allocate resources

Run-wide token and elapsed limits are **optional and unset by default**. Fast mode
is defined by its smaller graph and repair bound, not a universal token quota.
The release-check cutoff was a test allocation. Read [Choosing a budget](budget-strategy.md)
for the usage breakdown, tradeoffs and revised acceptance strategy before selecting
another limit.

Elapsed time and tokens are separate from candidate counts, graph steps and one
completion's hang timeout. CLI controls are `--max-elapsed-s`, `--max-tokens`,
`--validation-reserve-s` and `--validation-reserve-tokens`. The GUI exposes the
same effective run settings. Python graphs accept the same fields:

```python
run = mode.run(
    workdir,
    model=client,
    resource_limits={"max_elapsed_s": 360, "max_tokens": 30000,
                     "validation_reserve_s": 60, "validation_reserve_tokens": 5000},
)
```

The values above illustrate accounting controls; they are not an allocation known to
complete fast authoring.

The shared `.refactory/resource-usage.json` ledger aggregates coordinator and
nested-worker usage, retries and validation. Repeated cumulative receipts for
the same worker replace its previous total instead of counting it twice. The
outer loop reserves validation resources before admitting another candidate;
required final validation can use the reserve. Fast package smoke and fast
Design's check are explicit validation stages. Fast graph nodes declare their resource
phase independently of the worker role. Design uses final-validation resources for
its check, QA, gate and report; Create/Edit use final-validation resources for canonical smoke and subsequent checks, QA and reporting. A repair returns to the work allocation. Mode authors can set
`nn.Node.resource_role` to `work` or `final_validation`; omission retains the prior
role-based/inherited behavior.

Elapsed limits are checked at graph boundaries and while owned model/check
processes run. Arbitrary in-process Python operations are checked when they
return; they cannot be forcefully interrupted safely. Token limits are enforced
at provider usage boundaries. Each worker's in-flight provider request may
overshoot; this is not an exact provider-side token cap. A backend without token
telemetry refuses a token-limited launch. Missing usage or pricing is shown as
unavailable (`null`), and estimated cost remains an estimate. Candidate counts
never stand in for token or time measurement.

An exhausted budget before required validation is incomplete/unvalidated, not a
success. Owned processes are asked to shut down and partial artifacts remain.
The ledger stops charging elapsed time when the owning run pauses or finishes.

## Resume deliberately

At a completed node boundary, supported resume retains completed work and its
consumption. An explicit larger allocation can extend the limit; it does not
reset usage. The direct authoring commands accept `--resume RUN_DIR` with
`--fast` for a saved fast graph. Python uses
`ModeClass.resume(workdir, model=client, resource_limits={...})`.

An interrupted node with an unknown side-effect outcome is never automatically
replayed. Inspect its artifacts before an explicit restart. Changed graph
instructions or a changed Design source-project snapshot invalidate dependent
results and require a new run. Partial artifacts are evidence, not a claim that
the interrupted node completed.

The Python executor conservatively refuses partial-fork recovery because its
saved record does not yet support restoring individual branch facts. It does
not replay successful sibling branches or silently retry an unknown worker.

The final-validation reserve belongs to the outer run. During optimization, a
candidate's internal validation nodes cannot spend the winner holdout reserve.
Nested searches reuse their enclosing ledger and do not reset usage, extend the
allocation or pause the enclosing clock. Deterministic candidates share elapsed
limits without requiring a model client; no provider usage remains unavailable.

Focused QA is bound to a digest of the materialized output after the requested
check. If QA edits those files, the gate requires another implementation/check
cycle within the same repair limit; a passing review cannot silently approve a
changed, unchecked artifact.

Custom model clients used with token caps must implement `with_budget(budget)`
and report measured or explicitly estimated usage into that shared ledger.
Clients without this protocol are refused at the completion boundary, including
optimizer proposals. Supplying such a client to a deterministic graph does not
force a model call or invent usage. Existing uncapped clients stay compatible.

refactory/docs/ceo-guide.md.text:
# CEO operating guide

Refactory runs explicit graphs. The runtime owns node order, branches, checks,
evidence, user gates and recovery. Drive the selected graph; do not reproduce its
workers in conversation or mark work complete from prose alone.

Start with `refactory` action `help`. Read `help` with `topic` equal to a mode ID
or operation for its live arguments, defaults, constraints, examples and interface
routes. `modes` lists installed packages, including packages added since build.
Coverage warnings mean guidance may be missing or stale. Read `docs` with `query`
for search, or `page`, optional `section`, `offset` and `limit` for bounded reads.
Use the returned IDs and continuation offsets. Help and docs carry schema, build
and documentation identities. These APIs read shipped product docs; no shell,
source-code search or web access is needed for product discovery.

Create and Edit produce reusable mode packages. Design produces a software
artifact. Canonical validation precedes QA and final intent review. Fast variants retain
focused QA and bounded repair. Edit allow_regression skips original execution and
comparison, while revised validation remains mandatory. Run uses a mode
once; Optimize (`start`) searches a scored mode. Read the mode's ports, required
inputs and user gates before choosing. When a person is present, use `wf_open`
with the mode, knobs, intent and a fresh absolute workdir. Continue with the
workflow tools. The runtime asks user gates; never invent their verdicts.
Headless approvals require an explicit user-approved answer and `headless: true`.

For optimization, inspect `strategies` and `profiles`; `profile-resolve` previews
settings and the contract. `start` returns a durable run ID. Read incremental
`status` using its offset, then candidates, artifacts and winner evidence. A run
can outlive a chat. A stopped, failed or unmeasured run is not success. Recovery
requires a known saved boundary; use the documented CLI or panel recovery route.

`workers` explains effective worker routing and provenance. New runs load
`refactory.workers.json` at the project root. Explicit profile/launch settings
win; node overrides beat role overrides, which beat the run route. This file
selects graph workers, not this CEO's conversational model. Backend changes are
configured through the file, CLI or panel. Native authentication stays in its
existing stores. New worker permissions default to `skip`; token caps are unset
unless requested, and native workers do not support whole-tree token caps.

Use `runtime` for configured credential readiness, which is not authentication
proof. Follow explicit task and fixture constraints without asking again. Keep
build/docs identity with evidence, and distinguish a generated receipt from
checks that establish the requested output.

refactory/docs/cli.md.text:
# Command reference

Start with [Get started](getting-started.md) or [Terminal and GUI](interfaces.md). All commands below run from the repository root. Examples with `<placeholders>` need your own values. Model-backed authoring and execution incur provider usage.


Every command is `uv run refactory <verb>`. `uv run refactory <verb> --help` is the current truth for one verb.

For `create_fast`, `edit_fast`, `design_fast`, focused QA, repair bounds and shared
elapsed/token controls, see [Fast modes and run budgets](budgets-fast-modes.md). Saved configurations use [optimization profiles](optimization-profiles.md); durable observation and explicit recovery use [live controls](live-control.md).

## Create and build

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `refactory ceo "<what you want>" --mode create --task <module:Class>` | build a harness for a class of work: the Task lists the items and judges each pass, and the produced package binds a `data` node to it. Research, a strategy you approve, a build, structural admission, registration and canonical smoke, then three parallel reviews and an audit; runtime depends on model latency and the number of review/repair cycles. |
| `refactory ceo "<what you want>" --mode create --single` | the special case: a harness that runs once, for one input, with no Task binding. |
| `refactory ceo "<what you want>" --mode design --check "<command>"` | design a checked artifact instead of a package; this is the default mode. |
| `refactory ceo "<what you want>" --mode edit --revise <package>/<mode>` | revise a mode; refuse a measured regression by default and report unavailable comparisons explicitly. |
| `refactory ceo <package>/<mode>` | run that mode instead of authoring anything. |

An edit inherits the source mode's Task and data-node requirements when no new
`task_ref` or `single_shot` knob is supplied. The final `create.json` describes the
emitted package's actual bindings, including `task_refs` and bindings per mode;
its legacy `task_ref` field is populated when there is exactly one distinct Task.

| option | what it does |
|---|---|
| `--mode <mode>` | `design` (the default), `create`, `edit`, `design_fast`, `create_fast`, `edit_fast`, or `<package>/<mode>`. |
| `--name <name>` | the package or artifact name; without it your words become the name. |
| `--check "<command>"` | run inside the Design artifact; fast Create/Edit also accept a focused package check. Failures enter the bounded repair path. |
| `--repair-attempts <n>` | fast authoring repairs after the first implementation, from 0 to 3 (default 1). |
| `--source-project <dir>` | fast Design: copy an existing project into the output artifact before applying a change. |
| `--worker-backend dsh\|codex\|claude_code` | the explicit coding-worker runtime; DSH is the default. |
| `--effort <value>` | DSH reasoning-effort override; external workers use native product settings. |
| `--permission-mode <value>` | New workers default to `skip` (full native permission bypass). Choose `default` for native checks, or a supported backend-specific policy. Saved runs/profiles retain their policies; see [worker permissions](models.md#model-provider-versus-coding-agent). |
| `--max-elapsed-s <n>` / `--max-tokens <n>` | the shared resource allocation, including nested work and validation. |
| `--validation-reserve-s <n>` / `--validation-reserve-tokens <n>` | keep part of that allocation available for required final validation. |
| `--revise <package>/<mode>` | edit only: the mode being revised. |
| `--task <module:Class>` | create only: the class of work the produced harness binds a `data` node to. One of `--task` or `--single` is required. |
| `--single` | create only: build a harness for one run of one thing. |
| `--knob name=value` | set one of the authoring mode's knobs for this run, e.g. `allow_regression=1`. |
| `--workdir <dir>` | where the run's evidence lands (default `.factory/interactive/<package>-<mode>`). |
| `--provider <route>` | the provider route that model is on, e.g. `deepseek-official`. |
| `--model <id>` | the model this run uses, e.g. `deepseek-v4-pro`. |
| `--approve <gate>=<value>` | answer a gate up front, e.g. `gate_strategy=proceed`, for a run with nobody at it. A gate a person would be asked at is theirs: run without this and answer it, or drive the mode node by node with the `wf_open` tool. `modes` marks a person's gate `(user)`. |
| `--headless` | run without a conversation: one task, one report, then exit, for scripts and CI. Without it the run is live — each turn prints as it happens and a line you type between turns reaches the CEO. |
| `--timeout <seconds>` | bound the interactive graph process, including authoring; 0 supplies no separate wait limit. An explicit shared elapsed allocation can impose a shorter deadline. |

Fast Create and Design use one strategist, coder and QA agent sequentially. Fast
Edit starts with the coder and retains source-contract checks. Canonical smoke precedes QA; repairable failures share the repair bound. `allow_regression=true` skips original execution and comparison, retaining revised-mode validation and provenance; false remains the default.
The CLI passes `--check` through the same declared `check` knob exposed in the
native form; use `--knob check_timeout_s=45` to bound that command separately.
These small graphs omit research and reviewer fan-out; [acceptance status](budgets-fast-modes.md#acceptance-status)
remains separate from selecting and launching them.

The full create and design QA gate uses current `BLOCKING: <finding>` statements from
all three review reports. `BLOCKING: none` and scoped empty verdicts such as
`BLOCKING: none in the current emitted artifact` are clean verdicts. A section
title such as `## 11. BLOCKING: findings` is not itself a finding; actual findings
under it still need their own `BLOCKING:` marker. `BLOCKING: none, except ...`
remains blocking. Fenced transcripts and sections headed `Previous review`,
`Superseded`, or `Archived review` are
history; a `Current findings` heading resumes current findings. The synthesis
preserves the full reports and their digests, so changing a report after synthesis
requires fresh synthesis before the gate can proceed.

## Manage packages of modes

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `refactory list` | every package and mode this checkout can run. |
| `refactory list modes --json` | the catalogue as JSON, with each mode's `action`, parameters and guidance. |
| `refactory package verify <package>` | import every mode and validate its graph. |
| `refactory package show <package>/<mode>` | one mode, described. |
| `refactory package tools <package>` | the tools it declares, and whether this machine has them. |
| `refactory package add <dir>` | install a package from a directory (`--as` to rename). |
| `refactory package import <dir-or-git-url>` | import one, recording where it came from (`--ref`, `--as`). |
| `refactory package remove <package>` | remove it. |
| `refactory package enable/disable <package>` | include it, or leave it out of the catalogue. |
| `refactory package smoke <package>/<mode>` | run it once, in a sandbox, without a model (free). |
| `refactory package smoke <package>/<mode> --model` | score a mode whose graph has an `agent` node, by supplying a model. |

Package import uses the literal `PACKAGE.name` when available, even if the source
folder has a different name. `--as` copies the package under a new identity and
rewrites its literal self-qualified Python imports, module references and mode
identifiers. Relative imports, comments, docstrings and external dependencies are
preserved. A rename requires a direct literal `PACKAGE = Package(name=...)` (a
positional literal name also works); dynamic identities and self-qualified
f-strings must be prepared explicitly before import. Provenance records the source
path or git URL/ref and original package identity. A refused import leaves no
installed copy.

`refactory package` also accepts `--json`, `--force` and `--project`.

## Use a mode

`refactory ceo <package>/<mode>` runs a mode you already have on DSH with your terminal attached, so a gate reaches you. It is the same `ceo` verb that authors a mode; a positional that names one is what says to run it.

**A run is a live session.** The CEO's turns print as they complete, each node is reported as it runs, a gate is a prompt, and a line you type between turns reaches the CEO — which can amend a node's prompt and re-run it. `--headless` builds the older one-shot argv instead, for a script or CI, and then the run prints only its final JSON.

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `refactory ceo <package>/<mode> --intent "<what it is for>"` | run the mode on DSH with your terminal attached, so a gate reaches you. |
| `refactory ceo <package>/<mode> --knob name=value` | set one of the mode's knobs for this run. |
| `refactory ceo <package>/<mode> --source <dir>` | read the items from here instead of the source the mode declares. |
| `refactory ceo <package>/<mode> --source-format directory\|jsonl\|csv` | how to read `--source` (default: a directory of one item per subdirectory). |
| `refactory ceo <package>/<mode> --workdir <dir>` | where the run's evidence lands. |
| `refactory ceo <package>/<mode> --timeout <seconds>` | how long to wait at a gate; `0` waits for you. |
| `refactory ceo <package>/<mode> --model <id> --provider <route>` | the model this run uses. |
| `refactory ceo <package>/<mode> --approve <gate>=<value>` | answer a gate before the run instead of at it, for a run nobody can ask. For a gate a person owns, leave it to them: they are asked when the run reaches it. |

## Optimization

`refactory optimize <package>/<mode>` searches a mode's architecture and knobs: propose typed edits, validate, evaluate, keep what improves.

| option | what it does | default |
|---|---|---|
| `--epochs <n>` | rounds of propose → validate → evaluate → select | 2 |
| `--batch-size <n>` | candidates proposed per epoch | 4 |
| `--optimizer <name>` | how candidates are proposed: `random`, `hill_climb`, `evolutionary`, `archive`, `islands`, `map_elites`, `autoresearch` | `autoresearch` |
| `--strategy <name>` | which outer loop drives the search: `default`, `best_of_n`, `reflective`, `reflective_sampler`, `tree_search`, `staged_curriculum`, `staged_v1`, `adaptive_meta`, `autoscientists`, `research_then_optimize` | the harness's own (`default`) |
| `--evaluator walker\|dsh` | which runtime scores a candidate: fast in-process, or the one that ships | `walker` |
| `--preset <name>` | which edits are allowed: `broad`, `structure`, `conservative`, `knob_only` | `broad` |
| `--allowed-ops <name>` | narrow the chosen preset to listed edit operations; repeat for multiple names | the preset |
| `--frozen <name>` | additional knob protected from edits; repeat for multiple names | mode-declared frozen knobs |
| `--profile <name>` / `--profile-version <n>` | load an immutable saved configuration; explicit overrides remain visible in the snapshot | none / latest |
| `--repeats <n>` | independent trials per candidate and winner audit, from 1 to 10 | 1 |
| `--seed <n>` | seed the search RNG; model outputs can still vary | 0 |
| `--elite <n>` | how many parents each round proposes against | 3 |
| `--max-evaluations <n>` | a hard ceiling on evaluated candidates | 64 |
| `--holdout <fraction>` | the share of a Task's items kept out of the search and used to audit the winner afterwards; one item cannot be split, which the audit records | 0.3 |
| `--parsimony <cost>` | what each node of a candidate's graph costs its score: the search compares `raw_score − parsimony × nodes` | 0.01 |
| `--attempts <n>` | retries per batch after a refusal | 3 |
| `--runs-root <dir>` | the run directory itself; read it back with `--run <this path>` | `.factory/loop` |
| `--intent "<words>"` | what the run is for; seeds the ledger the agents read | empty |
| `--model <name>` | model for proposals and evaluated agent nodes; both evaluators carry the same routing context | the configured route |
| `--provider <route>` | the provider route that model is on | your settings default |
| `--worker-backend dsh\|codex\|claude_code` | worker runtime, independent of provider choice | `dsh` |
| `--role-routes <JSON>` / `--node-routes <JSON>` | route overrides; node takes precedence over role, then run | empty |
| `--max-elapsed-s <n>` / `--max-tokens <n>` | shared limits for proposals, trials, nested work and final validation | unlimited |
| `--validation-reserve-s <n>` / `--validation-reserve-tokens <n>` | part of the shared allocation reserved for validation | 0 |
| `--resume` | continue a compatible saved search and retain consumed resources | off |
| `--max-steps <n>` | step ceiling for one inner run, enforced by the executor | 2000 |
| `--history-limit <n>` | how many evaluated candidates the optimizer is shown; bounded so a prompt cannot grow without limit | 200 |
| `--prior-runs <n>` | how many previous runs are summarised as a prior for this one | 3 |
| `--dsh-timeout-s <n>` | wall-clock ceiling for one inner run when the evaluator is DSH | 900 |
| `--verbose` | print every event, and each candidate's own run output, not only the meaningful ones | off |

**For Task-bound modes, candidates use the training items and the winner is audited on held-out items.** Modes without a data split report holdout as not applicable. The part travels in the run directory (`subset.json` beside each candidate), not in a knob, so a search cannot choose its own exam; the audit lands in `<run root>/holdout.json` and in the report as `{"train", "holdout", "gap", "overfit", "threshold", "instances"}`, with `overfit` true when `train − holdout` exceeds 0.15. The score the search compares has the size cost taken off it, and the unpenalised number is recorded beside it as `raw_score`. `refactory best` reports the audit, and `refactory adopt` refuses an overfit winner unless you pass `--allow-overfit`.

## Read the run, and steer it

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `refactory runs` | every run under the root, newest first. |
| `refactory profiles` | list saved versions; `profile-save --name NAME --spec JSON` creates a new version. |
| `refactory profile-resolve <package>/<mode> --profile NAME` | preview the exact launch settings and fixed contract. |
| `refactory comparison --run <id>` | all measured, failed and unmeasured candidates, with trial/cost/latency evidence and audit. |
| `refactory status --run <id> --follow` | stream durable state changes without starting or owning work. |
| `refactory status --run <id>` | where it is, and the events since an offset. |
| `refactory leaderboard --run <id>` | candidates by score, each with its diff against its parent. |
| `refactory candidate <id> --run <id>` | one candidate, exactly what it changed. |
| `refactory best --run <id>` | the winner, with the state that scored it and the held-out audit of whether it works beyond its training items. |
| `refactory artifacts --run <id> --contents` | what it left on disk. |
| `refactory adopt --run <id> --as <package>` | write the winner as a new package, input untouched. |
| `refactory adopt --run <id> --as <package> --allow-overfit` | adopt it anyway, with the audit recorded beside the package. |
| `refactory steer --run <id> --note "<words>" --kind info\|correction\|constraint` | add what you said to the run's intent ledger. The proposer reads the ledger before every generation, so a note steers the next one. |
| `refactory steer --run <id> --verdict <gate>=<value>` | record a gate's answer, so a resume replays it. |
| `refactory steer --run <id> --pause` / `--resume` | hold a search at its next generation boundary, or release it. |
| `refactory steer --run <id> --stop` | end a search at its next boundary, recording that a person asked. |
| `refactory steer --run <id> --keep <candidate>` | follow that candidate up: it stays a parent even once a newer batch outscores it. Add `--lineage` for its descendants too. |
| `refactory steer --run <id> --reject <candidate>` | stop searching around that candidate: it leaves the leaderboard, so it cannot be proposed from, reported best or adopted. Add `--lineage` for the whole branch. |
| `refactory steer --run <id> --adopt [--as <package>]` | write the run's current winner as a package now, without ending the search. |
| `refactory stop --run <id>` | request interruption of its recorded owned process; the receipt distinguishes requested cancellation from confirmed termination. |

**A search says what it is doing while it does it.** `refactory optimize` prints the meaningful events as they happen — each candidate's score, the best so far, what the optimizer kept and refused with the running rule tally, each epoch's best, and the held-out audit — while the final JSON stays on stdout for a caller to parse. `--verbose` adds every event and each candidate's own run output, and `refactory status --run <id>` shows the same records, which is what the Web panel reads.

The read verbs pass through the console's own `--project`, `--runs-root`, `--after`, `--limit`, `--state` and `--contents` options.

## Everything else

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `refactory doctor` | check local configuration and missing setup; this does not test authentication or quota. |
| `refactory help [--topic <topic>]` | the operating guide, and the current mode and operation schemas. |
| `refactory docs [--page <page>]` | search and read the documentation shipped with this checkout. |
| `refactory workers` | the coding-agent worker configuration and the capabilities each backend reports. |
| `refactory runtime` | the resolved runtime and model route a run would use. |
| `refactory profile-save --name <name> --spec <JSON>` | save an immutable configuration version. |
| `refactory graph-control [--node <id>]` | control a graph run through the spine: pause, resume or stop it. |
| `refactory ui --port <n> --no-open` | start the [browser GUI](interfaces.md) without opening a browser. |


## Model selection and runtime limits

Read [Models](models.md) for managed credentials, resolved routing, worker receipts and unsupported backend capabilities. A random seed does not make provider responses deterministic. Candidate counts, elapsed time and tokens have separate limits; repeated trials and final holdout measurements consume the shared resource allocation. Token enforcement occurs at usage boundaries and can overshoot during an in-flight request.

For samples and resume on authoring APIs, use the documented Python Create/Edit/Design entry points and their `--help`; those flags are not all aliases on `refactory ceo`. [Authoring guide](tutorials/03-author-with-a-model.md).

refactory/docs/concepts.md.text:
# Concepts

Refactory makes an agentic workflow explicit, interactive and searchable. A mode can be small or elaborate: research and QA are graph choices, not requirements imposed on every harness.

![The mode and artifact workflows](assets/refactory-flow.svg)

## Packages, modes and Tasks

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Package** | A named collection of Python modes and their supporting operations |
| **Mode** | An explicit graph, declared knobs and input/output contracts; a scored mode also defines the objective used by optimization |
| **Task** | The source of work items, per-item preparation and verification used by a mode's data node |
| **CEO** | The conversational coordinator that drives the graph and delegates its agent nodes |
| **Outer loop** | A search that proposes, validates and measures permitted changes to a mode |

Shipped packages live in `refactory/refactory_packages/`. Created, imported and adopted packages live in the project's `.factory/packages/`. Both use the same registry. A package may be disabled without deleting it.

Create produces a reusable package; Edit produces a revised package and records where it came from. Design produces an artifact in `.factory/artifacts/`. Create and Design are deliberately unscored authoring modes: successful completion is governed by their graph's checks, not a numeric search objective. Standalone Design artifacts are not optimizer candidates.

## What a graph contains

| Node | Work |
|---|---|
| `op` | Invoke a Python operation |
| `agent` | Delegate a tool-using agent task; it can involve multiple model turns |
| `gate` | Route on a deterministic, agent or user verdict |
| `fork` / `join` | Dispatch independent branches and wait for their results |
| `data` | Run a subgraph over a Task's items |

Nodes declare inputs, outputs and facts. Runtime validation catches structural violations; the mode's own checks establish its application requirements. Neither a file's existence nor an agent's statement proves its content correct.

A user gate is an explicit control point. The runtime asks the person or uses their deliberately configured authorization; the coordinator cannot invent approval.

## Graph execution and interactivity

The CLI and GUI present the same underlying workflows. The CEO uses workflow tools to open a graph, see the due node, dispatch workers and record completion. The runtime owns the cursor and the gates. Its guard disables the CEO's direct coding and skill tools during graph execution.

Workers may use skills as supporting instructions. The graph's structure and durable run state remain the execution mechanism. A graph does not depend on an agent remembering a checklist in a skill document.

Steering notes are recorded and supplied to subsequent work. Explicit prompt edits and reruns change a selected node's execution. Notes do not automatically rewrite deterministic operations, and delivery does not prove semantic compliance. See [Terminal and GUI](interfaces.md) for the current timing and UI boundaries.

## State, knobs and protected requirements

A Python mode declares its initial graph with `build()`. After that, `state_dict()` contains the graph and knobs as serializable data. The optimizer edits this state; it does not rewrite `build()` or arbitrary source files.

Knobs are declared inputs and parameters with types, bounds and mutability. Use them to pass actual values into deterministic operations. An intent such as “count to twenty” is context; `target=20` supplies the input.

A scored mode's `score()` and `invariants()` are methods outside the editable state. The validator enforces those declared boundaries before evaluating proposals. Required artifacts that are not part of a numeric score need meaningful invariants and acceptance checks; a higher score alone does not establish that every user requirement survived.

## The configurable outer loop

Three choices are independent:

| Choice | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Strategy / outer loop** | Organize selection, proposal rounds and stopping |
| **Optimizer** | Propose candidate edits |
| **Evaluator** | Execute a candidate and measure its result |

The default walker evaluates the graph in Python and supplies a model client to agent nodes. The DSH evaluator lowers the graph and runs it through the shipping DSH runtime. Both carry the run's selected model/worker context to agent nodes; see [Models](models.md#model-selection-across-execution-paths).

Permitted edits can include knobs, prompts, nodes and edges, subject to the selected preset and invariants. A proposal is validated before it can spend candidate evaluation budget. Execution failures are recorded but cannot win.

For Task-bound modes, candidates use the training partition and the winner is audited on held-out items. A mode without a data split reports holdout as not applicable. The compared score can include a graph-size penalty; the raw score is retained separately.

A [profile](optimization-profiles.md) versions the search settings and objective; each run retains its own resolved snapshot. Opt-in repeats report actual trial count and variability, while shared budgets account for proposals, evaluations and validation. Adoption writes the exact eligible winner into a new package with its profile and audit provenance. It does not alter the source package or guarantee a future stochastic run will reproduce the same outputs. No-improvement searches are valid outcomes.

## Models, agents and runtimes

Cordis supplies plugin composition and service lifecycle. DSH supplies the current agent runtime, tools, sessions and model-provider adapters. Refactory supplies modes, graph execution/steering and the meta outer loop.

The model provider and coding-agent runtime are different choices. Today, choosing an OpenAI model still runs the DSH coding agent. Optional Codex and Claude Code workers require an explicit backend selection and their native setup; they are not enabled by a model-name change. [Worker capabilities](models.md#model-provider-versus-coding-agent) define the supported controls.

## What evidence means

Keep three questions separate:

1. Did the framework execute the declared graph and handle gates, steering, failure and cleanup correctly?
2. Did the artifact meet its declared acceptance checks?
3. How good was the model's output across the workload, and at what cost?

A checker can be too narrow, a valid workflow can generate a poor answer, and a model timeout can leave a correctly reported failed run. Preserve the exact result and use the appropriate measurements for each question.

Next: [get started](getting-started.md), [write a mode](tutorials/01-write-a-mode.md), [Tasks](datasets.md), or [architecture](architecture.md).

refactory/docs/contributing.md.text:
# Contributing

For anyone — person or coding agent — changing `refactory/`. It assumes you have
read [the architecture overview](architecture.md), and it is about the rules that
are not visible from the code alone: which invariants must hold, what will break
if you move something, and how to check your work.

## The commands

Run from the repository root.

```bash
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests/ -q                    # the suite
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests/ -q --run-integration  # ... plus the real-DSH runs
uv run python -m refactory_dsh.tools.gen_api_reference --check # docs match the code
uv sync --group reference                                      # add the test-time oracle
```

`tests/test_ir_parity.py` compares `refactory_dsh/ir.py` with the reference graph
language over every shipped mode. That reference is a **test-time oracle** and not
a runtime dependency: it lives in the non-default `reference` group, so a plain
`uv sync` does not install it and the parity tests skip with a reason
`--toolchain-gate` reports.

The DSH side, when you touch `packages/`:

```bash
pnpm run build                 # typecheck, then the host and client bundle passes
pnpm run test                  # the eight packages' vitest suites
pnpm run lint                  # oxlint
pnpm run typecheck
```

The gates the harness copy carried are gone with it. [Verification](verification.md)
names what replaced each one, what a contributor runs before pushing, and what is not
covered.

`.work/todo.json` tracks the work, and `tests/test_work_complete.py` **fails while
any item is open**. Each item records its issue number, the command that verifies
it, and the observed result; that test also checks the command names files that
exist, because two items once named test files that never existed and nobody
noticed.

## The environment, and what it hides

**Lean and mathlib are optional, and their absence is silent.** The Lean tests skip when `lean` is not on `PATH`; the mathlib tests skip when `MATHLIB_PATH` is unset. A skipped test cannot fail, so a green suite on a machine without them says nothing about the checker path — which is how two real defects hid. Every test that exercises a real external tool is marked `toolchain`, and one command reports which ran, which skipped and why, and fails if any did not run:

```bash
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests -q --toolchain-gate
```

No per-PR job installs Lean or mathlib (mathlib is a 7.4 GB checkout, and this suite is not in the DSH CI matrix), so those paths are verified on developer machines by that gate. A machine without the tools is expected to fail it and to say what it did not verify.

**A DSH profile is machine state, not a checkout artifact.** It is created with `dsh plugin --profile <name> add <package>`. This checkout owns two: `graph`, which the Python glue runs modes on, and `refactory`, which the GUI boots over the harness's own `web` template — the harness's `web` profile is never written to, so a plain `dsh --profile web` session shows no re:factory rows. `refactory` needs both the `ceo` preset layer and the web-surface layer — without the preset every session it creates without naming one stops, and without the surface the console and picker rows never mount. `install.sh` provisions both idempotently, `./refactory-dsh` heals a missing layer before booting, and `REFACTORY_SKIP_DSH_PROFILE=1` skips both. `refactory_dsh/dsh_profile.py` is the one place that answers "is the profile there, and what fixes it" — it owns the layer and target tables, emits the `init`/`add`/`remove` plan the installer and the launcher execute, and detects a harness profile an old install mutated; `refactory doctor`, the runner and the tests all read it. Martty is an **attached** target: the operator adds the preset layer to the profile they already have, and re:factory never creates it. Without the profile, anything that runs a mode on DSH stops at the first call.

**`install.sh` provisions the default install, not the optional parts.** It creates
`.venv` from `uv.lock`'s default (`dev`) group and installs the pinned pnpm workspace
with the eight packages' `lib/` built, then creates the DSH profiles above. It does
**not** install the non-default `reference` group — the parity oracle, added with
`uv sync --group reference`, whose tests skip with a reason without it — and it does
not create `refactory/vendor/srf/graphs`, the legacy graph directory for the
low-level `dsh --profile graph run` path; the public `uv run refactory ceo
<package>/<mode>` route supplies its own graph directory. `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
runs `install.sh` and asserts this default install, so the opt-ins stay opt-in.

**Use managed credentials for nested model execution.** Save the provider key through **Settings → Models → Edit → API key → Apply** in the DSH home used by the run. Exported keys and repository `.env` can serve the launching process, but nested smoke deliberately scrubs credential environment variables and changes `HOME`; the product carries the nonsecret DSH-home location so DSH can resolve its managed store. See [Models](models.md#credentials-for-nested-execution) for precedence and setup, and use `refactory doctor --provider deepseek-official --model deepseek-flash` to check downstream configuration before authoring. This check does not authenticate the key; unsupported custom runtimes report an explicit unverified warning. Deterministic modes, searches with `--optimizer random`, and offline tests do not need model credentials.

## The invariants

These are the rules the system is built on. Breaking one is not a style problem;
each exists because its absence caused a specific failure.

### The state is the authority after genesis

`build()` runs **once**, to produce the starting state. Every later architecture
comes from the state dict, because that is what the optimizer edits.

- Never read a knob's value in `build()`. A knob is consumed by a node at run time.
- Never make `build()` depend on I/O, the clock, or randomness — it must be pure,
  or `build() -> state -> build()` stops being an identity.
- `score()` and `invariants()` are **methods**, never state. That is what makes
  them unreachable by a proposal, and it is the whole protection. Do not put them
  in the state dict, and do not make a candidate able to influence them.

### A candidate is judged before it costs anything

`Optimizer.attempt` applies and validates the edit *before* the loop evaluates
anything. A proposal that would produce an invalid graph costs no budget.

- A new rule goes in `nn/validate.py` and in the `RULES` table. `tests/test_integrity.py`
  asserts the table and the emitted codes are the same set **in both directions**,
  so a rule that is emitted but unpublished fails the suite.
- The validator **refuses; it never repairs.** A repair hides the edit that caused
  the problem and makes the next failure unattributable.
- Macros are literal compositions of primitives. If you add one, express it as an
  `expand` into primitives rather than as new application logic, or it can produce
  a state no sequence of primitives could.

### Every knob is reachable, and every file is produced

- `V7` refuses a declared knob no node consumes **and** a node consuming an
  undeclared knob. A knob that looks like a search axis and is not is worse than
  no knob: the search spends batches learning nothing.
- `V6` refuses a node reading a file no node on a start-to-terminal path writes.
- `V11` refuses a declared port no node writes.
- `Loop.unreachable_knobs()` reports knobs that *this optimizer* cannot move even
  though they are declared and consumed. It warns rather than refuses, because a
  knob-only optimizer on a structural mode is a legitimate pairing.

### The journal is the only durable state

`journal.jsonl` is append-only and replayed. Do not add a second snapshot of the
population and keep it consistent by hand — that is what the system this replaced
did, and it produced real bugs.

- Anything a later step needs must be **journaled**, not derived. `generation`,
  `refusal_pressure`, and `bound` are all journaled for this reason: a resumed run
  that guessed them would take a different path.
- An invalid candidate is recorded as a `Rejection` with its reasons, never
  dropped in silence. `E-duplicate` exists because a silently dropped duplicate
  loses a batch slot and makes the run report a batch it did not try.

### The two runtimes must agree

The walker is a debug runtime; DSH ships. `tests/test_equivalence.py` runs the
same mode both ways and compares the score.

- If you change the executor, change nothing that makes a node behave differently
  on DSH. The lowering in `lowering.py` is the seam, and `refactory_dsh/ir.py` owns
  the IR it lowers into. `tests/test_ir_parity.py` holds that copy against the
  reference over every shipped mode: the serialization is byte-identical, and the
  reference's validator accepts the result except for two modes whose refusal is a
  limit of that validator, both recorded in `REFERENCE_REFUSALS` there.
- The IR has **no field for the facts a node produces**, so `write_declarations`
  writes them beside the graph and the runner reads them from the run directory.
  That is a known wart, not an oversight to "clean up" silently.

## The failure modes worth remembering

Each of these happened, and the shape of the code is the response.

- **A severed gradient.** The optimizer was not shown what the run learned.
  `backward()` produces the gradient and it is part of the API; `knob_attribution`
  includes `untried`, because *a value that failed* and *a value nobody tried* are
  different facts and a prompt that conflates them keeps re-proposing what it
  already knows.
- **Mutating operators that destroyed graphs.** Some rewrites produced structures
  that could not run. Hence: macros expand to primitives, the validator refuses
  rather than repairs, and validation happens before budget is spent.
- **A surface that lied.** Structural wins were counted from failed runs, and
  duplicates vanished. `structural_wins` requires `exit_ok`; duplicates are refused
  at the optimizer layer and `attempt == 0` is asserted in the tests.
- **Steps that deleted their own run.** When the loop became a mode, each node
  rehydrates from the journal — and `resume=False` means "start over", so the
  first version deleted the journal between two nodes of the loop's own run. Any
  node that reads the run must resume.

## Where to put a change

| you want to | change |
|---|---|
| a new mode | a package under `refactory_packages/` |
| a new validator rule | `nn/validate.py` `RULES` + the check, then the anti-drift test |
| a new edit operation | `nn/edits.py`: a primitive, or a macro that expands to primitives |
| a new optimizer | subclass `optim.Optimizer`, implement `propose`, register it |
| a new outer loop | subclass `outerloop.OuterLoop`, override the steps |
| a new strategy | `strategies.py`; a port of an SRF mode |
| a new artifact | declare a `Port` on the mode **and** write it from a node |
| a new way to read a run | `observe.py` (readers) or `history.py` (finished runs) |
| the loop's own steps | `loop.py` — and expect `loop_mode/loop` to need matching changes |

## Documentation

- The [API reference](api/reference.md) is **generated**; never edit it. Run
  `uv run python -m refactory_dsh.tools.gen_api_reference`. `tests/test_docs_api.py`
  fails when it is stale, when a documented symbol has no prose, or when a
  document names a module that does not import.
- The architecture overview's rule table is checked against `nn.RULES`, so adding
  a rule means updating the overview too.
- Prose belongs in the overview and the tutorials. A comment belongs where the
  reason for the code is local to it.

## What not to do

- **Do not add a second runtime.** The walker is for debugging; DSH ships. A third
  executor is a third set of behaviours to keep in agreement.
- **Do not silently accept an invalid candidate** to keep a batch full.
- **Do not default a missing referent.** `Package` resolution refuses a bare mode
  name rather than guessing a package, and the registry refuses a name that exists
  in both roots rather than picking one.
- **Do not repair a state.** Refuse it and report the reason.

## Public capability coverage

See [discovery](discovery.md) for the shared parser/mode contract, semantic review
metadata, offline generation and extension checklist. Run `pnpm run docs:generate`
after reviewed changes and `pnpm run docs:check` before building. New public
operations, mode schemas and worker capabilities require current explanations,
examples and explicit CLI/chat/panel routes.
