refactory/docs/datasets.md.text:
# Datasets and Tasks

A mode normally walks its graph once. A mode with a **`data` node** walks a subgraph
once per *item* — one benchmark instance, one row of a file, one directory — and an
item can carry its own prompt and its own verdict. That is how a benchmark or a
dataset becomes a mode instead of a script around one.

## A harness is for a class of work

What this system produces is a harness for a **class** of work — "write the build config for any Java buildroot", not "write the config for this buildroot". A mode that runs once is the special case rather than the default, because a mode that was tuned until one instance passed makes no claim about the next instance.

The `data` node is the harness's **input port**. What it is pointed at at run time — a bound Task's `instances()`, a directory, a JSONL or CSV file — is material rather than meaning, and a harness with its items written into the graph is a harness for exactly those items. `create` binds a Task by name and leaves the port open, and the validate gate refuses a package whose items are baked into the graph instead of read from the node at run time.

A class-of-work harness scores **per item**: its `score()` aggregates the verdicts the Task's `verify` returned for each pass, and the run reports the individual verdicts under the `item_scores` fact alongside that aggregate. That is what makes the score a statement about the class rather than about the one run that produced it.

## The node

```python
graph.add(nn.Node(
    "data", "data",
    subgraph_entry="work",     # the first node of the per-item subgraph
    subgraph_exit="work",      # the last one, included in every pass
    task_ref="my_pack.tasks:MyTask",   # where the items come from (optional)
    writes=("current_item.json",),
    produces=("item_scores",),
))
graph.connect("data", "finish")        # where the run goes after every item
```

The subgraph is reached **through the data node**, not by an edge: an edge into it
would run it once outside the iteration. Each pass writes the item to
`current_item.json` in the run directory, so an op or an agent node reads the item it
is working on rather than being told it in a prompt.

Items come from, in order of precedence: `inline_items` declared on the node; the
`source_path` read as `source_format` (`directory` — sorted subdirectories; `jsonl` —
one object per line; `csv` — a header row); or the bound Task's `instances()`. The
node's `limit` caps what is used. A source that is named and missing is refused by
name, because an empty selection and an unbound source must not look alike.

## Feeding it at run time

The graph declares the source the mode was built with, and a run may name another. That is what makes a harness usable on items it has never seen without editing the mode:

```bash
uv run refactory ceo java_build_pack/build --source /path/to/my/trees
```

The runner writes the choice into the run directory as `items.json`, and `load_items` reads it on both runtimes, so the walker and DSH iterate the same items. `--source-format` says how to read it (`directory` by default, or `jsonl`/`csv`), and an entry keyed `*` applies to every data node of the run while an entry keyed by node id wins for that node.

An item in a `directory` source is a subdirectory, and it may describe itself in an `item.json` beside its content — those fields reach the pass the way a Task's metadata does, which is how a harness learns an item's entry point. The directory's own name stays the id, so a described item cannot rename itself out of the selection it was listed in.

## The Task

A Task is three optional hooks, resolved by `module:Class` or by a name registered with
`register_task`. A reference that does not resolve is refused rather than run with
nothing judging the items.

```python
from refactory_dsh.task import Task, TaskInstance, VerifyResult

class CountingTask(Task):
    name = "counting"

    def instances(self):                      # the items
        return [TaskInstance(id="alpha"), TaskInstance(id="beta")]

    def setup(self, instance, workspace):     # before a pass
        ...

    def verify(self, instance, workspace):    # after a pass; None means "no opinion"
        return VerifyResult(passed=True, score=1.0)
```

There is no hook that writes the prompt. An item is data — it reaches the pass as `current_item.json` — and what the agent for an item is asked is the mode's own business, stated in its agent node's prompt template. Two places that both decide the ask is one place too many.

The verdicts are recorded as `item_scores` when the data node declares that fact, so
`score()` reads what the Task decided rather than a number the graph guessed.

## A worked example

A package with one data node bound to a two-item Task, whose subgraph is one op that
appends the current item's id, scores the mean of the Task's verdicts:

```bash
uv run refactory package smoke dataset_probe/dataset
```

```json
{"mode": "dataset_probe/dataset", "package": "dataset_probe", "exit_ok": true,
 "error": null, "score": 0.75, "iterations": 4}
```

`0.75` is the mean of `1.0` for `alpha` and `0.5` for `beta`: two passes, each with
its own item on disk, each judged by the Task.

A two-item Task proves the shape but not the claim. `java_build_pack` is the example that does the work the product is named for: its Task lists three small Java source trees, its one agent node writes `build.sh` for whichever item is on disk, and the Task runs that script and compares what the program printed with the output recorded beside the sources. The mode's score is the share of trees it built, and pointing the same harness at a fourth tree it has never seen is what the binding buys:

```bash
uv run refactory ceo java_build_pack/build --intent "build each Java tree the Task lists"
```

## Creating one

`create` makes you say which of the two things you are building, before it spends anything on a model:

```bash
# a harness for a class of work: the Task supplies the items and judges each pass
uv run refactory ceo "a harness that counts the items of any counting instance" \
  --mode create --name my_pack --task my_pack.tasks:CountingTask

# the special case: a harness for one run of one thing
uv run refactory ceo "a harness that counts to ten" --mode create --name my_once --single
```

Naming a Task is the whole directive: the produced package gets a `data` node bound to that Task, and the validate gate checks the package really has one rather than taking the prompt's word for it. A creation that names neither a Task nor `--single` is refused with both options named, because a harness built for one hardcoded example is the special case and must be asked for as one.

The validate gate refuses three shapes, each by name: a package that declares no data node when a Task was named, one whose data node is bound to a different Task, and one that closes its input port — items written into the graph as `inline_items`, or a data node that names neither a Task nor a source to read at run time. Asking is not the same as getting.

## On the runtimes

Both runtimes iterate the node the same way and produce the same facts. The walker
owns the whole loop and runs it in-process. DSH's spine walks the subgraph the way it
walks the rest of the graph, so the item loop is split across the loader's three
commands — `list` (how many items), `begin` (materialise one and run the Task's
`setup`), and `end` (run the Task's `verify` and record the score) — and each pass's
deterministic nodes run in-process while its agent nodes are handed to the subagents
the graph names. The loader is one implementation
(`refactory_dsh.nn.executor.load_items`), so the items a mode selects do not depend on
which runtime is running it. The composition supplies the command
(`dataCommand`, set by the `graph` bundle to `python -m refactory_dsh.items`); a graph
with a data node and no loader is refused at load rather than handed to the model,
because a model cannot enter a subgraph the cursor never enters.

`refactory/tests/test_equivalence.py` runs one data-driven mode on both runtimes and
compares the facts.

# CEO discovery and project-worker acceptance — 2026-09-27

This acceptance covers issues #253 and #254. It uses one new native CEO
conversation and one config-dispatched Codex worker. Existing adapter acceptance
in [release validation](release-validation-20260926.md) remains the evidence for
other backends; no three-backend or full-authoring campaign was repeated.

## Native run and identity

The run used the isolated `codex/ceo-discovery-project-workers` worktree based on
`8c3f2a61b738e8305e0d7b1ee10345b7deb91e3d`, with the implementation uncommitted.
Its returned build ID was
`3fe92e2189811c471ec44dae73e96ac644cff4f6e85935b40a82810c1759aaeb`;
documentation ID was
`188ca63a95177c6ace3e2d505551c714d963f050c0b9bcf0ef1791cf152ecbb9`.
Subsequent deterministic review fixes and reconciliation with merged authoring
changes change those IDs. This is evidence for the actual tested development
build, not a claim that a later commit ran another model acceptance.

The fixture `discovery_acceptance/worker_once` was installed after the build. It
has an `emit` agent (role `builder`) followed by a deterministic check requiring
`answer.txt` to contain exactly `42\n`. Live help listed it, including its missing
reviewed-guidance warnings. The project file contained:

```json
{"worker_backend":"dsh","node_routes":{"emit":{"worker_backend":"codex"}}}
```

The native CEO prompt required discovery through help, a mode-help read, a docs
search and page read, an effective-worker check, and one `wf_open` in a fresh
absolute work directory. It prohibited source archaeology, optimization, repair,
retry and out-of-graph delegation. No token cap was imposed. The CEO made ten
tool calls in eight steps: help, modes, mode help, docs search, workers, docs
page read, wf_open, wf_next, artifacts and wf_state. It used no shell, source
reader or web tool.

Session: `session-aa19f9b1-8682-4671-857c-db80ca251446`.
The CEO used the configured DeepSeek Flash selection. Summed assistant usage was
278,279 total tokens: 37,984 input, 238,080 cached input and 2,215 output;
643 reasoning tokens were reported within output. These figures are separate
from the native worker's usage.

Worker `worker-7c2827b6ce754da79d7d7729b4c61ef0` completed between
19:30:30.929 and 19:30:42.293 UTC. Its requested route was Codex with native
model/provider/effort selection and `skip` permissions. The actual native thread
reported `gpt-6-astra`, `openai`, `high`, Codex runtime `0.153.4`, adapter
`@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent` `0.1.5-rc.3`, and 45,249 measured tokens. The measurement
excludes nested workers. There was one attempt. Independent file inspection and
`checked.json` verified exact `42\n` output.

## Terminal and panel

Public terminal calls read workers, mode help and the shipped routing page, then
prepared the same fixture with `console open --workdir <fresh-directory>`.
The generated node specification selected Codex from the same project map.
This was preparation evidence and did not launch a second model worker.

In native Chrome, the Modes panel selected the runtime-installed fixture. Its
**Mode help and effective project workers** disclosure returned the same mode,
build/docs identities and effective project defaults. Runtime controls showed
**Use project defaults**, inherited permission policy and no token limit.
Attaching the existing run showed finished/done, both nodes complete, the actual
Codex route and measured usage, and verified output facts. No second panel model
launch was claimed. Deterministic tests cover the shared preparation and panel
argument mapping.

The canonical `artifacts` list returned zero entries for the custom fixture's
noncanonical filenames. The graph's check, independent file inspection and panel
outputs established success; the CEO disclosed that artifact-list limitation.

## Checks and cleanup

Focused checks cover file/environment/profile/explicit precedence, backend
switches, role/node maps, invalid native fields, nested and saved-run isolation,
CLI/chat preparation, live package discovery, docs bounds and integrity, stale
coverage, broken links, generated chat-to-parser mappings and panel controls.
Final focused validation after reconciliation with main `364eeffc85` passed:

- 145 Python tests across discovery, project configuration, workers, interactive
  preparation, worker permissions, profiles, recovery and API docs.
- 164 TypeScript tests across the tool, generated invocation contract, profiles,
  body and steering ledger (including the independently merged panel changes).
- `pnpm run build`, including offline docs/coverage checks, host/client typechecks
  and both production bundles; normal commit/push hooks.

Exploratory wider runs also encountered existing failures. A detached baseline at
`3fd35ac7c9` reproduced two legacy graph-cycle assertions in `test_nn.py`, seven
service-mock failures in `service.spec.ts`, and three GUI-loop failures involving
sandbox PID inspection, missing-run wording and a missing `cve_patch_pack`
fixture. The wider tool-live run passed 98/100 checks, with a sandbox stop-status
failure and the same stale missing-run wording assertion. These are not a claim
that the entire repository test suite is green.

Private transcripts, terminal JSON, requested-route provenance and the plan are
retained under `/private/tmp/refactory-discovery-acceptance-20260927`; graph
artifacts remain in this worktree's `.factory/discovery-acceptance-20260927`.
The owned server on port 60213 was stopped after acceptance; the worker had
already completed, and its owned Chrome tab was closed. The temporary project file was copied to evidence and removed.
No old run was resumed, credential contents were published, or original tracked
checkout was modified.

# Capability and documentation discovery

The CEO receives a compact [operating guide](ceo-guide.md) through its tool's
system prompt. `refactory help` returns that guide, current operation/mode IDs,
interface support and build/documentation identity. `--topic <ID>` reads actual
argument schemas and examples. Chat uses actions `help`, `docs`, `profiles`,
`profile-resolve` and `workers`; the native panel uses the same mode declarations.

```sh
refactory help
refactory help --topic counting_pack/fixed_step
refactory docs --query 'worker routing'
refactory docs --page refactory/docs/worker-routing.md --limit 6000
```

Docs return exact indexed page IDs, section IDs, resolved links and continuation
offsets. Reads are limited to 12,000 characters; search returns at most 12 bounded
excerpts. Only README and the public `refactory/docs` Markdown tree are bundled.
Runtime retrieval reads the installation's bundle, never project files, private
runs, credentials, swap files or arbitrary paths. Non-document links are identified
as repository assets. Shell/coding/web permissions of the CEO stay restricted.

Coverage targets shipped mode declarations and public console/CLI entry points.
Internal Python helpers are covered by the separate API reference generator,
not advertised as chat actions. Forwarding entry points such as `package` expose
their wrapper schema and supported terminal route; backend-native credential and
configuration flags remain owned by the native product and are deliberately not
chat configuration arguments.

The authoritative facts come from `console._parser()`, the CLI parser, profile
settings, worker capabilities, mode declarations and the installed package
registry. The generated chat schema and invocation mappings use those same
arguments. Interface declarations distinguish callable actions, `wf_open`,
terminal/panel routes and deliberately unavailable configuration controls. Worker
routing is a file/CLI/panel feature with read-only chat discovery.

`refactory_dsh/data/coverage.json` owns reviewed purpose, examples, documentation
links and interface routes. Its `reviewed_schema` binds that guidance to actual
public arguments, defaults and mode structure. Missing/stale metadata fails the
ordinary build with the capability ID, the behavior the CEO cannot reliably
choose/use, and repair instructions. Generation never updates semantic review
hashes automatically. Signatures are facts, not proof that an explanation works.

```sh
pnpm run docs:generate
pnpm run docs:check
pnpm run build
```

Generation is deterministic and offline: no model, credentials, network service
or vector database. It reuses the API reference generator and writes the full
installation docs bundle, [capability reference](api/capabilities.md), and the
TypeScript tool contract. Check mode fails stale artifacts and invalid links.
The build runs check mode first, so it cannot silently repair stale committed
artifacts. Build identity hashes version, schemas, reviewed metadata and docs;
documentation identity hashes indexed pages. Live mode schemas may differ after
installing a package; the help response shows coverage warnings in that case.

## Worked extension: mode

Register a mode normally and declare a new knob with its type, default, bounds
or accepted values, and a useful description. For example, add a frozen input
`target` and an integer `step` to a counting mode. The live catalogue immediately
shows these facts and its nodes/roles/gates/ports. Add a `modes` entry in
`data/coverage.json` explaining when to choose it, a working example such as
`{"knobs":{"target":5,"step":1},"explanation":"Reach five exactly."}`, its
public documentation page and CLI/chat/panel routes. Run `docs:generate` to get
the expected schema hash, review the guidance, and set `reviewed_schema` to that
hash. Regenerate and check. A later knob or graph change produces a new review
diagnostic. Newly installed modes still appear at runtime even without this
metadata, with a visible warning instead of a false claim of complete coverage.

## Worked extension: operation

Add the actual console parser and dispatch implementation, then add its operation
coverage entry: purpose, `examples` with console argument names, `doc`, and all
three interface routes. If it is a CEO action, `chat.fields` maps tool argument
names to actual parser destinations. The generator derives types, flags and
positionals, and the tool uses those mappings to invoke the console. Missing
required mappings and invalid example arguments fail generation. If it is file
or terminal only, omit `chat` and explain the supported route and why chat cannot
mutate it. `workers` and [project worker configuration](worker-routing.md) are a
worked example of intentionally read-only conversational support.

Run focused schema, negative coverage, docs retrieval and invocation tests. For
an exposed model workflow, demonstrate a small actual CEO discovery/docs/launch
case; deterministic schema checks alone do not establish model usability.

refactory/docs/getting-started.md.text:
# Get started

Start with a small offline search, then connect a model for authoring and interactive work. Run commands from the repository root.

## 1. Install

You need Git, [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) `^22.19` or `>=24`, and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). The installer sets up the pinned Node dependencies, Python environment, UI bundles and DSH graph profile.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh.git
cd refactory-dsh
./install.sh
uv run refactory list
```

The repository must be accessible to your GitHub account. `uv` manages the Python environment. Run `./install.sh` again after an update that changes dependencies or the UI bundles.

## 2. Try a search without a model

The shipped circle-packing example is deterministic. These options keep proposal generation and evaluation offline:

```bash
uv run refactory optimize circle_packing/adaptive \
  --optimizer random --preset knob_only --evaluator walker \
  --epochs 2 --batch-size 4 --max-evaluations 8 --seed 5 \
  --runs-root .factory/loop/first-search
uv run refactory leaderboard --run .factory/loop/first-search
uv run refactory best --run .factory/loop/first-search
```

Read the candidate changes, raw score and adjusted score. The latter includes the graph-size penalty. This mode has no dataset split, so its holdout is explicitly not applicable. Use a fresh run directory for a separate experiment.

Keep the winner as a new package:

```bash
uv run refactory adopt --run .factory/loop/first-search --as first_tuned
uv run refactory package verify first_tuned
uv run refactory package smoke first_tuned/adaptive
```

Use another package name if `first_tuned` already exists. Adoption preserves the original package.

## 3. Open the GUI and configure a model

```bash
uv run refactory ui --port 3081
```

Open the exact URL printed by the server, including its token. Choose this checkout as the workspace, then create a new session. A blank session can open the right sidebar's **Modes** tab; no introductory model message is needed.

In **Settings → Models**, configure a provider and save its API key with **Edit → API key → Apply**. Use the managed credential store for nested authoring and validation. An exported key or a repository `.env` alone does not survive nested execution's secret scrub. See [model setup](models.md#credentials-for-nested-execution).

```bash
uv run refactory doctor
uv run refactory runtime
```

Doctor checks local configuration, not authentication or quota. Runtime shows the nested defaults. Select a configured model in chat or use the CLI's `--provider` and `--model` options.

New coding workers default to **Skip permission checks**, including full native sandbox bypass for DSH/Codex. Their tools can access what your OS account can access. To retain backend checks, choose **Native permission policy** in the Modes panel or pass `--permission-mode default` in the CLI. Existing saved profiles and runs preserve their policy. [Worker permissions](models.md#model-provider-versus-coding-agent)

## 4. Choose the output you want

| Your goal | Use | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Build a reusable workflow | Create | A registered package of modes |
| Revise an existing workflow | Edit | A new package with provenance and comparison status |
| Build software or another artifact | Design | An artifact checked against the supplied command and brief |
| Use a workflow you already have | Run its mode | Its declared outputs and execution evidence |
| Improve a scored workflow | Optimize | Candidate comparisons, audit and a winner eligible for adoption |

Start an interactive terminal run:

```bash
uv run refactory ceo counting_pack/fixed_step \
  --knob target=20 --knob step=2 --intent "Count to twenty and explain the recorded result."
```

The knobs supply the operation's inputs; prose intent does not change deterministic inputs automatically. The conversational CEO uses a model even when the underlying mode is deterministic.

To author a small artifact:

```bash
uv run refactory ceo \
  "Build wordcount.py to count lines, words and characters in a UTF-8 file. Include sample.txt and verify the counts." \
  --mode design --name wordcount --check "python wordcount.py sample.txt"
```

Review the proposed design when asked. A command that merely prints counts does not by itself prove those counts correct; read the check evidence and review findings. Authoring can take substantial time because the current default modes include research and review stages.

To author a reusable mode, follow [Create and Edit](tutorials/03-author-with-a-model.md). Choose a [Task](datasets.md) for repeated items, or `--single` explicitly for a one-off harness.

## 5. Stay involved

In GUI chat, ask: “Open counting_pack/fixed_step with target=20 and step=2. Walk it one node at a time.” Ask to pause before a node, correct an instruction, or answer a gate. In the Modes panel, choose a mode and set its knobs: **Run once** executes it, including full and fast authoring modes; **Start** optimizes a scored mode. Chat supports stepwise authoring and user gates. Fast authoring uses smaller graphs with focused QA and bounded repair; see its [tested scope and resource choices](budgets-fast-modes.md#acceptance-status).

Attach the run's exact directory with **Existing run directory → Read this run** to follow persisted live activity, worker receipts and pending questions. Reading a run does not execute it. Use **resume** explicitly for a supported saved boundary after its owner stops; completed work and consumed resources are retained. [Interface guide](interfaces.md) explains what is interactive, what updates automatically, and when controls take effect.

Next: [command reference](cli.md) · [optimization tutorial](tutorials/02-optimize-it.md) · [write your own mode](tutorials/01-write-a-mode.md).

refactory/docs/hardening.md.text:
# Hardening: what the audit found, and what holds it now

Every issue closed before this pass was re-read against the code and probed for its
own acceptance criteria — by running them, not by grepping for identifiers. Five
were not finished, four of those while being marked done. This records each one, the
evidence, the fix, and the test that keeps it fixed, so the same claim cannot be
made twice.

Two probes also came back **clean**, and they are recorded because an audit that
only finds fault is not an audit.

---

## The method

For each issue: read its acceptance criteria as written, then write a probe that
would fail if the criterion were unmet, and run it. Grepping for a name proves a
name exists. Running the behaviour is what found these.

```bash
cd refactory && ../.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q
```

---

## 1. `check_package` executed generated code in the driver (#23)

**What the issue said.** create-mode writes Python and then something decides
whether it is usable, "which means loading it, which means executing model-written
code". The table named `create_ops.check_package: imports the generated package to
validate it — none — in-process, full access`.

**What the code did.** The docstring said *"A generated package is **never
imported here**"*. The body's tail was:

```python
package = load_fresh(name)              # importlib.import_module
for ops_module in package.ops:
    importlib.import_module(ops_module)  # model code, again
for mode_class in package.modes:
    problems.extend(_check_mode(mode_class))  # constructs the mode
```

Only the *structural* half ran in a subprocess. The semantic half — is the name
right, do the ops import, is the mode constructible, does it satisfy every
validator rule — ran in the driver with full access.

**The fix.**

- `sandbox.verify_sandboxed` now performs the whole check in its subprocess,
  including the package name, each declared ops module, and each mode's
  construction, score, knobs and validator rules.
- `register` and `smoke` needed the manifest only to *name* what was registered and
  which mode to smoke, and were loading the package to get it. They use the new
  `sandbox.describe_package`, which reads it out of process.
- `load_fresh` and `_check_mode` are deleted. No function in the driver loads a
  generated package any more.

**Held by.** `tests/test_create.py`: a test patches `importlib.import_module` to
record any import of the package's module prefix, runs `check_package` to a clean
result, and asserts the recording is empty. A second does the same for
`describe_package`.

**Known limit, stated rather than implied.** `registry.catalogue` and `registry.load`
still import packages to describe them, so *listing* a generated package still runs
it. That is a different boundary from create-mode's validation, and it is not fixed
here.

---

## 2. Run retention was declared and never applied (#24)

**What the issue said.** `memory(namespace, kind, retention)` where `retention` is
`run`, `project` or `global` — "the difference between a memory that dies with the
run and one that accumulates".

**What the code did.** `MemoryStore.forget_run_scoped` existed, with a docstring
reading *"Called when the run ends"*, and **nothing called it**. So a run-scoped
namespace accumulated exactly like a project one.

The cost is sharper than untidy files. `_evaluate` re-evaluates candidates when a
run resumes, and a run-scoped memory left on disk is read the second time — so a
resumed run would not be the run it resumed.

**A second gap, found while fixing it.** Memory did not cross to DSH **at all**:
`lowering` dropped it and `run.py` built its `RunContext` without a store. A mode
declaring a cross-run prior therefore worked in the walker and silently kept nothing
on the runtime that ships. Nothing reported the difference, because the running
example declares no memory.

**The fix.**

- `Loop._evaluate` forgets in a `finally`, so a crash or a stop applies the policy
  too, not only a clean finish.
- `lowering.write_declarations` carries the mode's memory declarations beside the
  node facts; `lowering.read_memory_declarations` reads them back; and `run.py`
  builds the store from them, with the same roots the walker uses.

**Held by.** `tests/test_declarations.py`: a run-scoped namespace is gone after
`forget_run_scoped`; project and global namespaces survive it; the loop's
`_evaluate` contains the call **and** a `finally`; the declarations survive the
lowering; and the node runner builds a store.

---

## 3. The strategies recorded their decision instead of applying it (#20)

**What the issue said.** "The deliverable includes all the SRF candidates
implemented on the new API. The abstraction is proven by the ports, not by the tests
for the abstraction."

**What the code did.** Five strategies took their distinguishing branch, counted it,
logged it, and called the ordinary path:

```python
def epoch_step(self, run=None, *, branch="mutate"):
    if branch == "merge": self.merges += 1
    else:                 self.mutations += 1
    run.log(f"branch={branch}")
    return super().epoch_step(run)     # the merge is not a merge
```

`reflective_sampler` stored `last_reflection` and read it nowhere.
`adaptive_meta` computed `meta` and logged it. `research_then_optimize` stored
`research_note` — `grep` found only the two lines that set and logged it.
`staged_curriculum` logged the stage and ran the ordinary step.

Measured, not argued: running all fourteen on identical input, **six produced
byte-identical leaderboards to `default`**.

The tests passed because they asserted the *counter* —
`test_reflective_takes_a_merge_branch_and_a_mutate_branch` checks
`loop.merges >= 1` — and a branch that changes nothing still increments a counter.

**The fix.** `ProposalContext.strategy` is a new channel carrying what the outer
loop decided for this iteration, so a decision reaches the proposer instead of only
the log. Each strategy now acts:

| strategy | what it now does |
|---|---|
| `adaptive_meta` | widens the batch by 2 on a stall — a real budget decision |
| `reflective` | builds a genuine merge: one parent's knobs taken from another, and it falls back to a mutation when the parents differ structurally rather than in their settings, because a no-op merge is refused as `E-noop` and loses the slot |
| `reflective_sampler` | drops a proposal that repeats an edit the run already refused |
| `research_then_optimize` | publishes its conclusion into the context |
| `staged_curriculum` | publishes which stage is running |

**Held by.** Six tests that assert the **effect**: the batch is wider, the merged
proposal takes the other parent's setting, a refused edit is not re-proposed, and
the decision is present in the context a proposer receives.

**Honest limit.** With `optimizer=random` the model-facing decisions (a research
note, a curriculum stage) reach a proposer that cannot read them, so four strategies
still match `default` on the tiny example. The channel is real; showing the
difference needs a model proposer.

---

## 4. A revision recorded a name, not a state (#13)

**What the issue said.** Provenance of *"what it was edited from, **at which
state**"*.

**What the code did.** `_revision_source` correctly handed the model the source
files. The record then said `revision_of: "circle_packing/adaptive"` and nothing
else. A mode is not a fixed thing — the outer loop edits it — so that names a class
which may have changed since, and the revision cannot be reproduced or diffed
against what it actually started from.

**The fix.** `edit()` resolves the source mode once, records its whole
`revision_of_state` plus a `revision_of_digest` (the same `candidate_id` the loop
uses, so a revision and a candidate that are the same state agree), and returns the
digest.

**Held by.** A test that runs a revision, reads the origin file, asserts the
recorded state is a full state dict, and that the digest matches both the result and
`candidate_id(state)`.

---

## 5. The lowering dropped `callable_name` (#21)

**What the issue said.** *"`FnNode.callable_name` already exists; do not invent a
command string."*

**What the code did.** Emitted `command: "python -m refactory_dsh.run <mod>:<fn>"`
and left `callable_name` unset. `callable_name` and `post_checks` appeared zero
times in `lowering.py`.

**Where the issue was right, and where it was wrong.** `callable_name` *is* a real
`FnNode` field — `factory/workflow/primitives.py`, round-tripped by
`factory/workflow/parity.py` — so the lowering was dropping something the language
has. But **DSH's spine does not model it**: `WorkflowNode` has `command`,
`evaluator_type` and `evaluator_command`, and `callable_name` appears nowhere in the
spine's source, which executes the command. A graph carrying only `callable_name`
would be a graph whose nodes never run.

**The fix.** The lowering emits **both**: `callable_name`, so the IR stays faithful
to the language and refactory's own tooling can read it, and `command`, because that
is what the runtime we ship executes.

**Held by.** Two tests: every op node carries both fields, and every declared
`callable_name` resolves.

**Not adopted, stated rather than skipped.** `AgentNode.post_checks` and refactory's
`ForkNode`/`JoinNode` are still unused. `post_checks` would duplicate a check the
executor already performs; adopting fork/join is a real design change, not a
fidelity fix, and is not done.

---

## 6. The documented commands, run as written (#31)

Ship readiness is not a feeling about the code; it is the claim that a person who has
never seen this repository can install it, follow the docs, and get the promised
result. That claim is testable, so it is a test: `tests/test_ship_ready.py` reads the
shipped documents, extracts every command line from their `bash` blocks, and runs it.

The gate checks four things, and each one found something:

| check | what it would catch |
|---|---|
| every `python -m refactory_dsh.X` a doc names imports | a tutorial pointing at a deleted module |
| every module's `--help` accepts the flags the doc shows | a flag renamed in code but not in the prose |
| the README links the architecture and the tutorials | a stranger with nowhere to go next |
| the docs the README promises exist on disk | a link to a file that was moved |

**The bug it found.** `python -m refactory_dsh.sandbox --help` printed its usage line
to **stderr** and exited **2**. Two things were wrong with that, and the second is the
worse one: a reader who asks for help is told they made an error, and a program that
captures stdout — which is how the doc gate itself reads a help page — saw nothing at
all. So the flag table was empty and the gate could not check the sandbox CLI, which
is where an unknown flag had to be caught by hand.

**The fix.** `sandbox.main` gained `usage()`, which is the one string both paths
print, and an explicit branch: `-h`/`--help` prints it to **stdout** and returns
**0**. The two cases that are genuinely misuse keep their old behaviour, because they
are a different decision and were already deliberate:

| invocation | stream | status | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `-h`, `--help` | stdout | 0 | a question, answered |
| no arguments | stderr | 2 | nothing was asked for; `test_the_sandbox_cli_needs_an_instruction` pins this |
| an unknown flag | stderr | 2 | not a command |

**Held by.** A test that runs `--help` against `sandbox`, `loop` and `console` and
requires both a zero status and non-empty stdout. It is not vacuous: the pre-fix
behaviour (status 2, empty stdout) fails exactly that assertion, which was run both
ways when the fix was made.

**The second finding was in the README, not the code.** It described the layout but
never linked `docs/architecture.md` or `docs/tutorials/`, so the entry point a
stranger actually opens did not lead anywhere. The README now carries a Documentation
table — architecture, tutorials, API, tool packing, hardening, contributing.

**Also regenerated.** `docs/api/reference.md` is generated from the code and had
drifted from it; the new `usage()` export made that visible. `test_docs_api.py` fails
when the two disagree, so the reference is checked rather than trusted.

**And the tracker's own commit field was not checked.** The gate asked a done item for
a non-empty `commit`, which `"(pending)"` satisfies, so six closed items carried one
and the field proved nothing. A recorded commit exists so a reader can go and look at
the change; `test_a_recorded_commit_is_one_git_actually_knows` now runs `git cat-file
-e` on every one, and all 23 done items resolve. Verified both ways: planting a
made-up hash fails the gate, and removing it passes.

**The install itself was run, not inferred.** `./install.sh` is the one command a
stranger executes, and everything above only proves the commands *after* it work. It
was run against this checkout: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `pnpm run build`,
the venv, the editable installs, and the registry listing all
completed with status 0. The build was then checked for the damage a build can do —
`git status` is clean, the Python suite is unchanged, the DSH-side specs pass, and the
doc gates pass — because "it exited 0" and "it left the tree working" are different
claims and only the second one matters.

**What this still does not prove.** It is not a clean clone: the submodules were
already initialised and the venv already existed, so the script's fresh-clone branches
were not exercised. A machine with neither was not available here.

---

## 7. The sandbox made an installed toolchain unreachable (#30)

Found by installing the tool and running the path, which is the only way it could be
found. Every Lean test in the repository **skipped** on this machine, with a reason
naming the missing binary — an honest skip, and one that hid a bug, because the
skipped tests were the only thing that would have executed the checker.

**What happened.** Lean 4.33.1 was installed. `registry smoke lean_pack/prover`
returned **score 1.0**: a real proof, accepted by the real checker, in one attempt.
`sandbox.smoke lean_pack/prover` returned **score 0.0** with `exit_code 1` and:

```text
error: no default toolchain configured. run `elan default stable` to install
```

Same mode, same machine, same theorem, two answers.

**The cause.** `run_sandboxed` sets `HOME` to the run's working directory. That is
correct containment — code we did not write should not read a user's dotfiles — but
elan finds its toolchains through `HOME`, so the sandbox pointed the checker at
`<workdir>/.elan`, which is empty. Proven by isolating the variable: `lake env lean`
on a trivial file succeeds with the real `HOME` and fails with `HOME=<workdir>`, and
in the failing case it *creates* `<workdir>/.elan/settings.toml` as a side effect.

This is not a Lean bug. rustup, pyenv, nvm, gvm and sdkman all locate themselves
through `HOME`, so containment alone breaks every per-user toolchain manager, and the
failure is a wrong statement about the machine: "no default toolchain configured" on a
machine where the toolchain is installed and working.

**The fix, in the declaration.** The manifest already existed to answer "can this
package run here"; it now also carries what the tool needs *at run time*. `Tool`
gains `env`, a tuple of `(name, value)` pairs, and `toolchain.tool_env(package)`
collects them from the package's **present** tools. `sandbox.smoke` forwards them into
the run. `lean_pack` declares `ELAN_HOME`.

Three properties make it hold rather than paper over:

| property | why it is the right shape |
|---|---|
| the value is resolved where the declaration is read | package code cannot compute it — by the time an op runs, `HOME` is the working directory |
| absent tools contribute nothing | forwarding for a tool that is not installed adds environment a run cannot use |
| applied *after* containment, and still secret-filtered | `HOME` stays the working directory, and a declaration cannot smuggle a credential in |

**Held by.** Four tests. One drives the mechanism on a synthetic package, so it holds
on a machine without Lean. One asserts the same probe sees **no** `ELAN_HOME` without
forwarding — the half that makes the first mean something. One asserts the secret
filter still applies to a declaration. One runs `sandbox.smoke` on the real mode with
the real checker. Every one of them was checked against the unfixed code: disabling
forwarding reproduces `score 0.0` and the elan message, so none passes vacuously.

**A test that had to change, and why that is the finding rather than a nuisance.**
`test_a_declared_tool_that_is_missing_names_the_fix_when_required` asserted that
`preflight("lean_pack")` raises `ToolMissing`. It passed on a bare machine and failed
the moment the declared tool was actually installed — it had quietly asserted that
Lean is *not* here. It now asserts the conditional truth, and the mechanism is tested
against a synthetic absent tool. `test_the_lean_declaration_names_the_toolchain_home`
is machine-dependent by design and carries `@needs_lean`.

**Verified, finally.** The Lean path had never run. It has now: `verified: true`,
`attempts: 1`, strategy `omega`, `exit_code 0`, and the axiom audit reports
`[propext, Quot.sound]` — no `sorryAx`, so the `#print axioms` check that separates a
proof from a `sorry` is exercising real output rather than a stub's. The suite runs
**562 passed, 7 skipped with Lean** and **558 passed, 11 skipped without it**; both
were run, because CI has no Lean and this checkout now does.

**Still unverified.** mathlib is not installed, so the mathlib problem and its
`[[require]] path` remain untested. The core-library problem is the one that ran.

---

## 8. Two defects mathlib found, and the optimizer SRF ships that we did not run

Closing #30 left two things unverified and one thing unported. All three are the same
kind of gap: a claim that was true of the tests and not yet true of the code.

### `mathlib` was installed, and the problem it exists for did not run

The package declared mathlib, the tool probe reported it, and the mathlib problem had
**never been executed** — the tests skipped with a reason naming the missing path. So
mathlib was installed: a `mathlib4` checkout, `lake exe cache get`, 7.4 GB. The
problem then scored **0.0**, and the reason had nothing to do with mathlib.

**Defect one: the statement did not parse.**

```lean
theorem sum_odd_eq_sq (n : Nat) : ∑ i in Finset.range n, (2 * i + 1) = n ^ 2 := by
```

```text
error: unexpected token 'in'; expected ','
```

`∑ i in s, f i` is the form most introductions show. This Mathlib does not accept it:
Lean reads `∑ i` as an ordinary binder and then wants a comma. The form that compiles
is `∑ i ∈ s, f i`, alongside the explicit `s.sum (fun i => ...)`, which was checked
side by side in one file to be certain which of them was wrong.

Worth being exact about why nothing caught it. Every test of this mode used a **stub
checker**, and a stub accepts whatever it is handed. A syntax error in the statement
is invisible to a test that never parses the statement.

**Defect two: the timeout abandoned the checker, and a timeout reads like a refutation.**

`timeout_s` defaulted to 60s. The first invocation against mathlib pays for importing
the library, which took longer than 60s cold; the same proof then took 22s warm. So
the run reported `verified: false` for a theorem that is provable, on a machine where
it was about to be proved. The default is now 180s, with the reason recorded at the
knob: a fact that costs a run its score must clear the cost of starting.

**A third thing, found while reading the record it produced.** The run's
`lean_version` fact came from probing `lean` on the PATH, and the project's checker is
not that compiler: a project requiring mathlib takes a `lean-toolchain` from the
dependency, so `lake env lean` ran **4.34.0-rc2** while the PATH had **4.33.1**. The
record named a compiler that decided nothing. `scaffold_project` now asks the checker
in the project directory once, right after the project exists, and `result.json`
carries `checker_version` — the compiler that actually decided.

**Held by.** Three tests: one pins the `∈` form and the `BigOperators` preamble with
neither Lean nor mathlib installed, so the syntax cannot drift back; one pins the
timeout default against the cost of a large import; one runs the real problem and
requires `statement_ok == 1`, `verified == true`, no `sorryAx`, and a
`checker_version` in the durable record. The first two are ungated — they are the
regression guards. The third is gated on `MATHLIB_PATH` and **ran**, not skipped.

### SRF's own optimizer was vendored and never used

`srf/lab/map_elites.py` is not one of SRF's thirteen modes; it is an optimizer SRF
keeps beside them — a multi-emitter MAP-Elites over mode and knob space, whose
distinguishing property is that it keeps **one champion per cell of a feature grid**
rather than one best candidate overall. Nothing in this repository referenced it. The
thirteen modes were ported and this was not, so the count of "SRF ports" was complete
against a list that omitted it.

Ported on the loop's own vocabulary: features are graph size, whether the candidate
was reached by moving structure or only settings, and the step budget it spends; the
archive refuses a weaker candidate in an occupied niche and accepts one in an empty
niche; selection draws parents from across occupied niches.

**It was put in the wrong bucket, and the count papered over it.** It was added as a
fifteenth `OuterLoop`, and `SRF_LAB_PORT_COUNT = 1` existed to make the totals add up
around that placement. MAP-Elites is a search policy, not a control flow.

### The two buckets were not what the code said

`outerloop.py` says *"most research ideas live here [in the proposer]"*. The registry
disagreed: every SRF-derived name was an `OuterLoop`, and the `Optimizer` registry
held two hand-written entries and no port at all.

The cause was structural, and finding it is what made the fix possible. `Loop`
handed a proposer `select_parents(self.config.elite)` — the top few — and
`Candidate.describe()` carries a score and the edits that produced it but **not the
state**. A proposer therefore saw only the elite's states. Island selection, a niche
grid and a tournament over an archive all need candidates the loop was not handing
over, so those five could not have been proposers however they were filed.

**So the contract changed, not the filing.** The loop hands over the evaluated
population and the optimizer selects; `ProposalContext.elite` carries the count an
optimizer with no parent policy should take, so widening the pool does not silently
change what the existing two propose. Four of SRF's thirteen modes — `scs`, `evox`,
`openevolve`, `karpathy` — moved to `optim/policies.py` as proposers, and
`map_elites` joined them there.

**The split is asserted** rather than described: `13 - len(SRF_OPTIMIZER_PORTS)` is
the loop count, every optimizer port must be in the optimizer registry, no name may
be in both buckets, and every registered name must be one or the other.

**Two defects came out of doing it**, both found by the new tests rather than by
reasoning:

- `MapElitesSelector.features` read `state["nodes"]`, and the nodes are at
  `state["graph"]["nodes"]`. `.get` returns `None` rather than raising, so every
  candidate landed in one cell — a niche grid that is a single bucket and looks like
  it is working. Caught by a test that aims at a known-empty niche.
- `island_of` derived the island from `hash(candidate.id)`, and Python salts string
  hashing per process, so the same candidate sat in a different island on a resumed
  run than it did when it was evaluated. Inherited from the original `IslandArchive`;
  invisible until a run is resumed or a test is run twice. It uses a digest now.

**Held by.** `test_optimizer_policies.py` — one test per policy, each naming the
difference that is the reason it exists, plus the two defect regressions and a test
that the loop still hands over the population. On the standard §3 standard, an
optimizer with no parent policy is asserted to breed from the elite *by id*, because
that ordering is what the loop used before and getting it subtly wrong changed the
search enough to lose a refusal a layer early.

---

## 9. Half of a fix, closed as if it were whole (#36)

Worth recording because it is the same failure the rest of this document audits, made
while auditing.

**What was claimed.** Issue #36's acceptance criteria list seven things, the first
being *"`lowering` can emit `user` (and `agent`) gates; a mode can declare where it
wants one"*. The ledger, the transform, the seeding guard, the fidelity gate and the
inert-when-unused property were all built and tested. The gates were not, and the
issue was closed with "landed in …" above a list that read as complete.

**What the code said.** `lowering.py` hardcoded `evaluator_type="fn"`, and `nn.Node`
had no gate kind at all. **A mode could not declare a pause point**, which is the
mechanism the whole steering design rests on: an intent ledger nobody can be asked
about is a file.

**The fix.** `Node.gate_kind` — `fn`, `user`, or `agent` — with three rules that make
the choice real rather than decorative:

- `fn` requires an evaluator, and the other two **refuse** one, because a gate with
  two answerers has an answer that depends on the runtime.
- `lowering` emits the declared kind and emits a command **only** for `fn`.
- A walker that meets a `user` gate **refuses**, naming the node, rather than
  inventing a verdict. A run that pauses cannot quietly decide for the person; an
  invented verdict is indistinguishable from one they gave. The answer arrives through
  explicit `RunContext.verdicts` standing authorization, or a one-use ledger
  decision scoped to the current review inputs. Interactive answers are consumed;
  a later gate visit asks again rather than replaying historical approval.

**And a second defect, found by an existing test rather than by this work.** The first
version of `Node.to_state` serialized `gate_kind` unconditionally, which changed
**every mode's state dict** — and therefore every candidate id the loop has ever
recorded, so a resumed run would no longer match itself and the search moved for
reasons that had nothing to do with the search. `test_no_batch_slot_is_silently_lost`
caught it as a vanished batch slot. A field at its default is now omitted.

**Held by.** Six tests: a mode can declare a person-answered gate and it reaches the
IR; a headless walk refuses one; a supplied verdict lets it proceed; an unknown
verdict is still refused; a gate cannot have two answerers; and the default is not
serialized. Verified both ways — restoring the hardcoded `fn` fails the first.

---

## Two probes that came back clean

Recorded because the point of an audit is accuracy in both directions.

- **`#16`, str knobs.** Probed by sampling a str knob 300 times through
  `edits.random_edit`, and by reading `Loop._other_value`. Both route through one
  `Knob.sample`, and the docstring says why: *"One sampler for the whole system, so
  the starting sweep and the random optimizer agree about what is reachable."* A str
  knob with declared values samples among them; one without gets `STR_MUTATIONS`.
  Implemented.
- **`#25`, path-aware metric integrity.** `nn.fact_produced`'s docstring and body
  both require the producer to lie on a `start → terminal` path. Implemented. (A
  first probe of mine was inconclusive — the off-path node I built was caught by
  `V2` for being unreachable, which is a different rule — and the probe was the
  thing that was wrong.)

---

## What this does not cover

- Listing a generated package still imports it (§1).
- The reflective/curriculum differences need a model proposer to show (§3).
- `post_checks` and fork/join are unused (§5).
- The GUI is not audited here at all. Its defects were tracked as issues #60–#73, and the panel's behaviour is held by `packages/client/ui-refactory/tests/` and [tutorial 7](tutorials/07-pick-and-watch-from-the-panel.md).

Two things that were on this list have moved off it, which is the point of keeping it:

- **mathlib is no longer untested.** It was installed and the mathlib problem ran, and
  doing so found two defects that no stub could have found (§8). The mathlib tests are
  gated on `MATHLIB_PATH`: they run where mathlib is present and skip with the reason
  where it is not, so a CI machine without it is honest rather than green by omission.
- **SRF's own optimizer is no longer unused.** `map_elites` is ported, counted
  separately from the thirteen modes, and asserted by name (§8).

refactory/docs/interfaces.md.text:
# Terminal and GUI

Both interfaces use the same mode catalogue and run artifacts. The terminal is useful for repeatable commands; GUI chat is useful for conversation and node-by-node control; the Modes panel exposes full search profiles, worker routing and shared resource settings.

## Pick the right surface

| Action | Terminal | GUI |
|---|---|---|
| Create, Edit, Design | `refactory ceo` with the authoring mode | CEO chat for stepwise control; select a full/fast mode and **Run once** for execution |
| Run an existing mode interactively | `refactory ceo package/mode` | CEO chat for stepwise control; **Run once** for execution |
| Configure and start optimization | `refactory optimize` | CEO chat can launch a saved profile through Refactory tools; Modes → **Optimize**: saved profile or explicit controls → **Preview launch contract** → **Start optimization** |
| Inspect an existing run | `status --follow`, `artifacts`, `comparison`, `candidate` | **Runs and pending questions** or **Existing run directory → Read this run**; live activity and Steering |
| Add instructions or answer gates | Conversation and `refactory steer` | Chat and the attached run's Steering controls |
| Keep/reject candidates, pause/resume, adopt | `refactory steer`, `refactory adopt` | Optimizer controls in Steering |

**Optimize → Start optimization** searches scored modes. **Run once** also runs enabled authoring modes, including `create_fast`, `edit_fast` and `design_fast`; supply their required knobs first. Each CEO session owns one open workflow at a time. Use a separate session and distinct work directory for another concurrent workflow; opening a viewer never claims ownership of the run.

For chat-driven optimization, name the scored mode and saved profile/version, ask
the CEO to launch it, inspect the completed search, adopt the exact winner and
smoke the adopted mode. Chat and panel have separate
[actual-use evidence](release-validation-20260926.md#gui-chat-optimization-follow-up);
selecting a model or optimizer alone does not prove that it ran.

## What runs the graph

The CEO calls `wf_open` and advances with `wf_next`. The runtime executes deterministic operations and function gates, tracks the cursor and routes branches. Agent nodes are delegated to coding/research workers. A user-owned gate asks the user.

While driving a graph, the CEO's direct coding and skill tools are disabled. A correction can change a node's prompt with `wf_edit`, then rerun it with `wf_redo`; the execution records the change and invalidation. Workers may use skills as supporting instructions, but skills are not the mode execution mechanism.

The same mode can run through the Python walker for evaluation. Agent nodes there use the configured model client; an agent completion can include multiple tool calls and model turns.

## Authoring evidence and comparison

Terminal CEO, Python/headless adapters, native chat and the panel use the same graph operations. Create/Edit stage the package, execute canonical smoke and route repairable failures back to the coder before review. Design runs its acceptance command before review. Full modes keep independent health, code, adversarial QA and Overwatch; fast modes retain one focused QA worker.

In Edit, the panel's **allow_regression** knob and chat's `allowRegression` option mean “skip original-mode execution and score comparison.” CEO uses `--knob allow_regression=true`; the direct Edit command uses `--allow-regression`. All default to false. Revised-mode correctness checks still run. `revision_note` explains an intentional skip, `before_score` and `regressed` remain null, and `after_score` records only the revised measurement. Historical reports remain readable.

Inspect `authoring-evidence.json`, `intent-audit.json`, `smoke.json` and `revision.json` in the exact run directory. A listed package is staging, not proof of completion. Missing evidence blocks success; changed source or later intent makes old review stale. [Developer contract and graphs](authoring-validation.md).

## Steering is precise about timing

- A note is persisted context. Delivery to a node is not proof of semantic compliance by its output.
- A deterministic operation consumes its declared inputs and knobs; a prose note does not rewrite it.
- The interactive CEO can honor a requested node boundary and apply explicit prompt changes. Changes do not retroactively alter completed work.
- Optimizer pause/resume/stop and population changes apply at generation boundaries. They may wait for an active model call or evaluation.
- A finished search has no next boundary. Its live controls are disabled/refused; explicit adoption can still apply immediately when the winner has the required audit.

Use the exact directory returned by the run, including for runs opened in chat. Do not infer an id from a mode name.

## Configure a launch

CLI and GUI share the same resolved configuration: strategy, optimizer, evaluator, starting/frozen knobs, permitted edits, epochs, batch size, candidate cap, retained parents, proposal attempts, seed, holdout and parsimony. The panel also exposes bounded repeats, resource limits/reserves, backend/provider/model/effort and role/node routing. Capability-aware controls disable unsupported external-backend options. See [profiles](optimization-profiles.md), [resources and fast modes](budgets-fast-modes.md) and [worker routing](models.md).

New workers select **Skip permission checks (default)**. This grants the tools OS-account access, including full DSH/Codex native sandbox bypass. Choose **Native permission policy** or CLI `--permission-mode default` to retain backend checks. Saved profiles and runs retain their effective policies.

A named profile version is reusable. A historical run's `resolved-profile.json` records the exact settings and contract it used. Save objective or required-artifact changes as a new version; preview again after changing launch settings. Task definitions, scoring and invariants remain owned by the mode.

Candidate counts do not substitute for time or token budgets. Repeated measurements and final validation consume the shared allocation. Candidate comparison keeps failed/unmeasured outcomes visible and reports unavailable cost/usage without inventing zero. Adoption keeps the exact eligible winner and its audit.

## Follow activity and questions

`refactory status --run RUN_DIR --follow` and the attached native panel read durable state and activity. The panel shows current/completed nodes, worker status and observed routes, usage, wait reasons, instruction-delivery receipts and output/check evidence. **Runs and pending questions** helps discover a gate waiting in another saved run. No estimated completion percentage is inferred.

Select a run to read its pending question and allowed verdicts. An answer is scoped to that run and invocation; a queued note or control is not proof that a worker consumed it. Reopening the view reconnects observation without starting work. See [live control and recovery](live-control.md) for timing, correction and ownership rules.

## Recovery and output

Pause/resume/stop controls apply at the owning graph or optimizer boundary; an in-flight worker may need to settle first. To correct a completed graph node, preview its affected results, then explicitly confirm the recorded revision. Prior evidence is archived and dependent results invalidated before rerun.

For a stopped graph owner, attach its saved run and press **resume**, or use `refactory graph-control resume --run RUN_DIR`. Both public paths have passed bounded acceptance: completed work, run identity and resource consumption are retained. Recovery is explicit and limited to a verified saved boundary. An unknown worker outcome, changed inputs/outputs or changed prepared configuration prevents automatic continuation. Reopening a mode can create a new invocation and archive outputs; it is not generic recovery. Native worker sessions are not resumed by this bridge. [Recovery details](live-control.md#recover-a-known-boundary) · [Work-directory lifecycle](tutorials/06-run-it-with-a-person.md#reusing-a-work-directory).

Created/adopted packages live in `.factory/packages/`, Design artifacts in `.factory/artifacts/`, and execution receipts in the selected run directory. A report's exact paths are authoritative. Task item results, aggregate score, execution completion and artifact quality are separate facts. Fast authoring, profiles, live control/recovery and worker routing have completed bounded CLI/GUI acceptance; see [validation status](../../README.md#release-capabilities-and-validation).


## Panel presentation

The Modes panel uses Refactory’s original two-gear identity and blue theme in both color schemes. **Configure a run**, **Activity & results**, **Graph controls** and **Steering** separate setup, observation and actions. Run and Optimize have separate launch actions while sharing inputs and the watched run. Help buttons explain fields, and clicking brief opens a large draft editor with Apply/Cancel. Advanced settings and package management expand without discarding inputs. A pending-question banner links to the available answers. Narrow and split panels stack the same controls; expanded panels place configuration beside activity.

The [panel guide](tutorials/07-pick-and-watch-from-the-panel.md#find-the-controls) describes navigation. [Presentation acceptance](panel-validation-20260927.md) and the [UX follow-up](panel-ux-validation-20260927.md) record native screenshots and bounded checks. [Upstream compatibility](upstream-compatibility.md) documents the published DSH dependency and pre-existing patch boundary.

## Project defaults and discovery

[Worker routing](worker-routing.md) documents `refactory.workers.json`, coder-only
selection and precedence. [Live help and docs](discovery.md) provide current-build
read-only discovery in chat and the terminal without source inspection.

refactory/docs/live-control.md.text:
# Live activity, control and recovery

A run directory is the durable identity shared by the terminal, native panel and owning runtime. Attach a viewer using the exact returned directory. Opening, closing or reconnecting a viewer does not execute work or cancel the run.

## Read live work

```bash
uv run refactory status --run /absolute/run --follow
uv run refactory runs
uv run refactory steer --run /absolute/run
```

The native Modes panel offers **Runs and pending questions** and **Existing run directory → Read this run**. Attached views stream persisted changes. Activity includes due/completed nodes, last event time, wait reason, worker receipts, requested and observed routes, available usage, instruction-delivery state and recorded outputs. No completion percentage is estimated from elapsed time. A missing observation remains unavailable.

Graph activity is appended to `.refactory/events.jsonl`; checkpoints, worker receipts and the resource ledger live beside it. Historical runs may lack newer records. An interrupted journal write is reported as a gap rather than fabricated progress. A worker context being prepared, a dispatch being observed, and an output satisfying a correction are different facts.

## Questions and ownership

Pending user gates retain their prompt and accepted verdicts. Select the run in the native panel and answer its waiting gate, use the owning CEO session, or record an explicit verdict:

```bash
uv run refactory steer --run /absolute/run --verdict gate_name=proceed
```

The allowed verdict comes from that gate. The answer is scoped to the run and invocation, not to whichever chat is visible. Reading or answering a persisted question does not grant a second session permission to drive the graph. Each CEO session owns its workflow; concurrent runs need distinct work directories. A native question left pending after a disconnect stays pending until a valid answer reaches the owner. A restarted owner must pass the recovery checks below.

## Apply a control at its boundary

Optimizer notes, keep/reject and pause/resume/stop apply at generation boundaries. Graph controls apply at the next graph boundary and can wait for admitted work to settle. External workers accept new instructions at a subsequent node boundary, not as an in-flight prompt edit. A queued control receipt is a request, not confirmation of application.

The native panel's **Graph controls** offers pause/resume/stop. The console exposes the same operations:

```bash
uv run refactory graph-control pause --run /absolute/run
uv run refactory graph-control resume --run /absolute/run
uv run refactory graph-control stop --run /absolute/run
```

Process cancellation is separate: `refactory stop --run RUN_DIR` requests interruption of its recorded owned process. Inspect the receipt and subsequent activity for confirmation; sending a signal is not proof that every worker terminated. Stopping a reader does not issue either kind of stop.

To change completed work, choose a completed node and prompt correction, press **Preview affected results**, inspect the invalidated nodes, then **Confirm correction and rerun**. The console equivalent is `graph-control preview --node NODE`, followed by `graph-control rerun --node NODE --text "CORRECTION" --revision REVISION` with the returned revision and the same `--run`. The owner refuses a stale preview. Prior evidence is archived and dependent results invalidated before execution; a note alone does not silently rewrite completed work. Unsafe replay plans, including unsettled concurrent work, are refused.

## Recover a known boundary

A live owner's resume control releases its boundary pause. If the old graph owner is gone, explicit resume can start a fresh owned process from the saved checkpoint. It preserves the run identity, completed work, route configuration and consumed resources. Larger resource limits are explicit allocations, not a reset of usage. The interactive entry point also accepts:

```bash
uv run python -m refactory_dsh.interactive package/mode \
  --workdir /absolute/run --headless --resume
```

Recovery requires a recognized checkpoint, a stopped owner, matching prepared configuration and unchanged fingerprinted inputs/outputs. It refuses a pending dispatched worker with unknown outcome or a failed/unknown last-node outcome. In-flight external product sessions are not resumed. Python executor partial-fork recovery is also refused because successful sibling facts cannot yet be restored safely.

Inspect side effects and outputs when continuation is refused. Use explicit invalidation where a valid replay plan exists, or start a new run deliberately. Reopening the mode is not an implicit retry. No mechanism here can infer whether an unacknowledged external side effect happened before a crash.

Release checks exercised live CLI observation and native gate answers, pause/resume, reviewed replay and owned stop. Separate registered dead-owner recovery checks passed through public CLI resume and the native Resume control, preserving completed artifacts, saved configuration and accumulated resources while executing only the remaining node. An unavailable-provider guard prevented model execution. See the [validation record](release-validation-20260926.md).

[Profiles and candidate evidence](optimization-profiles.md) · [Fast modes and resource recovery](budgets-fast-modes.md) · [Worker capabilities](models.md#model-provider-versus-coding-agent)
