refactory/docs/models.md.text:
# Models

DSH is the default coding worker. Configure its model routes in `~/.dsh/settings.yaml` or **Settings → Models**. The Modes panel exposes **Worker routing and shared resources** for Run once and saved optimization profiles. Supported entry points accept `--model` and `--provider` overrides without changing saved settings. The table below explains which execution paths receive those overrides.

## Where the list comes from

The adapter's catalogue is **advisory**: it is what pickers offer, not what the route accepts. The DeepSeek route ships `deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro` and `deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp`, and it will send any id you name — so a model that is not listed still works, it just is not offered. The settings document is hot-reloaded: nothing needs a restart.

## In the GUI

**Settings → Models.** Add a provider, paste its API key, optionally a base URL, and list the models — or press **Fetch available models** and pick from what the provider reports. **Add a custom provider** takes an id, a display name, one of three wire protocols (`openai-completions`, `openai-responses`, `anthropic-messages`) and a base URL, which is how a local server (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM) is reached. The page writes the settings document and the credential store for you; the composer's model picker then offers the new models.

## In the terminal

The same file, by hand:

```yaml
# ~/.dsh/settings.yaml
agent-default-model:
  provider: deepseek-official
  model: deepseek-v4-pro          # the default for every run that names none

llm-pi-ai:
  providers:
    openai:
      apiKeyEnv: OPENAI_API_KEY   # the *name* of the variable, never the key
    anthropic:
      apiKeyEnv: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
      models:
        - id: claude-sonnet-4-5
          contextWindow: 200000
    ollama:                       # a local OpenAI-compatible server
      displayName: Ollama
      api: openai-completions
      baseURL: http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1
      models:
        - id: qwen3-coder
          contextWindow: 262144
```

Keys are read from the environment (`DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, …, including a `.env` at the checkout root) or from the managed store at `~/.dsh/.credentials.yaml` that the Models page writes. A `llm-deepseek:` section overrides the direct DeepSeek route the same way: `models:`, `baseURL:`, `apiKeyEnv:`, `thinking:`, `reasoningEffort:`.

A local OpenAI-compatible server works through the same route, and still needs *a* key — pi-ai's OpenAI protocol asks for one, so name a dummy variable and export any value (`apiKeyEnv: LOCAL_TEST_KEY`, then `LOCAL_TEST_KEY=dummy`), or set an `Authorization` header.

## Choose a model for a run

```bash
uv run refactory ceo counting_pack/fixed_step --model deepseek-v4-pro
uv run refactory ceo "an idea" --mode create --single --model deepseek-v4-pro
uv run refactory optimize circle_packing/adaptive --provider deepseek-official --model deepseek-v4-pro
```

`--model` names the id and `--provider` the route; both fall back to `agent-default-model` in your settings, and neither writes anything back, so choosing a model for one run does not change the next. A route that does not exist is a loud failure (`NO_ADAPTER: no adapter registered for provider …`), not a quiet return to the default. The same two flags exist one level down, on `dsh --profile headless|graph`, which is what `refactory` calls.

## Model selection across execution paths

| Path | Where its model comes from |
|---|---|
| Terminal `ceo` | The selected graph-runtime provider/model, or saved defaults |
| Python Create/Edit/Design agent nodes | The supplied `DshModelClient`; its route/context is carried to supported nested validation |
| Optimization with the default `walker` evaluator | The supplied model client serves the reasoning proposer and evaluated agent nodes |
| Optimization with the separate `dsh` evaluator | The supplied client context is forwarded; explicit agent workers are dispatched through the same node bridge and route as the walker |
| GUI CEO and children | The owning session and worker configuration; inspect actual child execution when validating a route |

`refactory runtime` inspects configuration; `.refactory/workers/*.json` receipts establish the selected backend, observed runtime route, version and usage. Requested settings are separate from observed settings. Explicit `node_routes` override `role_routes`, which override the run settings; empty fields use the runtime defaults. Switching backend clears inherited provider/model/effort unless the override supplies them. A provider route declared in one DSH profile's settings is invisible to the nested headless runtime a DSH worker runs; declare such routes for workers with [`provider_config`](worker-routing.md) in `refactory.workers.json`.

A random seed does not make model outputs deterministic. Changing provider/model can change tool use, latency, cost and output quality; support for a protocol is not a performance guarantee.

## Model provider versus coding agent

DSH remains the default coding-agent runtime. It supplies the tool loop, sessions, delegation and working context; an OpenAI or Anthropic model can answer through its provider adapters. Choosing an OpenAI model does not switch the worker to Codex, and choosing a Claude model does not launch Claude Code.

Select `--worker-backend codex` or `--worker-backend claude_code` explicitly for an external node worker; `--worker-backend dsh` returns to DSH. The optional dependencies reuse DSH's named-provider registry, Codex app-server and Claude Agent SDK. They are dormant until selected and can be omitted from an installation that uses only DSH. A missing selected provider fails before execution. Native product settings and authentication remain authoritative; DSH credentials are not copied to either product.

For example, the direct interactive interface accepts:

```bash
python -m refactory_dsh.interactive counting_pack/fixed_step --worker-backend codex --model YOUR_CODEX_MODEL --headless
```

Refactory dispatches only the agent node's self-contained task, retains its declared outputs and runs graph-owned checks. The worker never owns graph order, user gates or scoring.

Each node worker receives its node identity, exact working directory, absolute
input/output paths and selected Python interpreter alongside the task and current
instructions. It uses the supplied API/reference context, performs that node's
required checks, writes its outputs and returns a brief completion response.
Delivery receipts and downstream graph operations remain runtime-owned; workers
are instructed not to rediscover that protocol from adjacent run histories or
repeat later stages. This orientation is active in both the Python executor and
native workflow path; it is guidance, not proof that a worker followed it.

New workers default to `--permission-mode skip` in the CLI, API and **Worker permission mode** control. This grants workers the access available to the OS account: DSH uses `danger-full-access` with approval policy `never`; Codex uses `dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`; Claude Code uses `bypassPermissions`. The setting applies to each launched runtime and does not change personal product settings. Use this mode only for tasks and inputs you trust.

Choose `--permission-mode default` (**Native permission policy** in the GUI) to retain the backend's native policy, which may deny file creation. Existing saved runs and profiles preserve their permission settings; historical snapshots without a recorded policy keep the native default. A backend switch resets an inherited backend-specific policy to `skip`. Codex also accepts `never`, `approve-for-me` and its full bypass name. Claude Code also accepts `dontAsk`, `acceptEdits`, `auto`, `plan` and `bypassPermissions`. Unsupported route combinations and permissions fail before launch. External per-call provider and reasoning-effort overrides are unsupported; select those through the product's native configuration. `--effort` is supported for DSH nodes.

| Adapter capability | DSH node | Codex node | Claude Code node |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model selection | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Cancellation/deadline | Owned runtime shutdown | Owned runtime shutdown | Owned runtime shutdown |
| Steering | Next node boundary | Next node boundary | Next node boundary |
| Resume in-flight worker / images / human questions | Not exposed by this one-shot bridge | Unsupported | Unsupported |
| Observed route | DSH model request | Native thread startup and reroute events | Native SDK initialization and observed model list |
| Token reporting | Measured request totals, including nested DSH agents | Measured native thread totals; nested coverage not established | Estimated SDK query totals, including Task workers; excludes helper calls outside that pipeline |

External workers refuse token-limited launches because complete nested accounting is not established. They support elapsed limits. Missing usage stays unavailable, never measured zero. Codex/Claude product sessions are ephemeral: receipts retain their identity for provenance, but never offer resume. A failed or cancelled worker is not automatically replayed. New instructions are delivered at an explicitly chosen node boundary; an already executing external worker cannot receive an in-flight edit. The native panel disables unsupported provider/effort/token controls for external backends and displays these limits. Switching backend clears incompatible inherited values; explicit unsupported overrides still fail validation.

Observe-only patches on the pinned DSH providers emit whitelisted route/usage metadata through Cordis. They do not copy raw protocol traffic, prompts, commands, paths, reasoning or credentials into the parent conversation. The protocol and product lifecycle remain owned by the existing provider bundles. Official integration contracts: [Codex App Server](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app-server), [Codex SDK](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex-sdk), [Claude Agent SDK](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview).

Worker receipts also feed [live activity](live-control.md); saved [profiles](optimization-profiles.md) retain requested routes in their exact launch snapshot. Configuration readiness is not execution evidence. DSH completed the bounded CLI and native GUI task. Codex and Claude Code completed the CLI task with explicit edit permissions and the native GUI task with the new `skip` default. Earlier native-policy failures remain documented as permission controls; see the [validation record](release-validation-20260926.md).

## Credentials for nested execution

Create/edit smoke and panel optimization launch further DSH processes. Their environment
is deliberately scrubbed, and the smoke process has a workspace-local `HOME`. Save the
provider key once through **Settings → Models** in the DSH home used by the run:
open the provider row with **Edit**, enter its **API key**, and choose **Apply**. The
product passes that nonsecret home location to nested model processes; keys remain in
DSH's managed store and are resolved by its credential service. Do not copy `.env`
files into generated packages or smoke directories. If an exported key shadows the
reference, the UI reports “Provided by the launch environment (read-only)”; launch
without that override before saving. DSH resolves keys in this order: inherited launch
environment, managed store, invocation-directory `.env`, then DSH-home `.env`. A stored
key overrides both `.env` layers, but not an inherited environment override. The launch
environment is a startup snapshot; changing the launching shell afterward does not
change the running GUI's credential source.

`refactory doctor --provider deepseek-official --model deepseek-flash` checks local
credential configuration through the same scrubbed subprocess boundary as smoke. Create
and edit perform this check before research. The check makes no model request: a
configured key is not proof of valid authentication, available quota, or network access.
The later real model smoke remains required. Provider-native authentication without an
API-key reference is reported as `native-auth-unverified`, not as a verified credential.

The local diagnostic uses the installed headless profile's supported file-backed
credential/settings services and adapter schemas. A replaced service or dynamic `!!js`
configuration, an external `DSH_CLI`, or a source-checkout launcher is reported as
`diagnostic-unavailable`: the doctor prints **WARN** and authoring continues with an
explicit unverified-readiness warning. The actual selected runtime performs its normal
checks. Confirmed missing references and malformed known credential/settings configuration
still stop authoring before research. The diagnostic never guesses a credential location.
DSH's normal profile loader may initialize a missing shipped headless profile; the check
makes no model request and does not write credential values. The local managed store is owner-only but does not
isolate credentials from generated code running as the same OS user; stricter isolation
requires a separate model-service boundary.

For a DSH source checkout, set `DSH_ROOT` to its root after installing its dependencies.
The source launcher resolves `tsx` and the checkout's TypeScript configuration there;
agent processes still run in their item directories. `DSH_CLI` continues to select an
external executable directly. A custom/source runtime must support the flags supplied
to it: upstream headless profiles without this fork's `--provider`/`--model` extension
can select their route through the profile's `agent-default-model` configuration.

## Inspect context before an interactive workflow

The CEO can use the existing `refactory` tool with `action: "runtime"` before `wf_open`. It reads the current session selection and the host-owned DSH home, then uses the same nested credential diagnostic as create/edit. It never asks you to copy credentials into a run or change a configured home. Missing and invalid configuration are reported as such; unsupported diagnostics stay unverified. Current-session reasoning effort is shown separately because credential readiness does not prove nested reasoning selection.

From the terminal, `refactory runtime` reports nested defaults as JSON; `--provider` and `--model` inspect an explicit route without changing settings. There is no current CEO session in that CLI call. The diagnostic does not authenticate or launch a mode. As with doctor, the normal DSH loader may initialize a missing shipped headless profile, but it does not write credentials.

## Completion deadlines and interruption

Worker contexts retain the selected Python environment (`VENV_BIN`, defaulting to
the checkout's `.venv/bin`). Tool commands receive it first on `PATH` and receive
the installed Refactory API on `PYTHONPATH`, even when their working directory is
a run's artifact directory. DSH's normal credential scrub still applies to child
processes; selecting a Python environment does not forward credential variables.

Token-limited DSH runs require the shipped in-process `spawn` and `fork` provider
composition. An additional named provider with unverified nested telemetry is
refused before a model request. Without a token limit, native descendants may run,
but their observations remain separate from the DSH parent's route: known DSH
tokens stay visible and total usage is explicitly unavailable. A completed DSH
request without valid usage likewise prevents claiming a measured total.

A `DshModelClient` deadline fails the completion without replaying its prompt: the
agent may already have written files or started tool work. Explicit transport
failures retain their bounded retry policy. On POSIX, a deadline or caller
`KeyboardInterrupt` raised in the thread calling `complete()` sends one SIGTERM
to the selected CLI and allows ten seconds for shutdown. The Python walker's
concurrent fork also owns a cooperative cancellation scope: a main-thread
interrupt stops queued branches and asks active shipped DSH clients to shut down
before propagating that original interruption. Cancelled branches are recorded at
the fork, without merging their facts or acknowledging its join. Each fork binds
an independent client copy; cancellation does not change the original client or
other runs. Completion polling retains one absolute deadline and accumulated
output, and cancellation also stops retry launches and backoff waits. The shipped CLI disposes its context and managed subprocesses,
including ordinary tool jobs launched in separate process groups. A separate CLI
session prevents terminal Ctrl-C from also delivering a second shutdown signal.
Valid work that finishes inside the deadline follows normal CLI disposal.

This is runtime-owned cleanup, not a scan or kill of process names. A runtime that
does not settle within the grace is forced to exit; the error says child cleanup
is unconfirmed and no retry follows. Custom launchers must implement their own
shutdown, and Windows termination does not provide the POSIX graceful signal
path. The local provider's macOS process-group fallback cannot contain arbitrary
descendants that escape its managed range. Python SIGKILL, abrupt parent death,
still need external supervision. Default process-wide SIGTERM now unwinds the owned Python model subprocess before exit.
Arbitrary in-flight Python operations are awaited, not forcibly interrupted;
custom model clients retain caller-thread serial execution and their own cleanup
contract. The client does not undo files written before failure or certify their reuse.

## Project defaults and discovery

[Worker routing](worker-routing.md) documents `refactory.workers.json`, coder-only
selection and precedence. [Live help and docs](discovery.md) provide current-build
read-only discovery in chat and the terminal without source inspection.

# Optimization profiles

A profile is a named, immutable version of search settings and the user's objective. A run writes its exact resolved settings, source identity, input fingerprints and validation contract to `resolved-profile.json`; changing the reusable profile later does not edit that run.

```sh
refactory profile-save --name small-search --spec '{"settings":{"optimizer":"random","edit_preset":"knob_only","epochs":1,"batch_size":2,"max_evaluations":2,"repeats":2,"max_elapsed_s":30,"validation_reserve_s":3},"contract":{"objective":"Compare a bounded pair of candidates","required_artifacts":[]}}'
refactory profiles
refactory profile-resolve circle_packing/adaptive --profile small-search --profile-version 1
refactory optimize circle_packing/adaptive --profile small-search --profile-version 1 --runs-root .factory/profile-demo
refactory comparison --run .factory/profile-demo
refactory adopt --run .factory/profile-demo --as profile_winner
refactory package smoke profile_winner/adaptive
```

Saving the same name creates a new version. CLI overrides are explicit and appear in the resolved snapshot. Profiles support the existing strategy, optimizer and evaluator; starting/frozen knobs, edit preset and a narrower allowed-operation list; epochs, batch size, evaluation cap, retained parents, proposal attempts, seed, holdout and parsimony; repeats, shared resources and worker/model routing. `refactory optimize --help` lists every option.

In the native Refactory panel, select a scored mode and expand **Optimization profiles and full search controls**. Select a saved version or edit controls and save a new version. The mode's existing knob fields choose starting values. **Preview launch contract** uses the same resolver as the CLI and launch service. Save objective or additional-artifact changes before launching. Existing live notes, candidate keep/reject, pause/resume/stop, explicit adoption and using the adopted mode once remain available.

**Candidate changes, measurements and validation** includes successful, failed and unmeasured states. Expand a candidate to inspect its lineage, graph/prompt/knob diff, raw and adjusted score, real trial count/variation, required-artifact outcome and duration. Missing token/cost telemetry is unavailable, never zero. Held-out winner validation is separate from training and never enters proposal context. The mode still owns Task definitions, scoring code and invariants; a profile cannot redefine them.

By default `repeats=1`. Opt in to 2–10 independent measurements per candidate and winner audit. Trials consume shared resources, including final validation. One failed or incomplete trial makes that candidate ineligible; its partial measurements remain visible. Ranking maximizes the mean validated score minus `parsimony × node count`. Cost and latency are descriptive rather than hidden selection advantages. A larger observed mean is not statistical proof; finding no improvement is a valid result.

Adoption records the exact winning state, profile snapshot and held-out audit in its provenance. Historical configurations without profiles remain readable. Profiles apply to scored modes, including generated Create/Edit packages; standalone Design artifacts have no separate optimizer.

See [shared budgets and fast modes](budgets-fast-modes.md), [model and worker routing](models.md), and [live controls and recovery](live-control.md) for the resource, execution and continuation contracts used by these settings.

# Packing a tool that is not Python

Audience: someone writing a package of modes whose work cannot be done in Python.
Every command below was run against this checkout, and the output shown is the
output it produced.

The library assumes a tool is a callable. An op is a function of the run context,
the validator resolves a node's `call` to a real object, and a package lists the
modules its modes call. Lean is not a callable. It is a proof checker with its own
file syntax, a build tool that gives a per-problem project a library path, and — for
anything past the prelude — a checkout of mathlib that the project names as a
dependency. `sympy_pack` is the same question in miniature: one importable module
that may or may not be installed.

`refactory_packages/lean_pack` and `refactory_packages/sympy_pack` are the worked
answers. They exist as a pair on purpose: one needs a toolchain, the other needs a
Python module, and a reviewer should be able to check that the *same* mechanism
handles both.

## The declaration lives in its own file

A package that needs something from the machine puts a `tools.py` beside its
`__init__.py` and assigns `TOOLS` to a tuple of `Tool`:

```python
from refactory_dsh.toolchain import Tool

TOOLS = (
    Tool(
        name="sympy",
        kind="python",
        probe="sympy",
        install=".venv/bin/pip install sympy",
        why="the exact algebra engine that decides whether a conjectured closed form is the right one",
    ),
)
```

A `Tool` has three required parts beyond its name — `probe`, `install` and `why` —
and `Tool.__post_init__` refuses a declaration that omits any of them. A declaration
that can say "absent" and nothing else is the failure this exists to replace, so it
is not a declaration the library accepts. `kind` is one of `binary` (a command on
`PATH`), `python` (an importable module) or `path` (a directory that must exist, where
`$NAME` expands from the environment). `optional=True` marks a tool only some of the
package's modes need.

`Package` gains no field for any of this, and the reason is not taste. Every field on
`Package` is validated by `Package.__post_init__` as a property of the package, and
whether Lean is installed is a property of the *machine*: it changes without the
package changing, and putting it on the manifest would mix a host fact into a value
the registry compares, copies for provenance and describes to a GUI. A separate file
also lets the registry read the requirement **before** the package is imported,
which is the case that matters. The usual way a missing tool announces itself is an
`ImportError` raised while importing the package's own ops, and the registry reports
that as `cannot import package sympy_pack: No module named 'sympy'` — a message
naming the symptom rather than the fix, and a false accusation whenever the package
is fine and the machine is not. `refactory_dsh/toolchain.py:read_tools` therefore
loads `tools.py` by path and never executes the package. A declaration may not use
relative imports for the same reason it may not import its own package: it has to be
readable when nothing else about the package is.

There is already a `tools` field on `Node`, and it is not this one. In the lowered IR
it is the agent's tool allowlist, which is a fact about what a model call may do
during a run. A package's requirement is a fact about the machine before the run
starts. Two unrelated facts behind one name is worse than two names.

## A declaration, not a cordis plugin

DSH composes capabilities as plugins, and a Lean capability would be one there:
something has to put a proof checker in front of the model, and that belongs in
`cordis.yml`. That seam answers *what can the running agent do*, and it is decided by
whoever writes the composition file. A package cannot reach it — the registry
discovers packages by scanning a directory, and the library is not allowed to know
any package by name — and it answers a different, earlier question: *can this
package's ops run on this machine at all?* That has to be answerable statically, by a
reader that is only reading, before any budget is spent. The two compose rather than
compete: the plugin gives the agent a Lean tool, and the declaration gives the package
a way to refuse to start without one.

## What verification does, and when

Three readers, one answer each, all of them static:

```bash
uv run python -c "
from refactory_dsh import toolchain
for status in toolchain.report('lean_pack'):
    print(status)
"
```

```text
lean: not on PATH as 'lean'
lake: not on PATH as 'lake'
mathlib: missing: MATHLIB_PATH is not set, so $MATHLIB_PATH names nothing
```

`uv run refactory package tools lean_pack` is the same answer as
JSON, with a `fix` field per entry holding the sentence the failure is built from:
`the tool 'lean' is not on PATH as 'lean'; the proof checker that decides whether a
candidate solution is a proof. Install it with: curl https://elan.lean-lang.org/elan-init.sh -sSf | sh`.

`refactory_dsh.toolchain.check` probes every declared tool, `report` does the same
per package, `preflight` refuses over the *required* tools that are missing, and
`require` answers for one tool and raises `ToolMissing` with the fix in the message.
`registry.tool_report` and the `tools` verb above are the same answer through the
registry, because the registry is what users already ask what a package is.

A missing tool is deliberately **not** a finding of `registry verify`. That command
answers "is this package well formed", and a package whose tool is absent is well
formed, listable and runnable-in-principle — reporting it there would make "this
checkout has no Lean" indistinguishable from "this package is broken". A `tools.py`
that cannot be read *is* a package defect, and that one does appear in `verify`. The
listing carries the difference where a person will actually see it:

```text
lean_pack/  Prove theorems in Lean 4 and score what the proof checker accepted.  [needs lean]
  lean_pack/prover                       prove a theorem in Lean and score what the Lean checker accepted
```

Absence must not make a package invisible. It must make it labelled.

## Provisioning: refuse, and name the fix

Nothing here installs anything. `Tool.install` is the exact command, and it is
quoted in every failure message, which is the whole provisioning story: the package
loads, the tool is declared, and the run that would have used it refuses at the point
of use.

Installing on demand was rejected for three reasons. A toolchain is not a per-package
affair — mathlib is gigabytes, and every package that needed it would fetch its own.
A run's budget is evaluation budget, and a download is not an evaluation. And a
package that mutates the machine it lands on is a package nobody can audit.

The same reasoning reaches inside the Lean project. `ops.py` writes no
`lean-toolchain` file, because pinning one makes `elan` download that exact compiler
as a side effect of evaluation; the project uses whichever toolchain the machine
already has. It names mathlib by `path` rather than by a git dependency, for the same
reason: a checkout the user has already built, never a fetch.

## The worked Lean example

`lean_pack/prover` states a theorem, writes a per-problem Lean project, attempts a
proof, and lets the proof checker decide. Its graph is:

```text
task_input -> tool_check -> scaffold -> attempt -> verify -> repair_gate
                                            ^                   |
                                            +---- reloop --------+
                                                                |
                                                      proceed -> finish
```

`tool_check` is a node rather than a comment because absence is the interesting
failure and it has to happen at step two:

```bash
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from refactory_dsh import registry
r = registry.resolve(Path('.'), 'lean_pack/prover')[1]().evaluate(Path('/tmp/pack-absent'))
print(r.exit_ok, r.iterations, r.error)
"
```

```text
False 2 tool_check: ToolMissing: the package lean_pack declares the tool 'lean' (the proof checker that decides whether a candidate solution is a proof), and it is not on PATH as 'lean'; the fix is: curl https://elan.lean-lang.org/elan-init.sh -sSf | sh
```

Two steps, no project directory, and a message that names the tool, what it is for,
and the command that fixes it. That is the difference between this and a
`FileNotFoundError` raised forty minutes into a run.

`scaffold` writes the project. The statement is its own file and stays a `sorry`,
because a candidate that could edit the statement it is judged against would be
proving a different theorem:

```lean
-- project/Problem.lean
theorem three_consecutive_sum (n : Nat) : n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3 * (n + 1) := by
  sorry
```

```lean
-- project/Solution.lean
-- the sum of three consecutive naturals is three times the middle one (omega)
theorem three_consecutive_sum (n : Nat) : n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3 * (n + 1) := by
  omega

#print axioms three_consecutive_sum
```

`project/lakefile.toml` is what makes those two files a problem rather than a
snippet: a `Problem` library for the statement, and for the mathlib problem a
`[[require]] name = "mathlib"` with `path` pointing at `$MATHLIB_PATH`.

`verify` accepts a solution on two conditions, and both come from Lean. The exit code
says the file elaborated; the axiom dump from `#print axioms` says what the proof
assumed. A `sorry` closes a goal and elaborates cleanly, so the exit code alone would
accept an unfinished proof — `sorryAx` in that dump is Lean reporting the hole
itself, rather than `ops.py` pattern-matching on tactic text. `score()` then reads a
fact the run produced:

```python
def score(self, run):
    if not run.facts.get("verified"):
        return 0.0
    return round(1.0 - 0.1 * (int(run.facts["attempts_used"]) - 1), 6)
```

The discount is what gives the outer loop a gradient. `verified` alone is binary, so
every candidate that proves the theorem would tie; charging for the attempts it took
makes "found on the first try" a better answer than "found on the fourth", which is
a real claim about a proof search.

The package ships two problems deliberately. `three_consecutive_sum` needs nothing
but the Lean prelude, so the package runs on a machine with a toolchain and no
library, and it is what the tests exercise. `sum_odd_eq_sq` states
`∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, (2 * i + 1) = n ^ 2`, which needs `Finset` and `ring` and
therefore needs mathlib — the problem that shows why the requirement is declared at
all. `MATHLIB_PATH` is what selects a checkout, and nothing downloads one.

Write `∑ i ∈ s, f i`, not `∑ i in s, f i`. The `in` form is what most introductions
show and this Mathlib rejects it — Lean reads `∑ i` as an ordinary binder and reports
`unexpected token 'in'; expected ','`. The package shipped the `in` form until mathlib
was installed and the problem was actually run; every test before that used a stub
checker, and a stub does not parse the statement it is handed.

Two more things mathlib teaches a package that declares it, both recorded in
`refactory/docs/hardening.md` §8: the first invocation pays for importing the library,
so a timeout tuned to a core problem abandons the checker and reports a provable
theorem as unproved; and the project takes its `lean-toolchain` from the dependency, so
`lake env lean` may be a different compiler than `lean` on the PATH — which is why
`result.json` records `checker_version` from the project rather than the PATH.

## The sympy mode, beside it

`sympy_pack/exact` asks for the closed form of a sum in `n` and checks a set of
conjectured forms against it. sympy derives the sum and then reduces the difference
between that and each conjecture; a conjecture is accepted only when the difference
reduces to exactly zero as a symbol in `n`, so a form that agrees at a few sample
points and is wrong is rejected. The seed checks one conjecture per identity and
every first conjecture is wrong, so it scores zero, and `candidates` is the lever:

```bash
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from refactory_dsh import registry
mode_class = registry.resolve(Path('.'), 'sympy_pack/exact')[1]
for candidates in (1, 4):
    mode = mode_class()
    state = mode.state_dict()
    state['knobs']['candidates']['value'] = candidates
    print(candidates, mode_class(state=state).evaluate(Path(f'/tmp/pack-sympy-{candidates}')).score)
"
```

```text
1 0.0
4 3.0
```

Two packages, one reader, one failure message. `registry tools sympy_pack` reports
the module as present or absent exactly as it reports the Lean binary, and
`toolchain.import_tool` is how the op asks: it requires the tool and hands back the
module it names, so the requirement and the import are one statement rather than two
that can drift apart.

## Packing your own tool

Write the modes first and let the failure tell you what is missing. When an op needs
something that is not a Python callable, declare it:

1. Add `tools.py` beside the package's `__init__.py`, with a `Tool` per requirement.
   Give each one the command that installs it and the clause saying what it is for;
   the library will refuse the declaration without both.
2. Call `toolchain.require(package, name)` as the first statement of the op that is
   about to use it, or `toolchain.import_tool` for a Python module. Derive the
   package name from `__name__` — `__name__.split(".")[-2]` — so the op keeps working
   under a rename and in the writable package root.
3. Shell out from the op, not from `build()`. `build()` is pure and runs once; the
   tool is used at run time, and the executor enforces that a node writes only what
   it declares, so write the project files through `ctx.write_text`.
4. Make `score()` read a fact the run produced. For a tool whose verdict is the
   answer — a checker, a solver, a verifier — that fact is the tool's own answer, and
   the mode is then optimizing something it did not decide itself.
5. Put the check in the graph if it can fail usefully: a node early in the pipeline
   that requires the tool turns "this machine cannot do this" into a first-step
   refusal with a reason the report carries.
6. Declare the tools *optional* when only some modes need them. A required tool a
   mode does not use makes every other mode in the package unrunnable for no reason.
7. Declare `env` for a tool that is found through the environment. See below — it is
   the difference between a tool that works from a shell and the same tool under the
   sandbox, and the failure is silent.

### The environment a tool needs at run time

A tool that is present is not yet a tool that is *reachable*. A sandboxed run is
contained by rewriting `HOME` to its own working directory, which is right — code
nobody reviewed should not read a user's dotfiles — but every per-user toolchain
manager finds its installation through `HOME`. `elan` reads `$HOME/.elan`; rustup,
pyenv, nvm, gvm and sdkman all do the same. Containment alone therefore makes an
installed tool unreachable, and the run reports the tool absent on a machine that has
it:

```text
error: no default toolchain configured. run `elan default stable` to install
```

That message is not about the package, and it is not about the machine. It is about
where the run happened.

Declare what the tool needs:

```python
Tool(
    name="lean",
    kind="binary",
    probe="lean",
    install=ELAN,
    why="the proof checker that decides whether a candidate solution is a proof",
    env=(("ELAN_HOME", os.environ.get("ELAN_HOME") or str(Path.home() / ".elan")),),
)
```

`tool_env(package)` collects the pairs from the package's **present** tools, and
`sandbox.smoke` forwards them into the run. Two properties are worth stating:

- **The value is resolved where the declaration is read**, in the driver, which can
  still see the real environment. Package code cannot compute it: by the time an op
  runs under a sandbox, `HOME` is already the working directory, so `Path.home()`
  there answers a question about the sandbox rather than about the machine.
- **`env` is applied after containment, and does not weaken it.** `HOME` is still the
  working directory; forwarding adds variables rather than restoring the caller's
  environment. The secret filter still applies, so a declaration cannot smuggle a
  credential into a sandbox — a tool that needed one to *run* would be a different
  design, not an exception to this one.

The worked example is Lean, and it is worth knowing how it fails, because it fails
quietly. `lean_pack/prover` scored **1.0 through the walker and 0.0 through
`sandbox.smoke`** on one machine: the same mode, the same theorem, the same toolchain.
The walker has the real `HOME`; the sandbox does not. Registering the mode and
smoking it are different code paths, so this is exactly the class of defect a single
path's tests cannot see.

The toolchain is checked by `registry verify`, `registry tools`, and the tests in
`refactory/tests/test_math_pack.py`; the tests that need Lean skip with the name of the
missing binary when it is not installed, because a checkout without it has to be
correct.

## Where to go next

- [The architecture overview](architecture.md) — the state model the declarations sit
  on top of.
- [Writing a mode](tutorials/01-write-a-mode.md) — the smallest mode, and the
  validator rules a package has to satisfy.
- [`refactory_dsh.toolchain`](api/reference.md#refactory_dsh-toolchain) — the module
  this page describes.

# Panel UX follow-up — 2026-09-27

Based on main `6e12c94ba6adcbbf08c26ac5b52782e2c9af3241` (PR #247). This follow-up separates Run and Optimize setup, adds contextual field help and expands the brief into a native dialog. It retains the original two-gear artwork and theme. The [panel guide](tutorials/07-pick-and-watch-from-the-panel.md#find-the-controls) describes the new navigation.

## Behavior and evidence

- Run shows **Run once**; Optimize shows **Start optimization**, search limits and folded advanced controls. Package, mode, inputs, routing, profile settings and the watched run remain shared. Switching views does not dispatch work. Hidden controls retain their DOM and values. The selected view is stored per tab and survives splitting or closing another dock pane.
- Field help works on hover, keyboard focus and click. Escape, scrolling or resizing dismisses it. Tooltips use a viewport-clamped portal so the panel does not clip them. Mode input descriptions come from the actual mode declaration.
- Brief is first and spans the form. Its dialog supports multiline drafts, Apply/Cancel, Escape and Command/Control+Enter. Cancel leaves the saved input unchanged; closing restores focus to the trigger. Applying text does not launch a run.
- The stock hero headline stylesheet is mounted with the Refactory hero, so plugin-effect teardown cannot leave the displayed logo without its presentation rules. Native clean reload confirmed the original logo with no stock headline or Preview badge.

Native Chrome checks used the existing disposable preview home on port 3095. No model calls or execution launches were needed for this follow-up. Checks covered both themes, a roughly 430 px panel, keyboard draft apply/cancel, reopening saved text, tooltip placement, Run/Optimize switching and persistence when a split pane was closed. Screenshots crop browser chrome and unrelated tabs; application pixels are unchanged.

| Surface | Native capture |
|---|---|
| Compact Run | [Run in a narrow panel](assets/panel-ux-20260927/run-narrow-dark.png) |
| Compact Optimize | [Optimize in a narrow panel](assets/panel-ux-20260927/optimize-narrow-dark.png) |
| Contextual help | [Evaluation limit explanation](assets/panel-ux-20260927/optimize-help-dark.png) |
| Large brief editor | [Dark](assets/panel-ux-20260927/brief-editor-dark.png), [light](assets/panel-ux-20260927/brief-editor-light.png) |

## Checks and boundaries

- `pnpm test:gui`: **163 passed in 10 files**. New tests cover intent switching, keyboard tab navigation, input identity and values, exact optimization dispatch, watched-run preservation, unsupported authoring optimization, tooltip interaction, brief apply/cancel and focus restoration. Branding tests cover hero unmount/remount.
- `pnpm build`: host/client typechecks and both production bundles passed.
- `pnpm lint` and `git diff --check`: passed.
- No upstream version, dependency, lockfile, compatibility patch, execution engine or run schema changes. All changes remain in local plugins and documentation; no upstream fork or new patch is introduced.
- Execution, graph activity and steering contracts reuse [the prior native acceptance](panel-validation-20260927.md). This UI-only follow-up does not rerun the broader historical suites or claim their baseline failures are resolved.

The setup views survive dock remounts within the tab lifetime; this does not introduce persistence across a full browser reload. Existing advanced controls and catalogue descriptions remain partly English in the Chinese shell. The title and hero presentation bridges still require inspection on upstream upgrades.

# Panel and branding validation — 2026-09-27

This is the presentation acceptance for #245, based on main `5d4df6482478948db0d6ff62b307190738f1583a`. It reuses [release validation](release-validation-20260926.md) for the unchanged execution contracts in #234–#237 and PR #244. All new native runs were small deterministic fixtures, with **zero model calls**. Historical model-backed runs were read only. No historical campaign was restarted and no new universal resource cap was introduced.

## Result

The original Refactory two-gear artwork now has transparent, theme-aware ink. Brand blue drives the panel, controls and status graphics. The initial HTML, favicon, manifest, welcome, sidebar and blank conversation identify Refactory; the blank conversation's stock headline and Preview badge are removed. Provider/model identities remain accurate.

The panel starts with **Package → Mode**, retaining the full package/mode ID at dispatch. Configuration, activity, steering and package management have distinct sections. Advanced controls fold without unmounting their values. A read-only workflow map renders actual checkpoint nodes and connections, including forks, joins and return edges. Running nodes pulse; waiting, paused, failed, completed and explicitly skipped nodes have text labels. Follow active can be disabled, nodes support keyboard inspection, and reduced-motion preferences disable animation. Old runs without topology keep their recorded-node list. Completion is execution evidence, not a claim that validation passed.

The intended hierarchy was shown before broad implementation, then refined using the owner's explicit direction to retain the two gears and blue identity, remove the logo background and add the two dropdowns and live graph. The captures below show the implemented native application, not the design mockup.

## Native evidence

Captured in Chrome against separate disposable DSH homes: baseline on port 3096, updated application on 3095, and a fresh updated launch on 3097. Images crop away browser chrome and unrelated tabs; application pixels are otherwise unmodified. The animation is a sequence of native screenshots, not a simulated graph.

| State | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Fresh welcome | [Upstream welcome](assets/panel-20260927/before-welcome.png) | [Refactory welcome](assets/panel-20260927/after-welcome-light.png) |
| Configured panel | [Expanded light](assets/panel-20260927/before-configured-light-expanded.png) | [Narrow light](assets/panel-20260927/after-configured-light-narrow.png), [narrow dark](assets/panel-20260927/after-configured-dark-narrow.png) |
| Pending question | [Original gate](assets/panel-20260927/before-question-light-expanded.png) | [Question banner and waiting map](assets/panel-20260927/after-live-map-question-dark.png) |
| Active execution | [Recorded activity](assets/panel-20260927/before-active-light-expanded.png) | [Active workflow map](assets/panel-20260927/after-live-map-active-dark.png), [actual node pulse](assets/panel-20260927/live-node-pulse.gif) |
| Completed execution | [Completed graph](assets/panel-20260927/before-completed-light-expanded.png) | [Completed map](assets/panel-20260927/after-live-map-completed-dark.png) |
| Saved failure | [Known failed validation](assets/panel-20260927/before-failure-light-expanded.png) | [Failure in narrow dark layout](assets/panel-20260927/after-failure-dark-narrow.png) |

Additional evidence: [package-scoped mode menu](assets/panel-20260927/after-package-modes-dark.png), [Chinese shell and light theme](assets/panel-20260927/after-locale-zh-light.png), [one run finishes while another remains watched](assets/panel-20260927/after-watch-isolation-dark.png).

![Package selection and active execution map](assets/panel-20260927/after-live-map-active-dark.png)

## Control and behavior parity

| Contract retained | Evidence for this change |
|---|---|
| Package/mode selection, disabled package Enable, declared knobs, full/fast authoring | Package menu enumerated the catalogue; `default_pack` showed only its six modes. Component tests cover package changes, exact mode IDs and the existing enabled/action guards. Catalogue and execution declarations are unchanged. |
| Run once versus optimization Start | Native `counting_pack/fixed_step` Run once used `step=2,target=7`, produced `value=8,steps=4`. Start used one epoch, one candidate and one evaluation with the existing random/walker settings. UI launch guard and tests prevent a duplicate pending Start; Run once keeps its independent guard. |
| Configuration, profile versions and routing | Native profile `polish-245-demo`, version 1, was saved/selected. Values survived disclosures, resize and light/dark/locale switches. Component tests retain input DOM identity and values. Profile/fast CLI regression tests passed. No routing precedence, permissions or saved schemas changed. |
| Live reads, reconnect and ownership | Watch/Read attaches an existing directory and receives durable state without executing it. The deterministic 15-second run `single-6eed6147-0638-4ab2-a466-a036374d56de` completed while `polish-245-control` stayed watched with its question intact. Stream tests cover late launches/results and retired reads. A targeted test covers Watch changing while Start's receipt is pending, including releasing the launch guard. |
| Questions, steering and graph controls | Native `polish-245-control` used the actual spine: prepare → user review → 30-second check → finish. The question banner linked to the native verdict controls. Pause/resume/stop and explicit correction preview were exercised at supported boundaries. A confirmed correction reran prepare at revision 2 and required a fresh gate answer. The final map followed waiting → running → completed. |
| Correction and recovery safety | Preview still displays invalidated results before confirmation; the real checkpoint was explicitly resumed by the deterministic fixture owner. No graph editor or alternate engine was added. Graph controls retain their run-keyed component and capability semantics. |
| Candidates, adoption/replay, usage and validation | Existing candidate, measurement, validation, adoption/replay and resource components remain reachable. Reuse the release acceptance for unchanged model-backed operations. No inferred percentages, aggregate scores or estimated usage were added. Missing usage remains unavailable. |
| Package import/enable/disable/remove | Existing handlers, arguments and package rows retained under Packages of modes. Package selection only changes local picker state. |
| Layout, focus and accessibility | Actual narrow (~403 px) and expanded (~790 px) panel, both themes, keyboard focus and native selectors inspected. Form state persisted. Long paths wrap in details and remain inspectable; notices and pending questions remain prominent. Graph nodes are keyboard buttons with full names/states; pulse is disabled by `prefers-reduced-motion`. |

Native fixture run paths belong to the isolated checkout's ignored `.factory` directory. The saved failed validation was only viewed, from the earlier release evidence; its defect was neither hidden nor rerun. Logs and authentication URLs are private test artifacts and are not committed.

## Branding and portability audit

| Surface | Verification |
|---|---|
| Initial document title, favicon, manifest | Fresh updated host response and native fresh launch; host-hook tests retain scripts and replace only app identity. The gear favicon was confirmed on the fresh process. |
| Sidebar and empty conversation | Native new session, both themes and English/Chinese locale; original gears and lettering retained, background removed, stock headline/badge absent. |
| Welcome | Native fresh English welcome; English and Chinese injected copy tested while retaining original component, acknowledgement and controller props. |
| Settings, notices, loading and errors | Native general/model settings and saved failure; source audit distinguishes product identity from provider/model/backend and package identifiers. Local loading/error presentation identifies Refactory. |
| Title changes and lifecycle | Tests retain session prefixes, replace only the exact product suffix, and dispose observers, slot contributions and styles. |
| Dependencies and extension boundary | Root DSH pin, workspace patch declarations and all eight existing compatibility patches unchanged. Frozen install and normal build succeed. Local host index/routes, browser slots/theme and read-only Python status supply all changes. |

There is no vendored upstream fork and no new patch. The install already had eight compatibility patches, so it should not be described as literally patch-free. See [upstream compatibility](upstream-compatibility.md) for upgrade checks, including the two isolated title/hero presentation bridges.

## Automated checks and remaining limitations

- Frozen offline install passed; host/client typechecks and production build passed.
- GUI tests: **156 passed in 9 files**, including package filtering, disclosure preservation, launch ownership, topology layout, state labels, keyboard interaction, branding and both welcome locales.
- Python `test_live_activity.py`, `test_profiles.py`, `test_fast_cli.py`: **56 passed**. Topology coverage checks real edges, forks/joins/return paths, skipped nodes, malformed/old checkpoints, command/prompt exclusion and unchanged checkpoint bytes.
- `pnpm lint` and whitespace check passed. Normal commit and push hooks are required for delivery.
- The broader Python CLI/profile selection had **68 passed, 6 failed**; the same six failures reproduced on the unchanged baseline. They concern stale doctor/catalogue/README expectations and legacy DSH profile stubs, not the UI or graph reader.
- The broader Refactory host selection had **109 passed, 10 failed**. The seven service-unit failures reproduce on baseline (older argv, authoring receipt and ledger expectations). The same three live failures also reproduce on baseline: two outdated unknown-run error strings and a stop/finished-state expectation. No host execution code was changed to suppress these failures.

Some existing advanced controls, runtime state labels and catalogue descriptions remain English when the shell is Chinese; the new package picker and principal panel labels follow the locale. The original logo remains raster-derived, suitable for current app sizes. The launcher still prints the underlying `dsh web` runtime URL label. The title and hero-wrapper bridges need rechecking on an upstream upgrade. This work does not claim a fully green repository-wide historical suite or repeat the completed model-backed acceptance.

refactory/docs/plans/pythonic-modes.md.text:
# Decisions: pythonic modes and the outer loop

This is the **decision record** for the refactory system. It says *why* the thing
is shaped the way it is, and it is the place a disagreement gets settled.

**The mechanics are not here.** How the state model, the validator, the edit
algebra, the loop, and the two runtimes actually work is
[the architecture overview](../architecture.md). This file used to carry both; the
mechanics were removed once they moved, because a document that describes an
implementation it no longer matches is worse than no document.

Status: the decisions below are **in force**. Each names the consequence that
holds it in place; a decision with no consequence is an opinion.

---

## Objective

Build "the PyTorch of the harness world": a mode is a Python class, its
architecture and parameters are a serializable `state_dict`, and optimizers
propose typed updates to that state.

The end state it was written against, and which now holds:

```
epochs=2, batch_size=4 on the ported circle_packing mode
→ a leaderboard with at least one accepted structural win
→ a rejection-cause histogram from the optimizer's internal validation loop
→ the whole thing driven by real model calls in the `optimizer` step
```

```bash
cd refactory && ../.venv/bin/python -m refactory_dsh.loop circle_packing/adaptive \
  --epochs 2 --batch-size 4 --optimizer random --seed 5 --runs-root /tmp/decisions
```

seed `0.795` → best `0.875` raw `0.955`, 1 structural win, rejections across `V2 V3 V4 V5 V6 V7
V10`, `I:fact_produced`, `E-shape`.

## Non-goals

- **No JSON compatibility.** JSON is the serialization format for state and run
  records. It is never an authoring or mutation surface. There is no importer from
  legacy JSON modes.
- **No new DSH core packages.** Everything lands under `refactory/`.
- **No GUI work in the Python system.** The loop is a Python process; the GUI is a
  view over its artifacts, and the panel, the console and the client specs are where
  that view is built and held.

## Decisions

| # | Decision | Held in place by |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Python is the source of truth. A mode is a `Mode` subclass. | `nn/mode.py` |
| D2 | `state_dict` carries **architecture and parameters** — the deliberate divergence from PyTorch, because the loop searches architecture. | `nn/mode.py`, `nn/validate.py` |
| D3 | The author writes `build() -> Graph`, pure. Genesis captures its output; thereafter the optimizer edits the state. | `V7` refuses a knob `build()` read |
| D4 | `score()` and `invariants()` are **methods**, never in the state. No optimizer can reach them. | structural, not defensive |
| D5 | Structural change is a first-class search operator, expressed as **typed data**, never code. | `nn/edits.py` |
| D6 | The validator replaces what `load_state_dict(strict=True)` gives PyTorch, because architecture is in the state. | `nn/validate.py` |
| D7 | Operators are **naive**: they reject, never repair. Repair corrupts the gradient by attributing a score to an edit that was not applied. | every refusal carries a code |
| D8 | The edit vocabulary is closed and enumerable: primitives, plus macros that are literally compositions of them. Broad by default, restrictable by preset. | `edits.names()`, `PRESETS` |
| D9 | The generate→validate→regenerate loop is **optimizer-owned**; the validator is one shared deterministic service. | `optim.Optimizer.attempt` |
| D10 | Op callables resolve from `"module:function"` strings. No package name is hardcoded in the library or the engine. | `nn/resolve.py` |
| D11 | An invalid proposal costs **zero** evaluation budget. | `attempt` validates before `forward` |
| D12 | Universal invariants always apply; a mode's `invariants()` cover what only the author knows. Removing work is a legitimate win when the score stays meaningful. | `nn.validate.fact_produced` |
| D13 | **Two extension points, deliberately separate**: `Optimizer` proposes and cannot run anything; `OuterLoop` owns the search. A proposer plugs into any loop; a loop can override any step. | `optim/base.py`, `outerloop.py` |
| D14 | **The loop is itself a mode.** Its eight steps are nodes, its gate loops back or leaves, and its `score()` reads the inner run's best score — so a further loop can search the loop. | `refactory_packages/loop_mode` |
| D15 | **The loop's output is a new artifact, never a mutation of its input.** `create`, `edit`, `design` and an adopting loop all produce something new, so the baseline stays measurable. | `create.py`, `edit.py`, `design.py` |

D13–D15 were decided after this record was first written, and are the reason the
mechanics sections were removed rather than updated: the shape of the optimizer
layer changed, and a plan that described the older single-class API was actively
misleading.

## Vocabulary

The PyTorch mapping is maintained in
[architecture.md §2](../architecture.md#2-the-pytorch-mapping), with its one
deliberate divergence stated there. It is not repeated here.

## What the first real run changed

Kept because the lesson generalizes, and because the same mistake is easy to make
again.

The first real 2-epoch run produced **no improvement**: seed `0.875`, best `0.875` (raw, before the size cost existed).
It was correct in every structural sense and useless as a search. Three defects,
all in the loop rather than the library:

1. **The starting population had no parameter contrast.** It was sampled across the
   whole catalogue, so `set_knob` was drowned by structural edits and epoch one
   evaluated candidates differing only in structure. All scored the same, so the
   gradient said nothing about which value of anything was worth having.
   *Now:* `init` **sweeps** — one candidate per movable knob, each at a value the
   default is not.
2. **The gradient said what had been tried, not what had not.** *Now:*
   `knob_attribution` carries `untried`.
3. **"Structural wins" counted runs that never ran.** *Now:* a win is a structural
   candidate that ran and scored.

**The lesson:** a validator can only reject what is *invalid*, and a search also
has to be given something *informative*. The first run was proof that those are
different properties, and that the second has to be designed rather than assumed.

# Preset UI follow-up — 2026-09-27

Based on main `78acf93b1a453474f09e487bc4431c5ddfe85928` (PR #248). The new-chat picker and Agent presets settings now offer CEO and Minimal only. CEO's description explains creating, running and improving Refactory workflows, coordinating agents and returning questions and results. Both English and Chinese copy are supplied.

## Behavior and native checks

- The native new-chat picker contains exactly CEO and Minimal; selecting each updates the current choice. An unsupported old default is normalized through the native selection controller when the picker loads.
- Settings has one Agent presets navigation button and two cards. Native View and Set as default actions are retained; extra-preset authoring is disabled. The CEO composition viewer opens successfully.
- Existing sessions retain their actual preset labels. The host roster, worker presets, CLI behavior and stored defaults are unchanged by UI filtering.
- Native Chrome verification used the disposable preview home on port 3095. No model calls or execution launches were needed. Captures crop only browser chrome and surrounding application space.

| Surface | Capture |
|---|---|
| Two-choice picker and CEO description | [Picker](assets/presets-20260927/picker-dark.png) |
| Settings cards and navigation | [Settings](assets/presets-20260927/settings-dark.png) |

## Checks and portability

- GUI suite: **170 passed in 11 files**. New coverage checks filtered snapshots, unchanged source data, locale copy, stable snapshot identity, old-default fallback, native errors and actions, slot replacement/disposal, and reversible duplicate-navigation suppression.
- Production build, host/client typechecks, lint and whitespace checks passed.
- Preset components and controllers are reused through public slot registrations in the local branding plugin. The pinned shell enumerates raw section registrations, so a scoped presentation observer hides its duplicate navigation button. Recheck that bridge and the typed preset faces on upgrades.
- Two development dependencies expose existing pinned upstream types and test stores. No upstream version or compatibility-patch changes, runtime preset deletion, or new fork. The existing eight compatibility patches described in [upstream compatibility](upstream-compatibility.md) remain unchanged.
