refactory/docs/rc2-home-isolation.md.text:
# Upgrading to 0.2.0-rc.2: isolate the harness home

This checkout pins `@deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.0-rc.2` and runs it through `node_modules/.bin/dsh`. That harness moves the global settings document aside on its first boot and imports it into the profile it booted. The move is a rename, so the global document stops existing at its old path. Run it against a home another harness generation already uses and the two generations contend for one `settings.yaml`.

Two harness generations can share this machine. They do not share a settings layout, and they must not share a home.

## What changes

| | the `dsh` binary on `PATH` | this checkout's `node_modules/.bin/dsh` |
|---|---|---|
| package | the operator's own DSH install (`dsh-tauri`, version `0.1.6-alpha.1`) | `@deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.0-rc.2` |
| settings layout | one global document | profile-owned configuration |
| migration on boot | none | `importLegacyDocument()` |

The migration is `importLegacyDocument()`, a method of the `SettingsForms` service in the package `@deepseek-ai/dsh-settings@0.2.0-rc.2`, at `lib/index.js` lines 346-363. The service schedules it from its constructor once the Loader settles: `ctx.root.loader.await().then(() => this.importLegacyDocument())` (line 339).

The method reads the document at `join(profile.home, "settings.yaml")` — the global file under the resolved harness home, not a per-profile path. It then does three things:

1. `const imported = \`${path}.imported\`` then `await rename(path, imported)` — the document is renamed **before the first write**, so a partial import never repeats.
2. Parses the renamed file and calls `this.update(section, values)` for each top-level section. Sections are written into the booted profile's `cordis.patch.yml`; a section the running composition rejects is logged and left only in the renamed file.
3. Logs `settings: imported %s into profile %s`.

This is intentional upstream behaviour. The harness deliberately migrates away from a single global document, and the rename-first ordering is what makes the import idempotent — the second boot finds no `settings.yaml` and returns at line 349. Do not patch it out, and do not edit `node_modules` by hand; the documented patch set in [Upstream compatibility](upstream-compatibility.md) covers five unrelated compatibility changes.

Section names are remapped through a small table before the write: `ui-developer-tools` and `ui-onboarding` both go to `ui-settings`, and `shell` goes to the platform's shell-sandbox entry.

## What the operator risks

Two failures, and the second is the serious one.

**The global document stops being the live file.** After the first rc.2 boot, edits made through the fork's GUI no longer reach the harness, and edits made through rc.2 no longer reach the global file. A section the running rc.2 composition rejects is reported with a `warn` line and is never written anywhere except the renamed file.

**The rename can be the only copy.** `rename(path, imported)` overwrites its target. There is no timestamp and no collision check. A home that is booted, restored by hand, and booted again loses the intermediate state: the second boot renames the restored file onto the same `settings.yaml.imported` name and replaces whatever the first boot left there. Verified against a throwaway home — two successive boots each produced a byte-identical copy of that boot's input at `settings.yaml.imported`, with no second file created.

A backup taken before the first boot is the only durable protection. Take it outside the home.

### The files that appear

Read from the live home on this machine:

```
~/.dsh/settings.yaml                            2516 bytes   the restored live document
~/.dsh/settings.yaml.imported                   2516 bytes   byte-identical to the above
~/.dsh/settings.yaml.imported-20261001-1813     2540 bytes   carries a timestamp
~/.dsh/settings.yaml.bak                         274 bytes
~/.dsh/settings.yaml.lost-20261001-145440         99 bytes   carries a timestamp
```

Only `settings.yaml.imported` — the plain suffix, no timestamp — is produced by `importLegacyDocument()`. Confirmed by grep: the string `.imported` occurs exactly once in that file, at line 350, and the interpolated name has no date component anywhere in the package.

The two timestamped names are **not** attributable to verified code. `settings.yaml.imported-20261001-1813` and `settings.yaml.lost-20261001-145440` exist on this machine, but neither this checkout, nor the fork's source, nor the pinned rc.2 packages contain the strings that would write them. Treat them as operator backups of unknown provenance. Their contents differ from every other variant, so they are not interchangeable with `settings.yaml.imported`, and they are unavailable after the fact to prove which file a given boot consumed.

Because `settings.yaml.imported` is overwritten in place, its modification time equals the live document's to the second on this machine — both `2026-10-01 20:23:06` — which is consistent with a rename out of a restore, but does not by itself date the import.

## The isolation remedy

Give each harness generation its own `DSH_HOME`. The environment variable is read by `@deepseek-ai/dsh-home-paths`'s `resolveDshHome()`; precedence is an explicit configured path, then `$DSH_HOME`, then `~/.dsh`. An empty or whitespace-only `DSH_HOME` is treated as unset, so the fallback is never the current directory.

Both harness generations honour `DSH_HOME`, so one variable separates them completely. This checkout's Python reads it in `refactory_dsh/dsh_profile.py:176-179` and `refactory_dsh/model.py:204`.

The examples below use `~/.dsh-rc2` for the pinned rc.2 harness and leave `~/.dsh` to the fork. Any two distinct absolute paths work; keep the rc.2 home outside `~/.dsh` so the rename can never reach the fork's document.

### (a) `./install.sh` — provisions profiles into the rc.2 home

```bash
cd /path/to/refactory-dsh
DSH_HOME="$HOME/.dsh-rc2" ./install.sh
```

`install.sh` exports `DSH="$HERE/node_modules/.bin/dsh"` and runs the plan from `dsh_profile.render_plan()` through it, so `DSH_HOME` selects where the pinned harness writes. Verified: with `DSH_HOME` set to a `/tmp` path, the script created `profiles/graph` and `profiles/refactory` under it and left `~/.dsh` untouched. `REFACTORY_SKIP_DSH_PROFILE=1` skips profile provisioning entirely.

The plan for a fresh home is four rows, in this order:

| row | profile | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `add` | `graph` | `@deepseek-ai/dsh-graph`, installed from `packages/bundle/graph` by path |
| `init` | `refactory` | copies the shipped `web` template's bundle list |
| `add` | `refactory` | `@deepseek-ai/dsh-refactory` — the `ceo` preset and roster |
| `add` | `refactory` | `@deepseek-ai/dsh-refactory-web` — console, picker, brand rows |

After it, the two homes hold:

- **`$HOME/.dsh-rc2`** — `profiles/graph` and `profiles/refactory`, plus everything the pinned harness writes later (`sessions/`, `storages/`, `.credentials.yaml`, `.anonymous-user-id`). It starts with no `settings.yaml`, which is what makes the first boot safe.
- **`$HOME/.dsh`** — the fork's `settings.yaml` and `settings.yaml.*` files, and the fork's `profiles/`. On this machine those are `graph`, `headless`, `martty`, `probe`, `refactory`, `refactory-web` and `web`, with `refactory` carrying `['@deepseek-ai/dsh-base', '@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app', '@deepseek-ai/dsh-refactory', '@deepseek-ai/dsh-refactory-web']`. No rc.2 profile is created there.

The project-local sharing between the two homes is unavoidable and harmless: `profiles/<name>` holds absolute symlinks, and both homes link to the same `packages/bundle/*` directories in this checkout. Each home keeps its own `profiles/<name>/package.json`, so writes stay separated.

### (b) `./refactory-dsh` — boots the GUI from the rc.2 home

```bash
cd /path/to/refactory-dsh
DSH_HOME="$HOME/.dsh-rc2" ./refactory-dsh --port 3081 --no-open
```

The launcher heals a missing layer into the selected home before booting, so it reads the same `DSH_HOME`. Verified against a `/tmp` home: it provisioned `graph` and `refactory` there. It ends in `exec "$DSH" --profile refactory "$@"`, so the whole session runs on the pinned harness from `$HOME/.dsh-rc2`.

### (c) the rc.2 GUI

`uv run refactory ui` is the same launcher by another route. `cmd_ui` resolves `_launcher()` to `REPO_ROOT / "refactory-dsh"` and calls it with `--port` and `--no-open`:

```bash
cd /path/to/refactory-dsh
DSH_HOME="$HOME/.dsh-rc2" uv run refactory ui --port 3081 --no-open
```

`refactory ui` accepts `--port <int>` (default: the launcher's own) and `--no-open`. Anything beyond those two flags has to go through `./refactory-dsh` directly.

### (d) the Python glue's model calls

The glue resolves its model home once, before containment rewrites `HOME`:

1. An explicit `DshModelClient(dsh_home=...)` path.
2. Nonblank `REFACTORY_MODEL_DSH_HOME`.
3. Nonblank `DSH_HOME`.
4. The original user home's `.dsh` directory.

Paths are trimmed, expanded and resolved to absolute paths. Whitespace-only
values are treated as unset. The model subprocess and graph runtime receive
both `DSH_HOME` and `REFACTORY_MODEL_DSH_HOME` set to that resolved path. Runtime
preflight inspects the graph profile in the same home, including an explicit
client override. A missing profile's repair command includes `DSH_HOME` so it
provisions the home the run will actually use.

```bash
cd /path/to/refactory-dsh
REFACTORY_MODEL_DSH_HOME="$HOME/.dsh-rc2" uv run refactory ceo "an idea" --mode design
```

Verified by probe: with `DSH_HOME=/tmp/probe-dsh` and `REFACTORY_MODEL_DSH_HOME=/tmp/probe-refactory`, `DshModelClient()._dsh_home` resolved to `/tmp/probe-refactory` and both child variables carried that value. With `REFACTORY_MODEL_DSH_HOME` unset, `DSH_HOME=/tmp/probe-dsh` was honoured. With neither set, it resolved to `/home/kai/.dsh`.

`model.py:184`, `:201` and `:202` read `REFACTORY_MODEL_EFFORT`, `REFACTORY_MODEL_ID` and `REFACTORY_MODEL_PROVIDER` — the route, not the home. They apply only when the worker backend is `dsh` and no routes were resolved, and they do not affect which home is used.

### Installation/session and model diagnostics

Installation and GUI provisioning use `DSH_HOME`, falling back to `~/.dsh`.
`REFACTORY_MODEL_DSH_HOME` selects model workers independently; it does not
redirect `install.sh` or `./refactory-dsh`. With `DSH_HOME=A` and
`REFACTORY_MODEL_DSH_HOME=B`, installation and the GUI target A, while model
workers and graph runtime preflight target B. The console tool explicitly forwards
its session `DSH_HOME`; the harness subprocess provider preserves the ordinary
`REFACTORY_MODEL_DSH_HOME` variable, so console model workers follow the same
precedence as the Python CLI. Contained workers carry the resolved client home
in their serialized context before `HOME` is rewritten.

`refactory doctor` reports both resolved homes. It checks the installation's
owned profiles and any attached Martty profile, and additionally checks the
model home's graph profile when the homes differ. It only reads and reports.
To provision a separate model home, run installation explicitly against it:

```bash
DSH_HOME="$HOME/.dsh-model" ./install.sh
DSH_HOME="$HOME/.dsh-rc2" REFACTORY_MODEL_DSH_HOME="$HOME/.dsh-model" uv run refactory doctor
```

### Stranded bundle selections: upstream follow-up (#286)

At the pinned `0.2.0-rc.2`, plugin-manager already has a deselect primitive:
`selectBundle(name, false)` removes a selected name without requiring a
corresponding dependency. The remote method `setBundleEnabled(name, false)`
wraps it. However, `dsh plugin --profile NAME remove PACKAGE` forwards to pnpm;
a name absent from `dependencies` makes removal fail, and `reconcile()` preserves
that selection. The upstream request is to expose deselection through the CLI,
or tolerate dangling selections in CLI removal.

The offline installer cannot simply call `./remote`: an import probe finds only
`TYPERT_REMOTE` and `default` protocol metadata, with no executable manager.
Constructing `PluginManager` without a host context fails while reading
`ctx.reflect`. The implementation also uses `ctx.profileContext`, a profile
writer lock, the owning context and loader/HMR services. A host RPC invocation
requires a running profile, whose startup can already fail on the stranded
selection. Calling an internal prototype with a fabricated host would introduce
another unsupported adapter. Keep the owned-manifest cleanup using the pinned
writer lock and atomic writer until a supported offline operation exists.

Registry and tarball checks on 2026-10-06 found `latest` and `next` still at
`0.2.0-rc.2`, with `alpha` at `0.2.1-alpha.1`. The alpha plugin-manager's
`lib/types/operations.js` is byte-identical to the pinned file; upgrading to that
alpha does not fix CLI reconciliation.

## Safe first run

Set `H` once per shell and use it throughout. Substitute your own rc.2 home path.

```bash
H="$HOME/.dsh-rc2"
```

1. **Back up the live document before anything else, outside the home.** `importLegacyDocument()` renames the file inside the home, so a backup left inside `~/.dsh` is itself a file the next boot can collide with.

   ```bash
   cp -p "$HOME/.dsh/settings.yaml" "$HOME/.dsh/settings.yaml.pre-rc2.$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
   sha256sum "$HOME/.dsh/settings.yaml" "$HOME"/.dsh/settings.yaml.pre-rc2.*
   ```

   Record the sha256. It is the reference for step 4, and it is the only comparison that distinguishes a `rename` from a `write`. On this machine the expected value is `1958a76fa29edd3382b29d6a52f3c0f1be1eebc93e1337d16b4bfd3f527664e7`. Copy it to a second location if it matters — a backup that shares a filesystem with the original is not a backup.

2. **Confirm the two homes are distinct and that the rc.2 home starts clean.**

   ```bash
   ls -d "$HOME/.dsh" "$H"
   ls "$H/settings.yaml" 2>&1   # expected: No such file or directory
   ```

   `No such file or directory` is the safe state. A file present here is a document this home's first boot would rename.

3. **Provision and boot rc.2 in the isolated home.** The first boot is the one that migrates.

   ```bash
   cd /path/to/refactory-dsh
   DSH_HOME="$H" ./install.sh
   DSH_HOME="$H" uv run refactory doctor
   DSH_HOME="$H" ./refactory-dsh --port 3081 --no-open
   ```

   Provisioning reads and writes only under `$H`. Verified against a `/tmp` home.

4. **Confirm the original is untouched.** While the GUI is running is the best moment to check, because the migration has already fired.

   ```bash
   sha256sum "$HOME/.dsh/settings.yaml"
   ls -la "$HOME/.dsh"/settings.yaml*
   ```

   The sha256 must still match step 1, and the `settings.yaml*` listing must be exactly the set step 1 saw. Any new `.imported` file, or a changed digest, means the rc.2 boot reached the fork's home: stop, and restore with the section below.

5. **Confirm the migration landed in the rc.2 home**, where it is expected and harmless.

   ```bash
   ls -la "$H"/settings.yaml* 2>&1
   ```

   At this point `$H` has no `settings.yaml` to import, so nothing should appear here either. If you deliberately placed a settings document in `$H`, seeing `settings.yaml.imported` there is the migration working as designed.

## Detecting that it already happened, and restoring

### Detect

The signature is a `settings.yaml`/`settings.yaml.imported` pair in one harness home, with the global document no longer live.

```bash
ls -la "$HOME/.dsh"/settings.yaml*
```

Two conditions confirm it:

- **`settings.yaml.imported` exists.** The rc.2 harness renamed the document rather than copying it. This file is a real document, not a stub, and is byte-identical to what the global file held at the moment of the rename when the rename was the last writer.
- **`settings.yaml` is absent, or its content is a restore.** If a file is present, its digest settles which: matching a backup you took means you already restored it, and does not mean the migration did not happen.

On this machine both files are present and byte-identical — sha256 `1958a76fa29edd3382b29d6a52f3c0f1be1eebc93e1337d16b4bfd3f527664e7` for each — which is the "migrated, then restored by hand" state. The rc.2 profile directories under `~/.dsh/profiles/` are the other marker: this checkout's rc.2 harness wrote them, and the fork never creates `graph` or a re:factory-owned `refactory` with those four bundles.

Compare every variant before choosing a file to restore from. They are not equivalents:

```bash
sha256sum "$HOME/.dsh"/settings.yaml* && ls -la "$HOME/.dsh"/settings.yaml*
```

The largest file is not necessarily the right one. `settings.yaml.imported-20261001-1813` on this machine is 24 bytes larger than `settings.yaml.imported` but hashes differently, and neither timestamped name is attributable to verified code.

### Restore

1. **Stop every harness process** on the affected home. A running rc.2 boot can rename what you restore, which is how a restore becomes the next loss.
2. **Diff before you copy.** Neither candidate is guaranteed to be the newer document.

   ```bash
   diff -u "$HOME/.dsh/settings.yaml" "$HOME/.dsh/settings.yaml.imported"
   ```

   An empty diff means the two agree and the choice does not matter. A non-empty diff means deciding which document you want, and that is a reading task, not a command.
3. **Restore the chosen file to `settings.yaml`**, leaving the source in place:

   ```bash
   cp -p "$HOME/.dsh/settings.yaml.imported" "$HOME/.dsh/settings.yaml"
   ```

   Do not `mv` the only copy back. `rename` destroyed the previous occupant of the destination once already.
4. **Record the new digest and keep a copy outside the home**, then re-run the detection command above. Expect `settings.yaml` present with the digest you just recorded, and the `.imported` file unchanged.
5. **Re-check the profile-owned configuration the import wrote.** Sections that were imported were written into the rc.2 profile's `cordis.patch.yml`, under `$H/profiles/<name>/`. A restore of the global document does not remove them, and a section present in both places is applied twice:

   ```bash
   grep -rn "agent-default-model\|llm-pi-ai" "$HOME/.dsh-rc2"/profiles/*/cordis.patch.yml
   ```

6. **Prevent the recurrence** by running step 3 of the safe first-run procedure above — every rc.2 invocation with an explicit `DSH_HOME`.

## What this document could not verify

- **The origin of the timestamped names.** `settings.yaml.imported-<stamp>` and `settings.yaml.lost-<stamp>` are present on this machine, but no verified source in this checkout, in the fork, or in the pinned rc.2 packages contains the code that writes them. They are described as observed files of unknown provenance, not as harness behaviour.
- **The exact date of the destructive import.** The `.imported` file's mtime equals the live document's, so it dates the rename that produced it but not the import that preceded it.
- **Word-for-word configuration of the rc.2 GUI under an isolated home.** Provisioning and the profile plan were executed against `/tmp` homes and verified. A full interactive GUI session on a fresh isolated home was not run, because that requires booting the pinned harness and making model requests. The launcher path, the `DSH_HOME` plumbing and the resulting profile set were verified.

# Bounded release validation — 26–27 September 2026

Implementation started from main `a339605c69` in an isolated clone. These checks concern execution, controls and reported evidence. They are not broad repository certification or a claim about generated-artifact quality. Historical evaluation campaigns stayed stopped. The original checkout and its user-owned swap file were left untouched.

## Readiness

**All four release capabilities have completed bounded acceptance:** fast authoring/resources ([#234](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/issues/234)), live controls/recovery ([#235](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/issues/235)), profiles ([#236](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/issues/236)) and worker routing ([#237](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/issues/237)). Each has separate CLI and native GUI evidence. All three fast modes completed their required validation; actual structural repairs and explicit unresolved failures were also observed. These results establish the tested contracts, not general artifact quality or token efficiency.

Implementation was merged in [PR #239](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/pull/239) and [PR #240](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/pull/240). [PR #241](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/pull/241) added the requested full-bypass worker default and positive native worker checks; [PR #242](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/pull/242) recorded successful public recovery. [PR #243](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/pull/243) corrected validation-reserve ownership; [PR #244](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/pull/244) finalizes fast stage scope, CLI forwarding, worker context and the package API correction. The records below retain unsuccessful attempts and capability limits as well as the positive evidence.

## Issue and interface evidence

| Issue | CLI evidence | Native GUI evidence | Remaining acceptance |
|---|---|---|---|
| [#234](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/issues/234) | All three fast modes completed required QA/checks and reports. Create used one structural repair; Edit retained score 0.5 with no regression. Capped failures remain below. The deterministic known-defect control reached the real unresolved QA gate. | All three modes completed checks, QA and reports. Edit used one structural repair with no measured regression; corrected Create completed without repair. Its earlier import failure is retained. The deterministic known-defect control visibly reported the failed assertion and unresolved gate. | Complete for the bounded tasks. Required checks, structural repairs and unresolved outcomes are distinct evidence. |
| [#235](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/issues/235) | Actual live `status --follow`, boundary resume, persisted questions and control receipts, and public recovery of a registered run after its owner stopped. | Pending gate discovery and verdict, pause/resume, reviewed invalidation/replay, concurrent ownership, owned stop, and native Resume of a registered stopped owner. | Both interfaces complete for supported boundaries. Unknown in-flight side effects and partial-fork recovery remain explicitly refused. |
| [#236](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/issues/236) | Versioned profiles, exact configuration, 2 candidates × 2 trials, failed required-artifact control, separated holdout audit, adoption and replay. | Saved-version selection, profile creation and objective edit into a new version, same bounded search, candidate comparison, actual keep/reject/resume, exact adoption and replay. | No stochastic improvement is claimed; missing cost/usage remains unavailable. |
| [#237](https://github.com/akashgit/refactory-dsh/issues/237) | DSH passed; corrected native Codex and Claude Code dispatch both passed artifact and graph checks with explicit native edit permissions. | DSH passed. Codex and Claude Code passed the exact artifact and graph checks with the new `skip` default; actual native routes and versions displayed. | Both interfaces complete. Unsupported capabilities and usage coverage remain explicit below. |

## Fast-mode outcomes

The original six fast checks selected a 150,000-token allocation, 360-second limit and at most one repair. Allocation is enforced at admission/completion boundaries: an in-flight completion can take the observed total beyond the threshold. This is not a strict provider-side token ceiling.

| Interface | Mode | Observed tokens | Outcome |
|---|---|---:|---|
| CLI | Create fast | 149,410 | Working allocation exhausted; no completed emission/QA |
| CLI | Edit fast | 147,289 | Working allocation exhausted; no completed emission/QA |
| CLI | Design fast | 162,349 | Focused check passed; QA artifact written; exhaustion before final gate/report |
| Native GUI | Create fast | 145,594 | Exhaustion during emission |
| Native GUI | Edit fast | 156,722 | Exhaustion during emission |
| Native GUI | Design fast | 169,929 | Exhaustion during emission |

These six runs consumed 931,293 observed tokens, including completion-boundary overshoot of the requested aggregate allocation. Earlier 60,000-token failures and a zero-model preflight failure are retained separately. Resource exhaustion is failure evidence, not successful authoring. The [budget strategy analysis](budget-strategy.md) reconciles these receipts to provider usage and explains the subsequent scoped changes.

After the public CLI check/timeout forwarding fix, worker orientation and focused
stage changes, two further CLI checks used the same 150,000-token/360-second
limits and one-repair bound:

| Interface | Mode | Observed tokens | Outcome |
|---|---|---:|---|
| CLI, revised | Design fast | 135,727 | Completed in 31.77 seconds: sequential strategist, coder and QA; actual check passed, gate and report completed; zero repairs |
| CLI, revised | Create fast | 156,775 | Emitted package text, then token exhaustion before handback/QA; no completed authoring result |

The completed Design run changed only the copied tiny helper artifact; its source
was retained. A file emitted by the failed Create worker is not evidence of
structural admission, focused QA or canonical smoke.

The final scoped checks retain the six-minute elapsed limit and one-repair bound.
At the user's explicit request, the subsequent checks omit the optional
cumulative-token cap. Usage remains measured, including cached input; these
completion results do not establish token efficiency or reduced cost.

| Interface | Mode | Observed tokens | Elapsed | Outcome |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| CLI | Create fast | 1,210,437 | 143.47 s | Completed after one structural repair; focused QA, canonical smoke and report passed |
| CLI | Edit fast | 831,836 | 132.58 s | Completed with zero repairs; canonical score 0.5 → 0.5, `regressed=false`; default/changed inputs and sibling mode retained their contracts |
| Native GUI | Design fast | 128,567 | 29.02 s | Sequential strategist, coder and QA; focused check, gate and report passed; zero repairs |
| Native GUI | Edit fast | 757,421 | 130.15 s | Completed after one structural repair of a package-name mismatch; focused QA/check, canonical smoke and report passed; score 0.5 → 0.5, no regression |
| Native GUI | Create fast, failed attempt | 723,770 | 101.56 s | Failed after one structural repair on an unqualified package import; no focused QA, canonical smoke or final success report; resources were not exhausted |
| Native GUI | Create fast, corrected example | 655,160 | 99.89 s | Completed with zero repairs; structural admission, focused check/QA, canonical smoke (score 1) and report passed |

Native Create failed after its one repair: the supplied framework API example
used an unqualified package import. That failed run is retained. Five targeted
regressions verified the narrow example correction. The corrected
native Create run completed without repair. The successful capped CLI Design
above supplies the sixth interface path; it was not repeated. Default and changed
inputs were independently checked for the generated packages; Edit retained the
existing contracts and score, and the Design source remained unchanged.

The explicitly registered `fast_defect_acceptance/known_defect` control ran once
through the public CLI with no agent nodes and an impossible model route. The
actual helper assertion failed; production `focused_check` and `gate_qa` recorded
`unresolved` at `repair_attempts=0`, and no `design.json` was written. It exited
in 2.25 seconds within a 30-second/1,000-token allocation. The automatic driver
reported zero model calls; token telemetry remained unavailable. This is
deterministic failure/gate evidence, not model-authored QA or successful repair.
The native GUI **Run once** control independently showed the failed assertion and
unresolved gate with the same zero-repair bound, no `design.json`, and no budget
exhaustion. Its ledger recorded 2.19 seconds; it also used no agent nodes and the
impossible model route. Both interfaces therefore exposed the actual known-defect
failure without claiming a model review.

## Profiles and live controls

The `bounded-search` version 1 profile used random proposals, the walker evaluator, knob-only changes, one epoch, two candidate evaluations, two trials each, seed 9, and a 30-second shared allocation with three seconds reserved for validation. Both interfaces retained the same effective search constraints and seed-state digest. The CLI request omitted default knobs while the GUI explicitly supplied those identical defaults, so their raw request context hashes differ. The exact adopted winner `83ebe63e958b` had raw score 0.875 and adjusted score 0.795. CLI and native replay retained best score 0.875; no improvement was found. A separate Task control kept training score 1.0 and held-out score 0.5 distinct and refused ordinary adoption of the overfit result. An invalid required artifact made the candidate fail rather than receive a fabricated score.

Native profile versioning preserved the prior objective when a new version was saved. An additional zero-model search exercised actual keep/reject/resume at a generation boundary with two already measured candidates. Its acceptance driver held that boundary long enough to operate each UI control; it did not fabricate candidates or result receipts.

The live graph check used the real Cordis spine, shell execution and user-question bridge with deterministic operations. An explicit verdict was consumed once. Pausing did not invent a verdict. Correcting a completed node required a revision-bound preview; prior owned artifacts/facts were archived, dependent checks invalidated and unrelated input retained. The new draft reached a fresh gate rather than reusing the prior answer. A separate native ownership check ran a 15-second deterministic one-shot A while watching B at that gate: A completed successfully and B retained its identity, pending question and steering ledger. Fixture-only setup mistakes and their honest refusal receipts are retained separately from product evidence. Actual checkpoint restoration reused completed work without rerunning commands. The subsequent registered public recovery checks below cover the terminal and native panel separately.

## GUI chat optimization follow-up

On main `6ca5a57a84`, a fresh native CEO chat independently exercised the public
Refactory tool path. Earlier GUI optimization evidence above covered the panel;
it did not establish a chat-launched search.

The chat selected `bounded-search` version 1 and launched exactly one
`circle_packing/adaptive` search, `gui-chat-optimization-20260927`. Its saved
configuration retained random proposals, walker evaluation, one epoch, two
candidate evaluations, two trials, seed 9, 30 elapsed seconds with three reserved
for validation, and no token cap. The search completed four measurements in
0.179 seconds. Winner `83ebe63e958b` tied the seed: raw 0.875, adjusted 0.795,
with no improvement. Holdout was explicitly not applicable to this mode without
a data node; the separate Task holdout controls above remain the holdout evidence.

In that same chat, public tool calls inspected the winner, adopted it as
`issue236_chat_verified`, and smoked `issue236_chat_verified/adaptive`: exit OK,
score 0.875, 21 iterations. The native chat displayed the final result. Session
`session-e34a04ad-45ac-4fed-a2cb-e1fbfca94a86` records the actual start, status,
candidate, adoption and smoke calls; no shell substitute launched the search.
Two package-only registry targets were refused, then corrected to qualified mode
IDs without restarting the search. Source and saved-profile hashes were unchanged.

The chat used DSH / `deepseek-official` / `deepseek-flash`, low effort. Its turn
took 62.13 seconds and 25 model completions: 905,387 measured tokens, including
847,744 cached input, 50,159 uncached input and 7,484 output. The deterministic
search used no model workers. Chat orchestration usage is separate from that
search ledger; no efficiency or monetary-cost claim is made. The chat performed
source discovery to identify profile arguments, which remains observed overhead.

### Chat changes the optimizer to autoresearch

A second request in the same native chat launched one fresh run,
`gui-chat-autoresearch-20260927`, with per-run overrides selecting `autoresearch`,
two epochs, batch/elite size one, two evaluations, one trial, one admission attempt,
no prior-run history, 180 elapsed seconds with 15 reserved for validation, and no
token cap. The selected proposer route was DSH / official DeepSeek Flash / low
effort / skip permissions. The saved profile and source remained unchanged.

The run completed in **29.47 seconds**. Starting with only the seed ensured that
the next evaluated candidate came from the actual model proposer. Candidate
`3e50cd6446e7`, recorded with origin `optimizer`, changed the mode's `budget` knob
from 3 to 8 and was evaluated successfully: raw 0.875, adjusted 0.795, equal to the
seed. Both proposer calls completed with no errors and measured usage of 13,532
and 11,833 tokens (25,365 total). Worker receipts and provider-request records
confirmed the requested route. No improvement is claimed.

The existing pipeline also proposed `e160c2dbcfa1` (`grid` 10 → 24) at the end of
the final epoch. It remained explicitly unevaluated, with no invented score. No
search retry, source correction, additional adoption or replay followed; the first
chat check supplies adoption/replay evidence.

The second chat turn completed in 54.52 seconds and 20 model completions, using
1,294,169 tokens including 1,267,712 cached input. This orchestration usage is
separate from the 25,365 proposer tokens. Repeated status polling contributed to
the chat overhead; the result demonstrates functional configuration and execution,
not efficient chat orchestration. Both searches ended, all proposer workers
completed, resource clocks paused, and the temporary GUI server was stopped.

## Native workers and permissions

Earlier apparent Codex/Claude successes were withdrawn: the named-provider patch had left DSH active. The dispatch fix disables that entry before inserting the selected native worker and refuses DSH fallback. A composition regression verifies the actual installed loader's match semantics.

| Corrected CLI backend | Native runtime/model | Permission mode | Elapsed | Usage | Result |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Codex | 0.153.4 / `gpt-6-astra`, OpenAI, high | `approve-for-me` | 8.24 s | 44,964 measured native-thread tokens; nested coverage unverified | Exact `42\n` and graph-owned Python assertion passed |
| Claude Code | Agent SDK 0.3.263 / `claude-opus-4-6[1m]` | `acceptEdits` | 72.84 s | 454,673 estimated SDK-pipeline tokens; helper calls excluded | Exact `42\n` and graph-owned Python assertion passed |

Both checks were single attempts with 120-second limits and no retry. External whole-tree token caps remain unsupported. Claude's own Python tool was denied by its native sandbox; its alternative byte check and the independent graph Python check passed. The native GUI default-permission attempts reported 44,405 Codex measured tokens and 46,668 Claude estimated tokens, but delivered no required file. Those are useful permission-failure controls and are not positive GUI completion evidence.

## Worker permission follow-up

At the user's explicit request, new workers now default to full native permission bypass (`skip`). Existing profiles and checkpoints retain their prior policies. The change was verified at `1762d11dca`, based on merged main `6d732dd9e4`. Each additional GUI check used **Run once**, one worker attempt, a 120-second elapsed allocation, no retry or repair, and the same fixed `worker_gui_acceptance/worker_once` task. Both delivered exact `42\n`, passed the independent Python artifact check, and visibly reached **finished / done** with `build` and `verify` complete.

| Native GUI backend | Actual native runtime/model | Elapsed including graph checks | Usage | Run identity |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Codex | 0.153.4 / `gpt-6-astra`, OpenAI, high | 9.15 s | 44,016 measured native-thread tokens; nested coverage unverified | `single-4df96cd6-8a2c-4261-844c-061a1e92ea3c` |
| Claude Code | Agent SDK 0.3.263 / `claude-opus-4-6[1m]` | 18.73 s | 77,887 estimated SDK-pipeline tokens; helper calls excluded | `single-48ddda32-0d15-4b20-8992-361ccc16dd9d` |

Requested permission `skip` was saved in each run and worker receipt. Installed-provider contract tests independently verify Codex's full-access sandbox/never-approve mapping and Claude's bypass mapping. DSH uses a scoped runtime patch, with no environment override leaking into explicitly restricted children. Fresh preparation, CLI/console context propagation and historical run/profile preservation are covered by 117 focused Python tests and nine native-controls component tests; host/client typechecks and builds passed. Previous positive CLI evidence is reused for unchanged worker dispatch and artifact contracts. No further worker model calls or old campaign restarts were made. A subsequent recovery fixture unexpectedly used a managed profile pointing to the older graph runtime and consumed 9,929 coordinator tokens before its completion-boundary cap stopped it; no node completed and no retry with model access followed. This failed fixture is retained separately from the successful worker evidence.

## Public recovery follow-up

A registered two-operation package completed `first`, queued a pause before `second`, saved its real graph checkpoint, and exited. Recovery then used the normal public operation against that stopped owner; no checkpoint or success receipt was fabricated. These checks ran against merged main `10cefa309a`.

| Interface | Public action | Run identity | Observed result |
|---|---|---|---|
| CLI | `refactory graph-control resume --run RUN` | `registered-recovery-cli-guarded` | Queued a fresh owner; reached done with first/second complete |
| Native GUI | Existing run directory → Read this run → resume | `registered-recovery-gui-guarded` | Showed paused, first complete and second due; after one resume, streamed finished/done with both complete |

Both runs preserved the first artifact, its exactly-once invocation marker, saved run configuration, invocation identity, knob value, requested route and accumulated resource accounting. Only `second` executed after recovery. A simultaneous public resume attempt while the first owner was active was refused. Reading the native run did not execute it, and completion appeared without a manual refresh.

The actual graph/headless profile packages were pinned to the isolated checkout. Both saved routes used the deliberately unavailable provider `refactory-no-model` and model `no-model`: the installed LLM registry was separately verified to reject it with `NO_ADAPTER`, with no fallback adapter invocation. The deterministic runtime reported `driver: automatic` and `driver_model_calls: 0`; usage remained unavailable instead of inventing measured model tokens. The earlier accidental coordinator call and a filesystem-watcher startup refusal remain separate failed fixture evidence. No model-enabled retry followed them.

## Verification limits

Initial focused integrated Python checks passed (168 tests), followed by the relevant worker regressions. The final fast-mode slice passed 124 focused Python tests, five new API regression cases, 27 native execution/steering tests and 19 documentation tests. One optional external graph-reference oracle was skipped. Host/client TypeScript checks, builds and normal commit/push hooks passed. Two deferred-stream UI regressions fail on the preceding implementation and pass with the fix that keeps watched run B's state and gates after run A completes. Existing unrelated test failures remain outside this change; no clean full-suite claim is made.

Raw receipts, run directories and local acceptance reports remain in the isolated task checkout. Credential files, token-bearing server URLs and private runtime logs are not published.

# Steering ledger acceptance — 2026-09-27

Based on main `8c3f2a61b738e8305e0d7b1ee10345b7deb91e3d` (PR #249). **Steering → View full ledger** opens a scrollable viewer over every recorded entry, including the original brief, past notes, corrections, constraints and gate history. Records remain oldest first with their timestamps and complete text. Search matches text, kind or timestamp and never changes the saved ledger.

## What changed

- A compact latest-note preview replaces the long inline list. The viewer keeps its current history while refreshing, labels failed refreshes, follows live appends and restores trigger focus on Close/Escape. Switching watched runs closes the viewer and clears its cached history.
- The ledger parser previously stripped accumulated text on every line, which removed paragraph breaks. It now accumulates each entry before trimming its outer whitespace, preserving blank lines and internal indentation in UI reads and dispatched ledger context. Existing ledger files need no migration or rewrite.
- Steering notes accept multiple lines. Submission disables the Add button until the result arrives; only a confirmed note clears its matching draft. A refused request or a newly typed draft retains the user's text.
- Steering remains append-only context delivered at supported boundaries. Reading history does not repeat gate approvals, alter the graph or rerun completed work. The existing explicit verdict and correction controls retain those responsibilities.

## Native evidence

Chrome checks used the disposable preview home on port 3095 and an isolated, completed local fixture at `.factory/interactive/steering-ledger-preview`. No model calls or execution launches were needed.

- Opened the original brief and all recorded notes; paragraph breaks and indentation remained readable.
- Searched an earlier correction and saw exactly one matching entry.
- Submitted a multiline note through the real panel, verified it persisted exactly on disk, and saw the draft clear after confirmation.
- Appended another note from the local ledger API while the viewer stayed open: its count changed from six to seven, the original brief remained, and search focus stayed in place.
- Closed with Escape and confirmed focus returned to View full ledger.

| Surface | Native capture |
|---|---|
| Full history and original brief | [Ledger](assets/steering-20260927/full-ledger-dark.png) |
| Earlier correction found by search | [Search](assets/steering-20260927/search-past-text-dark.png) |

Captures crop browser chrome and surrounding application space; application pixels are unchanged.

## Automated checks and limits

- GUI: **179 passed in 12 files**, including full history beyond a short recent list, literal text rendering, timestamps, search, refresh/failure retention, live appends, focus restoration, run switching, failed submissions and preserving a newer draft during confirmation.
- Focused Python checks: **5 passed** for multiline ledger/console round trips, retained gate history with one-use verdict consumption, and the existing agent-delivery suite.
- Production build, host/client typechecks, lint and whitespace checks passed.
- The broader steering + delivery selection has **eight existing failures**, reproduced with the exact unmodified `steering.py` from main. They concern legacy resume/verdict and citation expectations. One reference-IR test skips because the optional `remote-factory` oracle is absent. This follow-up does not claim that broader selection is green.
- No upstream dependency, patch, runtime API or ledger schema changes. The viewer uses the existing complete ledger payload and watch stream; the parser and UI fixes remain local to Refactory.

refactory/docs/tutorials/01-write-a-mode.text:
# 1. Write a mode

A mode is a Python class. This tutorial builds the smallest one that is worth
optimizing, runs it, and then breaks it on purpose so you can see the validator
refuse it.

Everything here is offline and takes a few seconds.

## The shape

A mode declares three things:

- **parameters** in `declare()` — what an optimizer may move;
- **structure** in `build()` — the graph, built once, pure;
- **a score** in `score(run)` — how a run becomes the number being maximized.

The graph is *data*. `build()` produces it once; after that the optimizer edits the
state, never the class ([why](../architecture.md#2-the-pytorch-mapping)).

## Write it

A mode needs a package to live in. Put it in the **workspace root**,
`.factory/packages/counter/` — the writable half of the registry, and the same
place `create`-mode writes its output. The shipped packages live beside it in
`refactory_packages/`, which is read-only.

So this goes at `.factory/packages/counter/__init__.py`:

```python
"""A counter package: one mode, and the ops it calls."""
from refactory_dsh.nn import Package

from .mode import Counter

PACKAGE = Package(
    name="counter",
    description="count up to a target, and score the count reached",
    modes=(Counter,),
    ops=("refactory_packages.counter.ops",),
)
```

`.factory/packages/counter/mode.py`:

```python
"""The counter mode."""
from refactory_dsh.nn import Graph, Knob, Mode, Node


class Counter(Mode):
    name = "counter"
    description = "count up to a target"

    @classmethod
    def declare(cls):
        return {
            "target": Knob(3, "int", lo=1, hi=9, description="where to stop counting"),
            "step": Knob(1, "int", lo=1, hi=3, description="how much each step adds"),
        }

    def build(self):
        graph = Graph()
        graph.add(Node(
            "count", "op", call="refactory_packages.counter.ops:count",
            knobs=("target", "step"), writes=("count.json",), produces=("value",),
            notes="add `step` until the count reaches `target`",
        ))
        return graph

    def score(self, run):
        # What the run fact says, never a knob: a score that reads a knob is a
        # score about the input rather than about the run.
        return float(run.facts["value"])
```

`.factory/packages/counter/ops.py`:

```python
"""The operation the counter's node calls."""
from typing import Any


def count(ctx: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    target = int(ctx.knob("target", 3))
    step = int(ctx.knob("step", 1))
    value = 0
    while value < target:
        value += step
    ctx.write_json("count.json", {"value": value})
    return {"value": value}
```

Three rules the code above obeys, each of which the validator enforces if you
break it:

- the node lists `knobs=("target", "step")` — a declared knob no node consumes is
  refused (`V7`);
- the node declares `writes=("count.json",)` — a read of a file nothing writes is
  refused (`V6`);
- `score()` reads `run.facts`, never `ctx.knob(...)`.

## Register and run it

The registry scans `refactory_packages/`, so the package is found by name:

```bash
uv run refactory package list
```

```
counter/  count up to a target, and score the count reached
  counter/counter                        count up to a target
```

```bash
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from refactory_dsh import registry
package, mode_class = registry.resolve(Path('.'), 'counter/counter')
mode = mode_class()
print('state keys:', sorted(mode.state_dict()))
print('score     :', mode.evaluate(Path('/tmp/counter')).score)
"
```

```
state keys: ['graph', 'knobs', 'memory', 'ports', 'version']
score     : 3.0
```

Note the state keys: the architecture (`graph`) travels with the parameters
(`knobs`). That is the divergence from PyTorch this whole system rests on.

## Validate it before running it

Validation is what makes a search cheap: an invalid candidate is refused before it
costs a run.

```bash
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from refactory_dsh import nn, registry
mode = registry.resolve(Path('.'), 'counter/counter')[1]()
print(nn.validate_state(mode.state_dict(), invariants=mode.invariants()))
"
```

```
[]
```

An empty list means runnable and scoreable. Now break it deliberately — point the
node at a file nothing produces:

```bash
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from refactory_dsh import nn, registry
from refactory_dsh.nn import edits
mode = registry.resolve(Path('.'), 'counter/counter')[1]()
state = mode.state_dict()
broken = edits.apply({'op': 'set_node_field', 'id': 'count',
                      'field': 'reads', 'value': ['nowhere.json']}, state)
for issue in nn.validate_state(broken):
    print(issue)
"
```

```
V6 [count]: reads 'nowhere.json', which no node on a path from 'count' to a terminal produces
```

That message is what an optimizer is shown *instead of* a failed run. It is why
the running example reports refusals as `V6: 4` rather than a batch of zeroes, and
why none of them cost evaluation budget.

The catalogue of edits is discoverable, so you never guess a field name:

```bash
uv run python -c "
from refactory_dsh.nn import edits
for op in edits.catalogue():
    print(op['op'], op['fields'])
"
```

## What to take away

- A mode is data from `build()` onward. The class is a *seed*, not the truth.
- Declare what a node reads, writes, produces, and consumes. The declarations are
  what the validator checks against, and a node that writes something it did not
  declare is an error rather than a surprise.
- `score()` reads facts. If it read a knob, optimizing would be circular.

Next: [optimize it](02-optimize-it.md).

refactory/docs/tutorials/02-optimize-it..text:
# 2. Optimize it

The loop searches a mode's architecture **and** its parameters. This tutorial runs
it, reads what it found, and reads the diff that explains the result.

Prerequisite: nothing. `circle_packing/adaptive` ships.

## Run it

```bash
uv run refactory optimize circle_packing/adaptive \
  --epochs 2 --batch-size 4 --optimizer random --seed 5 --runs-root /tmp/tour/run
```

```
{
  "mode": "circle_packing/adaptive",
  "optimizer": "random",
  "evaluator": "walker",
  "bound": "epochs",
  "evaluations": 8,
  "seed_score": 0.795,
  "best_score": 0.875,
  "raw_best_score": 0.955,
  "scoring": {"compared": "penalized", "parsimony": 0.01, ...},
  "holdout": {"status": "not_applicable", "train": 0.955, "holdout": null, "overfit": null,
              "note": "the mode has no data node, so it iterates no items and there is nothing to hold out"},
  "structural_wins": 1,
  "rejection_codes": {"E-shape": 1, "I:fact_produced": 4, "V10": 2, "V2": 3, ...},
  "report": "/tmp/tour/run/report.md"
}
```

Three things to notice:

- **A bound is always named.** `"bound": "epochs"` — a run never ends for an
  unstated reason. The other bound is `max_evaluations`.
- **The score improved**: seed `0.795` → best `0.875`, in 8 inner runs. Those are the numbers the search compares: the raw score with `0.01` taken off for each node of the candidate's graph. The unpenalised pair is beside them (`0.875` → `0.955`), so a harness that won on merit can be told from one that won on size. Here every candidate has 8 nodes, and the `duplicate` the search tried next has 9 — which is why it scores `0.865` raw `0.955` and loses to its parent.
- **Nothing is held out when there is nothing to hold out.** `circle_packing/adaptive` has no data node and iterates no items, so the audit records `holdout: null` and says why instead of inventing a number. A mode bound to a Task is audited on the items it was not tuned on.
- **Refusals cost nothing.** `rejection_codes` lists every proposal the validator
  rejected *before* it could be evaluated.

Execution failures remain in `failed_candidates`, with their errors, but cannot
win or be adopted. If every evaluated candidate fails, the report has no winner,
`exit_ok: false`, and the CLI exits nonzero. The holdout status distinguishes a
measurement from a failed or unavailable audit and from a mode with no split.
Adoption requires a completed audit for the current winner; `--allow-overfit`
acknowledges a measured gap but cannot override a missing or failed audit.
An explicit live Adopt request audits its current winner before writing the package;
a later winner receives its own audit. Legacy score records without an explicit
successful exit remain visible in history but are ineligible until re-evaluated.

Resuming a completed search through `LoopConfig(resume=True)` honors its existing
epoch and evaluation bounds. It can consume a queued selection change and audit
the resulting winner without spending another proposal epoch.

## The steps, in order

The loop is named after a training loop, and running it with `--verbose`-style
inspection shows the same eight steps a PyTorch loop has:

| step | what it did |
|---|---|
| `init` | seeded the population — the seed, plus one neighbour per movable knob |
| `forward` | ran the batch; the only step that spends budget |
| `loss` | turned the batch into one number |
| `backward` | read the traces into the gradient the optimizer receives |
| `optimizer` | proposed the next batch, validating before anything ran |
| `step` | installed the offspring that were genuinely new points |
| `scheduler` | closed the epoch and recorded what bound the run |
| `report` | wrote the leaderboard, the gradient, and the markdown |

## Read the leaderboard

```bash
uv run refactory leaderboard --run /tmp/tour/run
```

Each row carries the candidate, its score, and a **diff against its parent**:

```json
[
  {"id": "4caa88db3dbc", "parent": "b6f0d3c9e601", "score": 0.875, "raw_score": 0.955,
   "nodes": 8, "size_cost": 0.08, "structural": false,
   "edits": [{"op": "set_knob", "name": "grid", "value": 18}],
   "diff": {"knobs": {"grid": {"before": 10, "after": 18}}, ...}},
  {"id": "6061dbf4589f", "parent": "4caa88db3dbc", "score": 0.865, "raw_score": 0.955,
   "nodes": 9, "size_cost": 0.09, "structural": true,
   "edits": [{"op": "set_knob", "name": "grid", "value": 18}, {"op": "duplicate", "target": "accept"}]}
]
```

This is the point of a diff on a leaderboard: without it the table says which
number is bigger and nothing about why.

## Read one candidate in full

```bash
uv run refactory candidate --run /tmp/tour/run 6061dbf4589f
```

The `rendered` field is the human-readable form of the same diff, and the row also
carries what the run measured (`score`, `exit_ok`, `duration_s`).

## Read the report

```bash
cat /tmp/tour/run/report.md
```

```
# Outer loop — circle_packing/adaptive

Optimizer `random`, 2 epoch(s) of 2, batch 4, 8 inner run(s). Stopped because **epochs** bound the run.

Seed score **0.795** → best **0.875** (raw 0.875 → 0.955). The compared score is the raw one minus 0.01 per node of the candidate's graph.
```

The markdown carries a leaderboard, the structural candidates that scored, and a
section for why proposals were refused — because a reader needs the refusals as
much as the wins.

## Watch a run that has not finished

A run is a directory of files, so you can read it *while* it runs:

```bash
uv run refactory status --run /tmp/tour/run --after 0
```

`--after` takes a line count, not a timestamp: a reader polling wants the events it
has not seen, and a clock cannot tell it which those are.

`progress.jsonl` has one line **per candidate evaluated**, not per epoch — an epoch
can be an hour.

## Then watch it on DSH

The walker is the debug runtime. The same mode on the runtime that ships:

```bash
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests/test_equivalence.py -q --run-integration
```

```
6 passed
```

Tutorial [4](04-ship-it-on-dsh.md) walks through that in detail.

## What to take away

- A run is a **directory**, readable without a service — before, during, and after.
- The report says what happened *and* what was refused, and by which rule.
- Every candidate's state is in the journal, and its diff is one command away.

Next: [author with a model](03-author-with-a-model.md).

refactory/docs/tutorials/03-author-with-.text:
# 3. Author with a model

Create, Edit and Design are ordinary graphs in `default_pack`. Run them interactively through terminal CEO or GUI chat, or use their Python APIs. They call a model; duration and output quality depend on the workload, model and review cycles.

| Mode | Output | Completion evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Create | A new registered package of modes | Structural validation, reviews and canonical smoke |
| Edit | A revised package with source provenance | The same checks, plus comparison status where meaningful |
| Design | An artifact | The supplied check command and reviews against the brief |

Configure [managed model credentials](../models.md#credentials-for-nested-execution) first. These examples are starting briefs; inspect actual results rather than assuming a particular generated mode name or score.

## Create a reusable harness

```bash
uv run refactory ceo \
  "Draft and check a project README from a supplied brief. Declare the input and output contract clearly." \
  --mode create --name readme_pack --single
```

`--single` deliberately chooses a single-run harness. For a class of work, use `--task module:TaskClass` instead. The importable [Task](../datasets.md) lists inputs, prepares each item and verifies the result; Create binds the generated mode to it. The final `create.json` records the actual binding.

The current graph surveys existing packages, researches the problem, develops a strategy, asks you to approve it, emits files, validates them structurally, stages/registers the package, executes canonical smoke, then runs parallel reviews and an audit. Repair loops are bounded by the declared controls. Canonical smoke belongs to the runtime and returns repairable failures to the coder before sign-off. Reviews consume its receipts and use targeted checks for uncovered requirements.

A sample run does not establish quality on every future input. A failed inner execution is a failure, not a measured zero. Unavailable credentials/tools leave a blocked, unmeasured validation with an unblock reason; they do not trigger repeated coding or final success. Inspect `smoke.json`, `authoring-evidence.json`, `intent-audit.json` and the final report. See [the validation and audit contract](../authoring-validation.md).

When the mode needs a named input, declare it in the brief and through `--knob requires_input=<name>` on CEO. The Python Create entry point also supports `--input` and repeatable `--sample NAME=VALUE`; samples exercise supplied inputs rather than only defaults. Read that entry point's help for its own flags.

Inspect the generated package with:

```bash
uv run refactory package show readme_pack
uv run refactory package verify readme_pack
```

The catalogue/report names its generated mode IDs. Use the actual ID to run it. `package smoke` without `--model` is keyless; agent-containing modes need the model-backed path. Structural admission is not a guarantee of safe arbitrary generated code; see [hardening](../hardening.md).

## Edit an existing mode

```bash
uv run refactory ceo "Improve the search strategy while preserving its input and output contract" \
  --mode edit --revise circle_packing/adaptive --name revised_pack
```

Edit uses the Create graph with the source and revision intent. It writes a new package; the source remains available. The Python driver preserves the graph's canonical report rather than independently repeating keyless before/after passes.

Comparable deterministic executions use the same accepted sample inputs. A measured regression is refused by default; `--knob allow_regression=1` on CEO skips original execution and numerical comparison entirely, while still validating the revised mode. The default remains false. Model-dependent or incompatible-input comparisons are marked unavailable with a reason, not reported as non-regressions. Inspect `revision.json`, `before_score`, `after_score`, `regressed` and `revision_note`.

The Python entry point supports `--sample NAME=VALUE`, `--allow-regression` and `--resume RUN_DIR`. These are entry-point-specific flags, not all aliases on CEO. A supported resume keeps completed stages; rerunning an ordinary CEO launch is a fresh invocation, not generic continuation.

## Design an artifact

```bash
uv run refactory ceo \
  "Build wordcount.py for a UTF-8 input file. Include sample.txt and verify line, word and character counts." \
  --mode design --name wordcount --check "python wordcount.py sample.txt"
```

Design researches and prepares a design document for your approval, implements the artifact, executes the check and runs reviews. The check executes from the artifact directory. Its exit status establishes only what the command checks; correct semantics may need additional evidence. Visual deliverables need a rendered inspection, and exchange files need a suitable independent consumer.

The original brief, approved design and explicit steering remain the acceptance baseline. A README limitation or reviewer summary cannot silently waive requested behavior. If an external validation dependency is missing, preserve the artifact and report the unmet requirement honestly.

The artifact is published under `.factory/artifacts/<name>`, with its exact absolute path in the run report. Design does not register a mode or produce a numeric optimization objective. Use it when the deliverable is the artifact itself.

## Approval, time and evidence

Leave user gates interactive when you want to review the plan. `--approve gate_strategy=proceed` supplies deliberate upfront authorization for unattended work. Approval history and scope matter; [the interactive tutorial](06-run-it-with-a-person.md) explains them.

Create/Edit's `smoke_timeout_s` knob bounds each full smoke pass (default 3600 seconds); it is separate from an agent completion deadline and does not bound total authoring time. API flags and graph knobs are documented by their respective help/catalogue surfaces.

Use the exact work directory returned by the launch. Research, design, review, progress and final report files belong to that run. Do not confuse authoring evidence with an optimizer's `analysis/generation-*.md` records.

For a small task, fast Create and Design use one strategist, coder and focused QA agent sequentially; fast Edit goes directly to the coder and QA. They omit research and reviewer fan-out, allow one repair by default, and retain the required checks. All three fast modes completed bounded CLI/GUI acceptance, including required validation and actual structural repairs; see [fast modes and budgets](../budgets-fast-modes.md) for the tested scope, resource choices and retained failures. Users can define their own modes; research and QA are graph choices, and the platform does not require every mode to use the full authoring pipeline.

Next: [run with a person](06-run-it-with-a-person.md) or [drive GUI chat](05-drive-it-from-the-gui.md).

refactory/docs/tutorials/04-ship-it-on-d.text:
# 4. Ship it on DSH

The Python walker is a **debug runtime**. DSH is the runtime that ships. This
tutorial lowers a mode to refactory's IR, runs it on DSH's spine, and shows the two
agreeing.

A debug runtime that disagrees with the real one is worse than none, so the
comparison is a test, not a manual step.

## What "lowering" means

A mode is a `Graph` of `Node`s and `Edge`s. Refactory's own language has the same
vocabulary, and DSH's `workflow-spine` already executes it. So the seam is a
**translation of data**, not a reimplementation:

```bash
uv run python -c "
import json
from pathlib import Path
from refactory_dsh import lowering, registry

mode = registry.resolve(Path('.'), 'circle_packing/adaptive')[1]()
path, workflow = lowering.write_mode_graph(mode.state_dict(), Path('/tmp/tour/graphs'), name='circle_packing')
written = json.loads(Path(path).read_text())
print('nodes:', len(written['nodes']), 'edges:', len(written['edges']), 'start:', written['start_node'])
"
```

```
nodes: 8 edges: 8 start: task_input
```

Two details worth knowing:

- **The reference check is a test-time oracle, not a runtime step.**
  `tests/test_ir_parity.py` lowers every shipped mode through both `refactory_dsh/ir.py`
  and the reference and compares the bytes, so a graph that cannot lower is caught
  on the Python side. Install the reference with `uv sync --group reference`.
- **The IR has no field for the facts a node produces.** So
  `lowering.write_declarations(state, workdir)` writes them alongside the graph and
  the node runner reads them back from the run directory. That is a known wart of
  the boundary, not something to "clean up" silently.

## Run it on DSH

The `science` profile mounts the spine, so one command drives the whole graph:

```bash
node --import tsx/esm apps/cli/src/bin.ts --profile graph run \
  --mode circle_packing \
  --task "Call wf_next repeatedly until it reports done. Do nothing else." \
  --budget 1 \
  --graphs /tmp/tour/graphs \
  --workdir /tmp/tour/work
```

DSH runs every deterministic node itself. The CEO model is only there to call
`wf_next`; the ops run in-process against the same Python the walker uses.

The result is written where a reader can find it:

```bash
cat /tmp/tour/work/facts.json
```

## The gate: both runtimes must agree

```bash
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests/test_equivalence.py -q --run-integration
```

```
6 passed
```

That suite runs the same mode both ways and compares the score. It covers:

- the spine's own validator accepting the lowered graph;
- the same score from DSH and from the walker for the same seed;
- facts produced on disk by DSH becoming the same number through `score()`.

It is marked `integration` because it spawns a real session, which is why the plain
`pytest refactory/tests/` run reports it as skipped.

## Evaluating one candidate on DSH

Inside a loop you rarely want a whole run — you want one candidate scored by the
runtime that ships:

```python
from refactory_dsh.dsh_runtime import evaluate_on_dsh

result = evaluate_on_dsh(mode, state, workdir, timeout_s=900)
```

Then the loop selects its evaluator with a flag:

```bash
uv run refactory optimize circle_packing/adaptive \
  --epochs 1 --batch-size 2 --optimizer random --seed 5 \
  --evaluator dsh --runs-root /tmp/tour/dsh-run
```

`--evaluator walker` (the default) is fast and is for searching. `--evaluator dsh`
is the one that ships.

## The loop itself, on DSH

The loop is also a mode — `loop_mode/loop` — so the same machinery runs it:

```bash
uv run python -m pytest refactory/tests/test_loop_as_mode.py -q --run-integration
```

```
21 passed
```

Those tests drive the loop's eight steps as nine nodes on DSH's spine and assert
the gate routed `done` to the report, reaching the same best score as `Loop` does.

## What to take away

- The seam between the two runtimes is a **data lowering**, checked on both sides.
- The same fact has one home: the Python op writes it, DSH's node runner records
  it, and `score()` reads it either way.
- Anything that changes the executor must keep both runtimes agreeing, or the
  equivalence suite fails — which is the point of having it.

Next: [drive it from the GUI](05-drive-it-from-the-gui.md).

### One execution owns its run directory

`console run` and `ceo` keep the selected work directory exclusively owned from
before input/ledger preparation until their DSH process settles. A second run, or
`console open`, refuses an owned directory before archiving its invocation. Wait
for the owner to finish or choose another `--workdir`. Once it finishes, a new
invocation keeps the existing sequential archive behavior.

`.refactory/invocation.lock` is an inert rendezvous file for a local OS lock, not a
PID record. Leave it in place: normal exit, handled failure, and process exit
release the descriptor automatically, so an old file does not need manual stale
lock removal. On POSIX the owned DSH child inherits that descriptor; terminating
only its Python parent does not free the directory while DSH still runs.

This protects the Python launch/prepare boundary. `console open` alone owns only
its lowering call; a separate long-lived `wf_open` driver must manage its own
execution lifetime. It is not distributed locking, protection against external
file deletion, or general descendant-process containment. The Windows byte-lock
path protects the Python call; inherited-child behavior after abrupt parent exit
has only been established on POSIX. Timeout and direct interruption keep ownership until the launcher has awaited
the selected runtime's shutdown, as described below.


### Timeout and interruption await owned shutdown

On POSIX, `ceo` and `console run` request the selected DSH CLI's graceful shutdown
when their deadline expires or the calling thread is interrupted, and wait up to
ten seconds before forced-exit escalation. A deadline still fails; ordinary
nonzero child exits remain failures. An uncooperative runtime produces an explicit
forced-exit/cleanup-unconfirmed error. Files already written are not rolled back.

The console's intermediate Python owner participates in the same chain. Each
owned CLI has a separate session so terminal Ctrl-C is forwarded once, rather
than reaching DSH twice. On the main thread, a temporary handler converts default
SIGTERM into an unwinding exit and is restored afterward. Existing custom or
ignored handlers are preserved. Run-directory ownership remains held while this
cleanup is awaited, and normal terminal input/output stay inherited where they
were inherited before.

This is cleanup through the runtime's managed subprocess service, not signalling
arbitrary descendants. SIGKILL, worker-thread process-wide signals, custom signal
policies, Windows termination and escaped descendants still need their own
supervision. A CLI/runtime exit alone cannot certify arbitrary process-tree
quiescence. The actual acceptance check uses a real DSH-managed deterministic
child and unrelated sentinel; it is not a model or solver-performance result.

refactory/docs/tutorials/05-drive-it-fro.text:
# 5. Drive a workflow from GUI chat

GUI chat is the conversational interface to the same explicit mode graph used by the terminal. The adjacent [Modes panel](07-pick-and-watch-from-the-panel.md) offers direct controls for existing modes and searches.

## Open a session

```bash
uv run refactory ui --port 3081
```

Open the full URL the server prints. Select the checkout as the workspace and create a new session. Configure a provider and managed key under **Settings → Models** before model-backed work; see [Models](../models.md).

## Walk a small mode

Ask the CEO:

> Open counting_pack/fixed_step with target=9 and step=1. Drive it one node at a time. Tell me which node is due before doing its work.

The CEO uses `wf_open`, then `wf_next`. The runtime runs deterministic operations; the CEO delegates agent nodes and waits for their results. User gates ask you in chat. Its direct coding and skill tools are disabled while it drives the graph.

Knobs set actual operation inputs. Prose intent describes what you want; it does not silently replace `target` or `step`.

## Author a mode or artifact

Be explicit about the output:

> Use Create to build a reusable single-run harness for drafting and checking a project README from a brief. Call the package readme_pack. Open its workflow and let me review the strategy before building it.

For a class of work, supply the importable Task reference instead of the single-run choice. [The authoring guide](03-author-with-a-model.md) explains both.

> Use Design to build wordcount.py and sample.txt, with a check command of `python wordcount.py sample.txt`. Show me the design before implementing it, and verify the reported counts.

Design produces an artifact rather than a registered mode. Its supplied command and reviews determine acceptance. The current full authoring modes include substantial research and review; [fast modes with focused QA](../budgets-fast-modes.md) use smaller graphs and completed bounded CLI/native GUI acceptance. Required checks and repair limits still apply.

## Steer and correct

You can say:

> Pause before the implementation node so I can review the plan.

> Preserve the existing command-line interface. Add that as a constraint for the remaining work.

> That node used the wrong assumption. Change its prompt and rerun it; show me which dependent results become stale.

The CEO uses workflow state, steering and edit/redo tools. A delivery receipt shows which instruction reached work; inspect the outputs to judge compliance. An already running worker may not receive a change immediately. See [the interface guide](../interfaces.md#steering-is-precise-about-timing).

A session owns one open workflow. Use another session with a distinct run directory for independent work. Reopening a mode can start a fresh invocation; it is not equivalent to resuming an interrupted one.

## Follow a run in the panel

The original two-gear Refactory lockup identifies empty chat. Open **Modes** for the blue configuration and activity cards. Advanced routing, profiles, search controls and packages expand independently; required questions remain prominent above the controls. See the [panel guide](07-pick-and-watch-from-the-panel.md#find-the-controls).

Copy the exact run directory reported by chat into **Existing run directory → Read this run**. The attached status and Steering sections refer to that directory. The attached view streams persisted graph/worker activity, wait reasons, completed nodes and pending questions. Reading or reconnecting does not execute the run; [supported recovery](../live-control.md#recover-a-known-boundary) requires explicit resume.

For optimization, select **Optimize** in Modes, choose a scored mode, set its starting inputs and search limits, and press **Start optimization**. Search methods and saved profiles are expandable. Inspect candidates and use the optimizer-specific steering/adoption controls. Use **Run once** for an authoring mode after supplying its required knobs, or chat for stepwise control and approval gates.

The same run can be inspected from a second terminal:

```bash
uv run refactory status --run <exact-run-directory>
uv run refactory steer --run <exact-run-directory>
```

Replace the placeholder with the actual directory. [The command reference](../cli.md) lists note, gate and search controls.
